q: A payments company processes orders through Amazon SQS and occasionally sees the same order delivered twice, causing duplicate charges when the consumer retries. Which design makes processing idempotent?
options: Store a deduplication key for each order in DynamoDB with a conditional write, and process the charge only when the conditional write succeeds
Enable SQS long polling so duplicate messages are collapsed before delivery
Increase the visibility timeout so the same message cannot be received twice
Switch to an SNS topic so subscribers receive each order exactly once
explain: DynamoDB conditional writes on a unique order key ensure only the first delivery wins; retries find the key and skip the charge. SQS standard queues are at-least-once, long polling and visibility timeouts do not remove duplicates, and SNS also delivers at least once.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A trading platform must process stock orders for each account in strict sequence, while unrelated accounts can be processed in parallel. Which queue configuration meets this requirement?
options: Use an SQS standard queue with the account ID as a message attribute
Use an SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID
Use an SNS standard topic with one subscription per account
Use a Kinesis stream with a single shard for all accounts
explain: FIFO queues preserve order within a message group ID, so using the account ID keeps each account's orders sequential while different groups scale in parallel. Standard queues and SNS standard topics are best-effort ordering, and a single Kinesis shard serializes everything unnecessarily.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An order service uses an SQS FIFO queue but throughput is capped even though orders belong to thousands of different customers. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The queue uses server-side encryption, which limits FIFO throughput; disable encryption
The visibility timeout is too short; increase it to raise throughput
The message group ID is set to a constant value, serializing all messages; set it to the customer ID instead
FIFO queues support only one consumer; add a second queue for overflow
explain: FIFO throughput scales by message group; a constant group ID forces single-threaded ordering. Encryption and visibility timeout do not cap group parallelism, and adding queues does not fix a serialized group.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A logistics firm wants an event bus that routes shipment events to different AWS accounts based on event content, with an archive for replay. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon SNS with message filtering policies and no archive
Amazon SQS with a dead-letter queue used as an event archive
AWS Step Functions with a state machine per shipment event
Amazon EventBridge with cross-account event buses, content-based rules, and an event archive for replay
explain: EventBridge provides content-based routing, cross-account bus-to-bus delivery, schema handling, and archives with replay. SNS filtering has no archive/replay, SQS is point-to-point queuing rather than a routed bus, and Step Functions orchestrates workflows rather than routing events.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A retailer publishes OrderCreated events and three independent teams each need their own copy to process at their own pace, with failures isolated per team. Which pattern should the architect choose?
options: Publish to an SNS topic and subscribe a separate SQS queue for each team
Publish to a single SQS queue that all three teams poll competitively
Publish to EventBridge and invoke three Lambda functions directly with no queues
Write events to one Kinesis shard consumed by a single consumer group
explain: SNS fan-out to per-team SQS queues gives each team an independent copy, independent retries, and a dead-letter queue. A single queue would let one team consume another's messages, direct Lambda invocation lacks durable per-team buffering, and a single shard limits throughput.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A streaming ingestion pipeline using Kinesis Data Streams has hot shards and throttling while other shards sit idle because events from one popular device dominate. How should the architect fix partitioning?
options: Use the event timestamp alone as the partition key for all records
Choose a partition key with higher cardinality, such as device ID combined with a random suffix for the hottest devices, and reshard as needed
Increase the retention period so hot shards can catch up
Enable server-side encryption to distribute records more evenly
explain: Partition keys determine shard assignment; low-cardinality or skewed keys create hot shards, so higher-cardinality keys distribute load. Timestamp alone still concentrates current traffic, and retention or encryption do not change shard distribution.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company needs guaranteed ordering of clickstream events per user session and the ability to replay the last 24 hours after a consumer bug. Which service should it select?
options: Amazon SQS standard queue with the session ID as an attribute
Amazon SNS FIFO topic with a single subscription
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with the session ID as the partition key
Amazon EventBridge with an archive of clickstream events
explain: Kinesis preserves order per partition key and retains records for replay from any shard iterator position. SQS standard and EventBridge do not guarantee per-key stream ordering with replay, and SNS FIFO is for fan-out messaging, not high-volume stream replay.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A microservice must not lose events when its downstream database is briefly unavailable, and it must retry with backoff rather than dropping messages. Which pairing provides this behavior?
options: Deliver events directly from SNS to the service's HTTP endpoint with no queue
Write events to CloudWatch Logs and have the service search them on recovery
Publish events to EventBridge with the service as a Lambda target and no retry policy
Deliver events to an SQS queue consumed by the service, with a visibility timeout, redrive policy, and dead-letter queue
explain: An SQS queue durably buffers work, and visibility timeout plus redrive to a DLQ gives controlled retries without loss. Direct HTTP delivery can drop failed calls, Logs is not a work queue, and Lambda targets alone do not provide the same durable, inspectable backlog.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An architect is choosing between SQS standard and FIFO for a high-volume image-processing backlog where duplicate processing is harmless but cost and throughput matter most. Which choice is correct?
options: Use a standard queue, which offers higher, effectively unlimited throughput and at-least-once delivery that the idempotent workers can tolerate
Use a FIFO queue because standard queues cannot scale beyond 300 TPS
Use a FIFO queue because standard queues delete messages after one delivery attempt
Use an SNS FIFO topic because queues cannot be consumed by Auto Scaling workers
explain: Standard queues provide near-unlimited throughput and at-least-once delivery, a good fit when workers are idempotent. The 300 TPS figure applies to FIFO without batching, standard queues redeliver until expiry, and SNS topics are not polled as work queues.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A SaaS provider needs to decouple a burst-prone checkout API from a fulfillment service so the API returns quickly during flash sales while no orders are lost. Which design achieves this?
options: Have the API call fulfillment synchronously and add retries in the client
Have the API write orders to an SQS queue and return a tracking ID, with fulfillment consuming asynchronously
Store orders only in an in-memory cache on the API servers until fulfillment recovers
Scale the fulfillment service vertically and keep the synchronous call
explain: Queuing decouples the burst from fulfillment, accepting work durably while consumers process at a sustainable rate. Synchronous retries amplify load, in-memory storage loses orders on failure, and vertical scaling does not remove the coupling.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A financial workflow requires that a notification be sent to email, an archive copy stored, and an analytics job started for every completed transaction, all triggered independently. Which integration pattern is most appropriate?
options: Write the event to a single SQS queue and let the three consumers race to read it
Use a Step Functions state machine that calls all three consumers sequentially in the API request
Publish the transaction event to an SNS topic with subscriptions for the email, archive, and analytics consumers
Store the event in DynamoDB and poll the table from each consumer every minute
explain: SNS fan-out delivers an independent copy to each subscriber in parallel. A single queue delivers each message to only one reader, sequential orchestration in the request path adds latency and coupling, and polling is inefficient and error-prone.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An EventBridge rule forwards events to a Lambda function, but some events fail schema validation downstream because producers keep adding unexpected fields. How should the architect detect this early?
options: Add the events to an SQS dead-letter queue and inspect them monthly
Enable VPC Flow Logs to capture the malformed event payloads
Require producers to send events through a Kinesis stream for validation
Use EventBridge Schema Registry with schema discovery and validate events against the registered schema in the producer pipeline
explain: Schema Registry discovery surfaces producer schema changes and enables contract validation before bad events propagate. A DLQ only captures failed deliveries, Flow Logs do not inspect payloads, and Kinesis does not validate schemas.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company routes events between Regions for disaster recovery and needs the secondary Region to receive the same domain events with minimal custom code. Which approach should it use?
options: Use EventBridge global endpoints or cross-Region bus-to-bus rules to replicate events to the secondary Region's event bus
Replicate the SQS queues with S3 Cross-Region Replication
Use Route 53 failover records to redirect event producers at the DNS layer only
Copy events nightly with a DataSync task between Regions
explain: EventBridge supports cross-Region routing between buses and global endpoints with failover, purpose-built for event replication. S3 replication does not move queue messages, DNS failover does not copy events, and nightly file sync is neither real-time nor event-aware.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A notification system sends SMS and push messages and must prevent the same alert being sent twice within a five-minute window for the same incident. Which configuration provides this?
options: Use an SNS standard topic with a high delivery retry count
Use an SNS FIFO topic (or SQS FIFO queue) with content-based message deduplication enabled
Use an SQS standard queue with long polling enabled
Use EventBridge with duplicate events filtered by a Lambda authorizer
explain: FIFO deduplication suppresses duplicates submitted within the five-minute deduplication interval. Standard topics and queues offer no deduplication, and EventBridge does not deduplicate based on content in this way.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A fleet of web servers keeps user session data in local memory, so requests fail whenever a server is replaced by Auto Scaling. How should the architect make the tier stateless?
options: Store sessions on an EBS volume attached to each instance
Pin each user to one instance with sticky sessions permanently
Move session state to Amazon ElastiCache (or DynamoDB) and keep no session data on the instances
Write sessions to the instance's local ephemeral store with replication disabled
explain: Externalizing session state to ElastiCache or DynamoDB lets any healthy instance serve any request, so replacement is harmless. EBS and local stores tie state to one instance, and permanent stickiness masks rather than removes the coupling.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A stateless API needs fast, shared access to frequently read product data that changes only a few times per day. Which store best fits as a shared cache?
options: Amazon S3 Standard-IA with one object per product lookup
An EBS volume shared by mounting it on each API server in turn
Amazon Redshift with a materialized view refreshed daily
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis with the product data cached and invalidated on update
explain: ElastiCache provides sub-millisecond shared cache access for all stateless instances. S3 IA has retrieval cost and latency unsuited to per-request lookups, EBS is single-attach block storage, and Redshift is an analytics warehouse, not a request cache.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An application stores uploaded contracts in memory on the upload server before processing, losing files when the server scales in. What is the correct redesign?
options: Upload contracts directly to Amazon S3 and pass only the object key to downstream processing
Upload contracts to a larger instance type with more memory
Replicate the in-memory files between servers using cron and rsync
Attach an instance store volume and back it up weekly
explain: S3 provides durable, shared object storage decoupled from compute, so scale-in loses nothing. Bigger instances and local volumes still tie files to a host, and ad-hoc replication is fragile.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Lambda-based API occasionally needs to remember a user's workflow progress between invocations across days. Where should that state live?
options: In a global variable in the Lambda function code
In Amazon DynamoDB, keyed by user and workflow ID, read and written by each invocation
In a file written to the Lambda execution environment's /tmp directory
In an environment variable updated by the function at runtime
explain: DynamoDB is durable external state that survives across invocations and days. Globals and /tmp persist only opportunistically in a reused environment, and environment variables cannot be changed by the function at runtime.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A gaming leaderboard needs single-digit-millisecond reads and writes for millions of players with automatic scaling and no servers to manage. Which database should the architect pick?
options: Amazon RDS MySQL with a large instance and read replicas
Amazon Redshift with distribution keys on player ID
Amazon DynamoDB with on-demand capacity
Amazon ElastiCache alone as the system of record
explain: DynamoDB delivers consistent single-digit-millisecond performance at scale with on-demand capacity. RDS would need sharding at this scale, Redshift targets analytics, and a cache alone is not a durable system of record.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A containerized checkout service running on Fargate must share feature-flag configuration that updates centrally without redeploying tasks. Which approach keeps the tasks stateless?
options: Write updated flags to each task's local filesystem through a sidecar file copy
Store flags in an EBS volume attached to the longest-lived task
Embed flags in the container image and rebuild tasks for every change
Read feature flags from a central store such as DynamoDB or AppConfig at runtime instead of baking them into task memory or local files
explain: Centralized external configuration lets ephemeral Fargate tasks start with current settings and be replaced freely. Local files, attached volumes, and image rebuilds reintroduce state or slow, heavyweight change cycles; Fargate also does not support persistent EBS attachment per task in this manner.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An architect reviews a design where each application server writes its audit trail to a local disk file that is collected weekly. What is the main architectural risk and correction?
options: The trail is lost if a server fails before collection; stream audit records to a durable shared store such as S3 or CloudWatch Logs instead
The risk is CPU overhead; move the file writes to a larger instance
The risk is disk cost; compress the local files more aggressively
There is no risk if the servers run in a Multi-AZ deployment
explain: Local disk state disappears with the instance; durable shared logging removes that single point of loss. Instance size and compression do not fix durability, and Multi-AZ placement does not protect instance-local files.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A web tier must serve personalized pages but remain horizontally scalable behind an ALB with no session affinity. Which combination achieves this?
options: Enable ALB sticky sessions with a one-week duration cookie
Store session and personalization state in DynamoDB or ElastiCache and keep instances interchangeable
Keep a local copy of each user's profile on the instance that first served them
Use a single large instance so affinity is never needed
explain: Externalized state is what allows the ALB to send any request to any instance, enabling true horizontal scaling. Long stickiness, local profiles, and a single instance all defeat that goal.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company ingests streaming click data, needs to transform it with SQL-like queries, and wants analysts to query the curated data in S3 without managing servers. Which pipeline fits?
options: RDS for ingestion, with analysts connecting directly for ad-hoc queries
SQS for ingestion and Redshift Spectrum without a catalog
Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion, a transformation step, and Amazon Athena over a Glue Data Catalog for querying data in S3
EMR clusters left running permanently for occasional analyst queries
explain: Kinesis handles streaming ingestion, S3 plus Glue Data Catalog plus Athena gives serverless querying. RDS is not a streaming store, Spectrum still needs catalog metadata, and always-on EMR wastes cost for intermittent queries.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Nightly CSV files land in S3 and must be converted to Parquet, partitioned by date, and registered for querying. Which serverless service should run the conversion?
options: AWS Lambda functions triggered hourly to rewrite each file manually in memory
Amazon Athena jobs that rewrite the bucket in place automatically
AWS DataSync tasks configured to convert file formats during sync
AWS Glue ETL jobs with crawlers to update the Glue Data Catalog
explain: Glue ETL is built for large-scale format conversion and partitioning, with crawlers maintaining the catalog. Lambda memory and runtime limit large conversions, Athena queries rather than performing managed ETL pipelines, and DataSync copies files without format conversion.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A data team wants to run ad-hoc SQL directly against JSON logs stored in S3, paying only for data scanned, with no infrastructure to provision. Which service should they use?
options: Amazon Athena
Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster
Amazon EMR with Hive
Amazon RDS with foreign data wrappers
explain: Athena is serverless, queries data in place in S3, and charges per data scanned. Redshift and EMR require provisioned capacity, and RDS is not designed to query object storage ad hoc.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Sensor data arrives through Kinesis Data Streams and must be delivered to S3 in near real time, with a simple format conversion and buffering. Which delivery mechanism is simplest?
options: A fleet of EC2 consumers that poll the stream and write files hourly
Kinesis Data Firehose with S3 as the destination and format conversion enabled
SQS queues that batch records and flush them daily
Step Functions state machines invoked per record to write each object
explain: Firehose is the managed delivery service for Kinesis streams to S3, handling buffering and format conversion. Custom EC2 consumers, queues, and per-record state machines add operational burden for a standard delivery task.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A pipeline must join a Kinesis stream with a reference table, detect anomalies in a Lambda function, and store results in DynamoDB. What must the architect watch most closely?
options: The DynamoDB table's provisioned throughput in a different account
The Kinesis stream's S3 bucket policy for the reference table
Lambda's Kinesis event source polling, shard scaling, and iterator age so records do not expire before processing
The Lambda function's VPC route table for internet access to Kinesis
explain: Lambda polls each shard and processes records in order; if processing lags, iterator age grows and records can expire past retention. Throughput, bucket policies, and VPC routing are secondary to keeping up with the stream.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An analytics team needs a catalog so that Athena, Glue, and EMR all see the same tables over the same S3 data lake. Which component provides that shared metadata?
options: A separate Hive metastore maintained on an EC2 instance per tool
S3 bucket tags describing each table's schema
Redshift external schemas recreated in each tool
The AWS Glue Data Catalog
explain: The Glue Data Catalog is the central metastore shared by Athena, Glue, and EMR. Per-tool metastores drift apart, tags do not hold table schemas, and recreating schemas per tool duplicates administration.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A serverless pipeline occasionally produces malformed records that fail transformation and are silently dropped. How should the architect make failures visible and recoverable?
options: Configure an error destination such as an SQS dead-letter queue or an S3 error prefix for failed records, with alarms on its depth
Increase the transformation function's memory until failures stop
Extend the stream retention and assume failures will self-correct
Disable transformation validation so all records pass through
explain: An explicit error destination captures failed records for inspection and reprocessing, and alarms surface the problem. More memory does not fix malformed data, retention does not reprocess, and disabling validation corrupts downstream data.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company wants a fully serverless pipeline that lands raw events in S3, catalogs them, transforms them into a curated zone, and serves BI queries, with orchestration of each stage. Which orchestration choice fits best?
options: A cron job on a single EC2 instance coordinating all stages over SSH
AWS Step Functions coordinating Glue jobs and Athena queries triggered by EventBridge schedules and S3 events
Manual runbooks executed by the data team each morning
SQS messages that each stage polls on its own schedule with no central workflow
explain: Step Functions gives visible, retryable, serverless orchestration across Glue and Athena. Cron over SSH is a single point of failure, manual runbooks do not scale, and uncoordinated polling makes dependencies and failures hard to manage.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A loan approval workflow has steps that wait days for human review, must survive compute restarts, and needs a full execution history. Which service should orchestrate it?
options: AWS Lambda functions chained by direct invocation
Amazon SQS queues with a custom status table polled by workers
AWS Step Functions Standard workflows
AWS Step Functions Express workflows
explain: Standard workflows support long-running, durable executions with waits, retries, and auditable history for up to a year. Lambda chaining loses executions on failure, custom queue polling reinvents orchestration, and Express targets high-volume short-duration work.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team wants long-running durable steps inside code-first workflows where each step checkpoints its result and can sleep for weeks without paying for idle compute. Which capability matches?
options: Standard Lambda functions using recursive self-invocation to wait
EC2 instances kept running so in-memory workflow state is preserved
SQS FIFO queues holding the workflow's in-progress variables
Durable Lambda functions (durable execution) with checkpointed steps and durable waits
explain: Durable execution in Lambda checkpoints step results and suspends during waits without compute charges. Recursive invocation is fragile and billed, always-on instances pay for idle time, and queues transport messages rather than checkpointing workflow state.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An order workflow must run a payment step and a fraud check in parallel, then continue only when both succeed, retrying each independently on failure. Which Step Functions feature models this directly?
options: A Parallel state with per-branch Catch and Retry configuration
A single Lambda function that calls both services sequentially
A Map state that iterates over a list of orders
An SQS queue with two consumers racing to complete the steps
explain: The Parallel state runs branches concurrently with independent retry and error handling. Sequential calls lose parallelism, Map iterates list items rather than distinct branches, and racing consumers do not model a join.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A workflow processes thousands of line items and must run the same validation step for each item concurrently with controlled parallelism. Which Step Functions construct should be used?
options: A Choice state that routes each item to a different workflow
A Map state (including distributed Map for very large datasets) with a maximum concurrency setting
A Wait state that delays each item before validation
A single Lambda function looping over all items in one invocation
explain: Map states apply a step to each list item with configurable concurrency, and distributed Map scales to large datasets in S3. Choice routes, Wait delays, and a single looping Lambda hits timeout and memory limits.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A multi-step media workflow fails intermittently at a third-party API step; the architect must avoid restarting completed expensive steps on retry. What design provides this?
options: Re-invoke the entire workflow from the beginning with a new input
Store progress in a text file on an EFS volume mounted by each step
Step Functions' built-in state persistence with Retry and Catch on the failing step so completed states are not re-executed
Have each Lambda function call the next one directly so failures cascade back
explain: Step Functions records each state's completion, so retries resume at the failed step. Full restarts repeat expensive work, file-based progress is brittle, and direct chaining has no durable resume point.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A workflow must pause until an external system calls back with approval, which may take hours, without holding any running compute. Which Step Functions pattern applies?
options: A Lambda function that sleeps in a loop until the callback arrives
An SQS queue that the workflow polls every second
A Wait state fixed at the maximum possible approval time
A task token with a callback pattern: the state waits until the external system returns the token via SendTaskSuccess
explain: Callback task tokens let a state pause indefinitely with no compute running until the external system responds. Sleeping Lambdas time out and cost money, polling wastes resources, and a fixed wait cannot react when approval arrives early.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A central security account must receive GuardDuty and login events from 50 member accounts in near real time for analysis. Which EventBridge design achieves this?
options: Create a central event bus in the security account and configure bus-to-bus rules (with resource policies) forwarding events from each member account's bus
Give the security account IAM users in each member account to poll CloudWatch Logs
Replicate each account's SQS queues into the security account nightly
Share a single SQS queue across accounts and disable its access policy
explain: EventBridge supports cross-account delivery to a central bus with resource-based permissions, designed for this aggregation pattern. Polling logs is slow and manual, queue replication is not a native pattern, and removing a queue policy breaks access control rather than enabling sharing.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Events published in one Region must trigger processing in another Region because the processing service is only deployed there. Which approach is simplest and native?
options: An S3 replication rule that copies the event payloads as objects
An EventBridge rule that targets an event bus in the destination Region
A VPC peering connection carrying the event traffic between Regions
A Lambda function in the source Region that invokes a Lambda in the target Region over the public internet
explain: EventBridge rules can target a bus in another Region natively. Object replication, VPC peering, and custom cross-Region invocation add latency, code, or networking that the bus-to-bus rule avoids.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company wants failover for event ingestion so that if the primary Region's endpoint is impaired, ingestion automatically continues in a secondary Region with the same routing. Which feature should it configure?
options: Two unrelated event buses with producers manually reconfigured during an outage
Route 53 latency records pointing producers at whichever bus responds
EventBridge global endpoints with health checks and automatic failover to the secondary Region
An SQS queue replicated by a scheduled Lambda copy job
explain: Global endpoints provide a single ingestion endpoint backed by Route 53 health checks that fail over between Regions. Manual reconfiguration is slow, DNS records alone do not replicate bus configuration, and copy jobs introduce lag and duplication risk.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An architect must ensure events from a partner account are accepted only from that account's specific event bus and no other source. How is this controlled?
options: Put the bus in a private subnet so only trusted traffic reaches it
Require producers to include a shared secret in the event detail and check it in every target
Enable default encryption and rely on it to authenticate producers
Use a resource-based policy on the target event bus that allows PutEvents only from the partner account and bus ARN
explain: Event bus resource policies scope which accounts and buses may put events. EventBridge is not placed in subnets, shared secrets in payloads are a weak custom control, and encryption protects confidentiality, not source authorization.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team runs Kubernetes workloads on-premises and wants the same EKS control-plane experience and tooling in AWS with managed node operations minimized. Which service should they standardize on?
options: Amazon EKS with Fargate profiles or managed node groups for the data plane
Amazon ECS with EC2 launch type and self-managed Kubernetes installed on top
AWS Elastic Beanstalk with Docker containers
Amazon Lightsail containers with manual scaling
explain: EKS provides managed Kubernetes in AWS, and Fargate profiles remove node management for pods. ECS does not run Kubernetes, Beanstalk abstracts containers but is not Kubernetes, and Lightsail lacks enterprise Kubernetes features.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A batch rendering workload on ECS needs to scale task count automatically based on the depth of its SQS job queue. Which scaling mechanism should be configured?
options: Cluster Autoscaler configured for the ECS cluster's EC2 instances
Application Auto Scaling for ECS services using a target-tracking or step policy on the queue's ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible per task
Manual service updates by an operator watching the queue
Lambda concurrency scaling applied to the rendering tasks
explain: ECS service auto scaling via Application Auto Scaling adjusts desired task count from queue metrics. Cluster Autoscaler is a Kubernetes concept for node scaling, manual updates do not react to bursts, and Lambda concurrency applies to functions, not ECS tasks.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Developers want to run containers without provisioning or patching any servers, with per-task IAM roles and VPC networking, and no Kubernetes requirement. Which option fits best?
options: Amazon EKS with self-managed node groups on EC2
Docker running on a fleet of manually managed EC2 instances
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate
AWS Lambda with container images limited to 15-minute jobs only
explain: ECS on Fargate is serverless container execution with task IAM roles and VPC networking. EKS self-managed nodes require patching, manual EC2 fleets add operations, and Lambda is for functions, not general long-running container services.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An EKS cluster's pods remain Pending during traffic spikes even though the cluster has spare pod IP addresses. Node CPU and memory are exhausted. Which component resolves this automatically?
options: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler increasing replica counts further
Application Load Balancer target group health checks replacing nodes
ECR lifecycle policies freeing space for new nodes
Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) scaling the node group based on unschedulable pods
explain: Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter add nodes when pods cannot be scheduled for lack of resources. HPA only creates more pods, worsening the backlog, and load balancer checks or image policies do not add capacity.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Kubernetes service on EKS must scale replicas from 2 to 20 based on CPU utilization at 60 percent. Which configuration achieves this?
options: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler targeting the deployment with a 60 percent CPU utilization metric
A Vertical Pod Autoscaler that restarts pods with larger requests
Cluster Autoscaler with a minimum node count of 20
An ECS service auto scaling policy attached to the deployment
explain: HPA adjusts replica counts from metrics such as CPU. VPA resizes individual pods instead of replica counts, Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes not replicas, and ECS policies do not apply to Kubernetes deployments.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company needs to give an ECS task permission to read one specific S3 bucket without granting the EC2 hosts or other tasks that access. Which mechanism provides this isolation?
options: An IAM user with access keys stored in the container image
An ECS task role (with a separate execution role) scoped to that bucket, assumed by the task at runtime
The EC2 instance role shared by every task on the host
A bucket policy that allows access from the VPC regardless of principal
explain: Task roles give each task its own least-privilege credentials, distinct from the execution role used to pull images and logs. Keys in images are a security risk, instance roles over-grant, and VPC-based bucket access is too broad.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Microservices on ECS need service-to-service discovery and connectivity without managing a separate service mesh data plane. Which built-in capability should the architect enable?
options: Manually maintained /etc/hosts entries in each task
A NAT gateway configured as a service registry
Amazon ECS Service Connect
AWS Global Accelerator in front of every internal service
explain: Service Connect provides ECS-native service discovery, connectivity, and traffic telemetry without sidecar management overhead. Hosts files do not scale, NAT gateways route internet traffic, and Global Accelerator is for global user traffic, not internal mesh discovery.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team migrating to EKS wants AWS-managed ingress that provisions load balancers from Kubernetes Ingress objects. Which component should they install?
options: The Cluster Autoscaler with ingress mode enabled
A DaemonSet that runs NGINX on every node as the only option
ECR with a load balancer lifecycle policy
The AWS Load Balancer Controller, which provisions an ALB (or NLB) from Ingress and Service annotations
explain: The Load Balancer Controller watches Ingress resources and creates ALBs with target groups for pods. Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes, a DaemonSet ingress is self-managed rather than AWS-provisioned, and ECR manages images, not ingress.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Container startup is slow because images have grown to several gigabytes with unused tooling. Which practice most directly reduces pull and startup time and attack surface?
options: Use multi-stage builds (or minimal base images) so only the runtime and application artifacts ship in the final image
Store the image in multiple ECR repositories to parallelize pulls
Increase the Fargate task CPU so image extraction runs faster
Disable image scanning so pulls are not delayed
explain: Multi-stage builds strip build tools and intermediate layers, shrinking images and attack surface. Repository duplication, bigger tasks, and disabling scans do not reduce image size and weaken security.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An ECS service must deploy a new version gradually, shifting 10 percent of traffic first and rolling back automatically on alarms. Which deployment capability provides this?
options: Replacing all tasks at once by setting minimum healthy percent to zero
ECS rolling deployments with deployment circuit breaker, or a blue/green deployment through CodeDeploy with weighted ALB target groups and alarm-based rollback
Manually stopping half the old tasks and starting new ones
Using an SQS queue to buffer users during a full cutover
explain: Controlled deployments with circuit breakers or blue/green weighting shift traffic gradually and roll back on CloudWatch alarms. Full replacement risks total outage, manual steps are error-prone, and queues do not version application traffic.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Internal services across several VPCs and accounts need to communicate by service name with access control, without complex VPC peering or route management. Which service simplifies this?
options: A full mesh of VPC peering connections with hand-edited route tables
Public ALBs for every internal service with IP allow lists
Amazon VPC Lattice service networks with service associations and auth policies
Transit Gateway used as an application-layer service directory
explain: VPC Lattice creates a service network that connects services across VPCs and accounts with name-based access and IAM auth policies. Peering meshes do not scale, public load balancers expose internal services, and Transit Gateway routes packets, not application services.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team using ECS Service Connect wants per-request visibility into latency and errors between services. What does Service Connect provide for this?
options: Automatic database query tracing inside each task's application code
VPC Flow Logs restated as application request metrics
A requirement to add a custom sidecar container the team must build and patch
Built-in traffic telemetry (metrics, logs, and traces via integrations) collected from the Service Connect proxy without code changes
explain: Service Connect's managed proxy emits connection and request telemetry without application changes or self-managed sidecars. Flow Logs are network-level, database tracing is unrelated, and the proxy is AWS-managed rather than a custom sidecar to patch.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Two services in different accounts must communicate privately, and the consumer should address the provider by a stable DNS name with IAM-based authorization. Which design fits?
options: Publish the provider as a VPC Lattice service in a shared service network and authorize the consumer account with a resource policy and auth policy
Expose the provider through a public NLB and share its DNS name
Create a VPC peering link and hard-code the provider's private IPs in the consumer
Replicate the provider's containers into the consumer account nightly
explain: VPC Lattice supports cross-account service sharing with DNS names and IAM authorization. Public exposure, hard-coded IPs, and container replication are insecure, brittle, or unnecessary.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An architect compares VPC Lattice with a traditional service mesh for a small ECS and Lambda environment. Which factor most favors Lattice here?
options: Lattice requires installing Istio control planes in each VPC
Lattice is fully managed with no sidecar proxies to deploy or patch, and it works across VPCs, accounts, containers, and Lambda
Lattice only works between EC2 instances in one VPC
Lattice replaces the need for any IAM policies on services
explain: Lattice's value is a managed, sidecar-free connectivity layer spanning compute types and accounts. It does not require Istio, is not limited to one VPC, and it complements rather than replaces IAM authorization.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A service mesh rollout keeps failing because sidecar injection breaks a legacy container that cannot tolerate a proxy. What alternative keeps managed connectivity for that workload?
options: Force the sidecar by running the legacy container in privileged mode
Move the legacy service to a public subnet so the mesh can reach it
Front the legacy service with VPC Lattice (which needs no sidecar in the workload) instead of a sidecar-based mesh
Rewrite the legacy application before any connectivity work can proceed
explain: VPC Lattice provides connectivity and access control without injecting a proxy into the workload, suiting sidecar-intolerant apps. Privileged mode adds risk, public exposure is worse, and a rewrite is disproportionate.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A CI pipeline pushes images to Amazon ECR, and compliance requires blocking deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities. Which ECR capability supports this?
options: ECR lifecycle policies that expire unscanned images after 30 days
ECR replication that copies images to a second Region for review
Tag immutability that prevents overwriting a scanned tag
ECR image scanning (basic or enhanced with Inspector) with pipeline checks on scan findings before promotion
explain: Scanning on push detects vulnerabilities so the pipeline can gate promotion on findings. Lifecycle policies manage retention, replication copies images, and immutability protects tags but does not assess vulnerabilities.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: ECR storage costs grow because hundreds of untagged and old development images are never cleaned up. Which configuration addresses this automatically?
options: ECR lifecycle policies that expire untagged images after a set period and keep only the newest N tagged images
A Lambda function that deletes the entire repository weekly
Switching the repository to private from public to reduce storage
Enabling scan on push so old images are quarantined
explain: Lifecycle policies automate retention by age, count, and tag status. Deleting whole repositories destroys needed images, visibility does not change storage, and scanning assesses vulnerabilities rather than expiring images.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A production repository must guarantee that a released image tag can never be silently replaced by a different image. Which ECR setting enforces this?
options: Enable encryption at rest with a customer managed key
Enable tag immutability on the repository
Replicate the repository to another account after each release
Set a lifecycle policy to keep the last 10 images
explain: Tag immutability prevents a tag from being overwritten once pushed. Encryption protects data at rest, replication copies content, and lifecycle retention limits count but still allows tag reuse if mutability is on.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Lambda API experiences throttling during launches because many concurrent executions start at once across the account. Which controls should the architect apply?
options: Increase the function's memory until throttling stops
Put an SQS queue in front of every synchronous API call
Request a concurrency quota increase if justified and set reserved concurrency for the critical function (and provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive paths)
Move the API to a single large EC2 instance behind an ALB
explain: Lambda scales by concurrency; quotas, reserved concurrency for protection, and provisioned concurrency for warm starts address throttling and cold starts. Memory affects per-invocation power, queues change the invocation model, and abandoning serverless is unnecessary.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A critical Lambda function must always have capacity available even when other functions in the account spike and consume the regional pool. Which setting guarantees this?
options: Provisioned concurrency alone with no reservation
A higher function timeout
An increased ephemeral storage size
Reserved concurrency for the critical function
explain: Reserved concurrency carves out capacity that other functions cannot consume. Provisioned concurrency pre-warms instances but does not reserve pool capacity, and timeout or storage settings do not affect scheduling capacity.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Users report high latency on the first request after idle periods for a Lambda-backed API where consistent low latency is a launch requirement. Which feature removes most cold starts?
options: Provisioned concurrency configured for the function's expected baseline traffic (with Application Auto Scaling if needed)
Reserved concurrency set to the account limit
SnapStart is irrelevant; instead increase the deployment package size
A cron EventBridge rule invoking the function every minute with no configuration
explain: Provisioned concurrency keeps initialized environments ready, eliminating most cold-start latency, and can auto scale. Reserved concurrency only reserves pool capacity, larger packages worsen cold starts, and ad-hoc warmers are unreliable hacks.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An ECS service's tasks are CPU-saturated at peak while its desired count stays fixed, causing timeouts. Which scaling policy best matches demand automatically?
options: A scheduled scaling action that doubles tasks every Monday regardless of load
Target tracking scaling on the service's ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization (or a custom metric) via Application Auto Scaling
Cluster capacity providers with managed termination protection only
Manual capacity reservations reviewed monthly
explain: Target tracking continuously adjusts task count to hold the chosen utilization. Scheduled actions ignore actual demand, capacity providers manage infrastructure rather than service targets, and manual reviews cannot react to peaks.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Kubernetes workload must scale pods on a custom application metric (requests per second per pod) rather than CPU. Which setup provides this?
options: Vertical Pod Autoscaler set to auto mode
Cluster Autoscaler reacting to the custom metric directly
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler using an external or custom metrics adapter (for example, metrics from Prometheus or CloudWatch) for the requests-per-second metric
An ECS scaling policy applied to the EKS service
explain: HPA can consume custom and external metrics through adapters. VPA resizes pods, Cluster Autoscaler scales nodes based on pending pods rather than app metrics, and ECS policies do not govern Kubernetes.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A serverless data API on Lambda must absorb a sudden tenfold traffic increase for a product launch without pre-provisioning servers. What inherent property and setting combination should the architect rely on?
options: A fixed pool of EC2 instances warmed before the launch
Provisioned concurrency set to one instance to control cost
An ALB with a fixed target group size sized for average load
Lambda's automatic scaling with an account concurrency limit verified/raised ahead of launch and downstream services (such as DynamoDB on-demand) scaled to match
explain: Lambda scales automatically per request; the launch risk is the account concurrency ceiling and downstream bottlenecks, so both are addressed in advance. Fixed pools and single provisioned instances contradict the burst requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An application runs containers on ECS and functions on Lambda, and both must scale on the same business metric published to CloudWatch. Which service coordinates scaling policies for both?
options: Application Auto Scaling, which manages scalable targets for ECS services and Lambda provisioned concurrency (and other resources) from CloudWatch metrics
AWS Auto Scaling groups, which cover both ECS tasks and Lambda
Systems Manager, which adjusts desired counts through runbooks only
The AWS Load Balancer Controller reacting to the metric
explain: Application Auto Scaling is the common scaling service for ECS, Lambda provisioned concurrency, DynamoDB, and others. Auto Scaling groups manage EC2 instances, Systems Manager runbooks are not a scaling policy engine, and the controller manages ingress.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A public web application needs path-based routing to several microservices, host-based rules, and integration with AWS WAF. Which load balancer should front it?
options: Network Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer
explain: The ALB operates at Layer 7 with path and host routing and native WAF integration. The NLB is Layer 4 without content routing, the Classic Load Balancer is legacy, and the Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party appliances.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A latency-sensitive trading feed needs a static IP, extreme performance at millions of requests per second, and TCP/UDP pass-through without HTTP inspection. Which load balancer fits?
options: Application Load Balancer
API Gateway HTTP API
Network Load Balancer
CloudFront distribution
explain: The NLB provides static IPs, ultra-low latency Layer 4 handling, and TCP/UDP support. The ALB adds HTTP processing, API Gateway is for API management, and CloudFront is a CDN for cacheable content rather than raw TCP feeds.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team exposes internal microservices to other VPCs without traversing the internet and wants each service reachable as an endpoint in consumer VPCs. Which technology should they use?
options: VPC peering with public DNS names for each service
NAT gateways in each consumer VPC pointing at the provider
CloudFront with private origins in each VPC
AWS PrivateLink with VPC endpoint services fronted by a Network Load Balancer
explain: PrivateLink exposes a service through interface endpoints in consumer VPCs, keeping traffic on the AWS network with controlled access. Peering shares whole networks, NAT provides outbound internet, and CloudFront is an edge CDN, not a private service fabric.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A startup needs a managed API front door with request validation, throttling per client, API keys, and direct integration to Lambda, without managing servers. Which service should it choose?
options: Amazon API Gateway
An Application Load Balancer with Lambda target groups only
A self-hosted NGINX tier on EC2
Amazon CloudFront with custom origins
explain: API Gateway provides validation, throttling, keys, and native Lambda integration as a managed service. ALB-to-Lambda lacks API management features, self-hosted proxies add operations, and CloudFront caches content rather than managing APIs.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An EKS application needs TLS termination at the load balancer using certificates from ACM and routing by hostname to different services. Which configuration delivers this?
options: A NodePort service with certificates stored as plain text in a ConfigMap
An Ingress resource managed by the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisioning an ALB with an ACM certificate and host-based rules
A ClusterIP service exposed through a NAT instance
An NLB with TLS policies applied to HTTP headers
explain: The controller creates an ALB from Ingress annotations, terminating TLS with ACM and routing by host. NodePort with plaintext certs is insecure, ClusterIP is internal only, and NLBs do not route on HTTP headers.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A global SaaS API must protect its origin from direct internet access while its ALB is reached only through CloudFront. Which design enforces this?
options: Make the ALB internal and give CloudFront its private IP
Publish the ALB DNS name only in the application code
Put CloudFront in front of the ALB and restrict the ALB security group (or use a custom header plus WAF/origin access controls) so only CloudFront can reach it
Enable ALB deletion protection so the origin cannot be bypassed
explain: Restricting origin access to CloudFront (via managed prefix lists/security groups and header checks) prevents bypass. Internal ALBs cannot be CloudFront origins over the internet, hiding a DNS name is not a control, and deletion protection guards configuration, not traffic.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A CloudFront-distributed site must rewrite URLs and normalize headers at the edge with sub-millisecond latency and no need for full Lambda runtime features. Which option is best?
options: Lambda@Edge functions on origin request for every rewrite
An ALB rule set performing the rewrites at the origin
A WAF rule that rewrites URLs before forwarding
CloudFront Functions attached to viewer request/response triggers
explain: CloudFront Functions run at viewer triggers with very low latency and lightweight JavaScript, ideal for simple rewrites and header manipulation. Lambda@Edge is heavier and better for complex logic, ALB rules act at the origin after the request travels there, and WAF inspects rather than rewrites URLs.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A media site needs to run complex authorization logic at the edge, including calls to external identity data and larger code packages, before serving protected content. Which edge compute choice fits?
options: Lambda@Edge, which supports larger packages, longer runtimes, and network access compared with CloudFront Functions
CloudFront Functions, which support arbitrary network calls
S3 Object Lambda for every page request
Route 53 resolver rules that evaluate authorization
explain: Lambda@Edge offers fuller Lambda capabilities for complex edge logic. CloudFront Functions cannot make network calls and are tightly limited, Object Lambda transforms S3 object retrieval only, and Resolver rules handle DNS.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A static marketing site on CloudFront wants A/B testing of a landing page decided at the edge without hitting the origin for the decision. Which approach works?
options: Duplicate the distribution and ask users to pick a link
Use CloudFront Functions (or Lambda@Edge) to assign a variant cookie and route/rewrite to the variant content at the edge
Use Route 53 weighted records between two origins for each page view
Store both pages in one S3 object and let browsers choose
explain: Edge functions can set and read variant cookies per viewer and serve the chosen variant without origin logic. Duplicate distributions and DNS weighting act at coarser granularity and cannot maintain per-user stickiness per request, and browsers cannot select inside a single object.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A chat application needs persistent two-way connections where the server can push messages to connected clients, with connection management handled by AWS. Which API type should be built?
options: API Gateway REST APIs with clients polling every second
An SNS topic that browsers subscribe to directly
Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs with routes for connect, disconnect, and message handling backed by Lambda
A Kinesis stream that browsers read with long polling
explain: WebSocket APIs maintain persistent connections and push via the @connections API, with Lambda handling routes. Polling REST wastes resources and adds latency, browsers cannot subscribe to SNS directly as a chat transport, and Kinesis is a backend stream, not a client connection layer.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A live sports app must broadcast score updates to hundreds of thousands of connected fans with minimal custom infrastructure. Which pattern scales best?
options: A single EC2 instance holding all WebSocket connections in memory
REST endpoints that fans refresh manually
SQS queues created per connected fan
API Gateway WebSocket APIs (or a managed pub/sub such as AppSync subscriptions/IoT Core) storing connection IDs and fanning out updates on score events
explain: Managed WebSocket/pub-sub services handle connection scale and fan-out; connection IDs stored in DynamoDB enable targeted pushes. A single instance is a bottleneck and failure point, manual refresh is not push, and per-fan queues are unmanageable.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A collaborative editing tool uses WebSocket APIs and must send a message to one specific connected user from a Lambda function. What information and API does it need?
options: The user's connection ID (stored at $connect time, for example in DynamoDB) and the API Gateway @connections POST endpoint for that connection
The user's IP address and a direct TCP connection from Lambda
The WebSocket route key resent to the client through SNS
The connection's IAM access key generated at connect time
explain: Server-initiated pushes require the connection ID captured during $connect and a POST to @connections. Lambda cannot open direct TCP to clients behind the gateway, route keys select inbound handlers, and no per-connection access keys exist.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A SaaS provider serves tenants with strict data isolation requirements in regulated industries, where each tenant gets dedicated resources, while other tenants share pooled resources. Which model describes offering both patterns deliberately?
options: A pooled-only model where regulated tenants accept shared tables
A hybrid multi-tenant design: siloed deployments for regulated tenants and a pooled model for standard tenants, chosen per tenant tier
A siloed-only model that forces dedicated stacks for every free trial
A single-tenant model marketed as multi-tenant
explain: Tiered SaaS commonly mixes silo for high-isolation tenants with pool for cost-efficient tiers. Forcing one extreme either violates isolation needs or destroys trial economics, and single-tenancy is not multi-tenancy.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: In a pooled multi-tenant application using Amazon Cognito, each request must be scoped so a user can only ever act within their own tenant. How is tenant context enforced?
options: Trust a tenant ID sent in a request header without verification
Give each tenant a separate Cognito user pool but share one database with no tenant key
Include a tenant identifier claim in the Cognito token (via groups/custom attributes and a pre-token hook if needed) and enforce it in the API and data layer on every request
Rely on the frontend to hide other tenants' data
explain: Tenant context must come from the authenticated token and be enforced server-side in APIs and queries. Unverified headers are spoofable, shared data without a tenant key leaks, and frontend hiding is not a security control.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A pooled DynamoDB table serves many tenants, and the provider must guarantee at the database layer that a tenant's queries return only their rows, plus offer tenant-specific encryption for premium tenants. Which combination provides this?
options: Use one shared sort key for all tenants and filter results in the browser
Encrypt the whole table with one key and describe it as tenant-specific
Store all tenants in one item collection with no partition key separation

Enforce tenant partitioning in keys with IAM/Lake-style row-level controls where applicable, and use per-tenant KMS keys (or envelope encryption with tenant keys) for tenant-specific encryption; for strict DynamoDB row security, scope access through the application with tenant-aware policies and leading-key conditions
explain: Tenant-scoped keys and access conditions keep queries within a tenant, and per-tenant keys deliver true tenant-specific encryption and crypto-shredding. Browser filtering, a single shared key, and unseparated storage all fail isolation.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company wants to add a customer-support chatbot using a foundation model without training or hosting the model itself, with pay-as-you-go API access and choice of models. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon Bedrock, invoking a foundation model through its API from the application
Amazon SageMaker training jobs to build a model from scratch
Amazon Comprehend custom classifiers trained on support tickets
Amazon Lex alone with no language model for open-ended questions
explain: Bedrock provides managed access to multiple foundation models via API, ideal for generative support chat. Building from scratch in SageMaker is disproportionate, Comprehend classifies rather than generates, and Lex alone handles intent-based dialogs, not open-ended generation.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A regulated enterprise runs Bedrock workloads in several AWS accounts and must keep model usage, guardrails, and provisioned throughput governed centrally while teams build independently. Which pattern fits?
options: One shared account where all teams share a single IAM user for Bedrock
A multi-account strategy with a central account governing Bedrock model access, guardrails, and logging, and workload accounts invoking models under organization policies
Each team negotiating its own model access with no central logging
Bedrock invoked only through personal access keys stored in code
explain: Central governance with separate workload accounts balances control (access, guardrails, audit logging) with team autonomy, a documented multi-account Bedrock pattern. Shared users and embedded keys destroy accountability, and ungoverned per-team access violates the regulation premise.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock application must prevent the model from producing disallowed content and from leaking personal data in responses. Which Bedrock feature should be applied?
options: A larger provisioned throughput so unsafe responses return faster
CloudFront signed URLs in front of the model endpoint
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with content filters and denied topics, plus PII detection and redaction
S3 versioning on the bucket holding prompts
explain: Guardrails evaluate inputs and outputs for blocked content, denied topics, and sensitive information. Throughput, signed URLs, and versioning do not inspect model text.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Knowledge workers need answers grounded only in internal policy documents, with citations, and the system must refuse when the documents do not contain the answer. Which architecture provides this?
options: A foundation model fine-tuned once on the policies with no retrieval
A keyword search page that returns whole PDFs to users
A Bedrock agent with web browsing enabled for missing answers
Retrieval Augmented Generation with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, grounding responses in retrieved document chunks and returning citations
explain: RAG over a knowledge base retrieves current policy passages at query time and supports citations and grounded responses. One-time fine-tuning goes stale and cannot cite, raw search shifts reading to users, and web answers violate the internal-only requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock-powered assistant's answers degrade after a document update because the knowledge base still serves old content. What operational step was missed and how is it automated?
options: The knowledge base data source was not re-synced after the update; schedule or trigger ingestion sync (for example, on S3 object events) to re-index changed documents
The foundation model must be retrained after every document change
The Guardrails configuration must be recreated
The vector store must be deleted and the account's model access re-requested manually each time
explain: Knowledge bases index documents at ingestion; changed sources require a new ingestion job to refresh embeddings and chunks. Foundation models are not retrained per document, guardrails do not hold content, and manual store recreation is unnecessary when sync exists.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company wants consistent low-latency Bedrock responses during a product launch with predictable model capacity rather than on-demand limits. Which option should it purchase or configure?
options: Reserved concurrency for a Lambda wrapper as a substitute for model capacity
Provisioned Throughput for the chosen Bedrock model (or model units sized to launch traffic)
An S3 transfer acceleration endpoint for prompts
A second knowledge base to split user traffic
explain: Provisioned Throughput reserves model inference capacity in Bedrock. Lambda concurrency does not create model capacity, transfer acceleration is for S3 uploads, and extra knowledge bases affect retrieval, not generation throughput.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Developers in three accounts need to experiment with different foundation models but finance needs per-team cost visibility for Bedrock usage. Which setup supports this?
options: One shared account and a spreadsheet updated manually
A single inference endpoint shared with no logging enabled
Separate workload accounts (or tagged resources/inference profiles) per team with Bedrock logging and cost allocation by account and tags in Cost Explorer and billing reports
Blocking model experimentation so costs stay uniform
explain: Account separation plus application inference profiles and invocation logging attribute Bedrock spend per team. Manual spreadsheets are unreliable, unlogged sharing hides usage, and blocking experimentation defeats the goal.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock application must keep prompts and responses entirely within the company's VPC boundary for compliance review. Which configuration addresses the network path?
options: Call Bedrock over the public internet but encrypt prompts in the application
Place the application in a private subnet with no route to any Bedrock endpoint
Use a NAT gateway and security groups alone to claim private connectivity
Use an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) for Bedrock Runtime so API traffic stays on the AWS private network
explain: PrivateLink endpoints keep Bedrock API calls off the public internet. Application-level encryption still traverses public paths, a subnet with no route simply breaks access, and NAT still sends traffic over the internet gateway path.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An architect must choose a foundation model in Bedrock for long-document summarization where input documents routinely exceed 100,000 tokens. What is the primary selection criterion?
options: The model's context window must accommodate the documents plus instructions and output, verified against Bedrock model specifications
The model with the lowest listed name alphabetically
Any model, because Bedrock automatically splits documents across models
The model that supports the most knowledge bases per account
explain: Context window limits determine whether long documents fit in one request. Model names carry no capability signal, Bedrock does not silently shard prompts across models, and knowledge base limits are unrelated to prompt size.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A generative AI feature must log every Bedrock invocation, including prompts, responses, and usage, to a central location for audit. Which setting enables this?
options: Rely on Lambda function logs from the calling code printing prompts manually
Enable Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs and/or S3 in the governing account configuration
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the application subnets
Turn on S3 access logging for the prompt bucket only
explain: Bedrock invocation logging is the native audit trail for model calls. Hand-printed logs are incomplete and risky, Flow Logs show packets not payloads, and bucket access logs do not record invocations.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An operations assistant must look up inventory, create purchase orders, and check shipment status by calling the company's existing APIs in response to natural-language requests. Which Bedrock capability orchestrates this?
options: A Bedrock Knowledge Base alone, which can execute API transactions
A foundation model given the APIs' credentials in its system prompt
Amazon Bedrock Agents (AgentCore runtime where applicable) configured with action groups that invoke Lambda functions wrapping the company APIs
SageMaker endpoints hosting the inventory database
explain: Bedrock agents reason over a task and invoke action groups (Lambda-backed tools) to perform real operations. Knowledge bases only retrieve text, embedding credentials in prompts is unsafe and does not execute calls, and SageMaker hosts models, not API orchestration.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock agent sometimes calls the wrong tool when two action groups have similar purposes. What is the most effective correction?
options: Increase the agent's underlying model provisioned throughput
Give the agent administrator permissions so any tool call succeeds
Remove parameter validation so calls never fail
Improve each action group's description and the agent instructions so tool purposes and parameters are unambiguous (and tighten OpenAPI schemas for the actions)
explain: Tool selection depends on the names, descriptions, and schemas the model reasons over; clarifying them fixes mis-selection. Throughput, excess permissions, and removing validation address neither selection quality nor safety.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An enterprise wants to deploy AI agents built with different frameworks by different teams, with a consistent managed runtime, memory, identity, and tool access. Which service provides that platform?
options: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, providing runtime, memory, identity, gateway/tools, and observability for agents regardless of framework
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases used as an agent runtime
AWS Step Functions renamed as the agent platform for all frameworks
Amazon EKS alone with each team building its own agent infrastructure from scratch
explain: AgentCore is the purpose-built platform for deploying and operating agents with managed runtime, memory, identity, and tool gateway capabilities. Knowledge bases serve retrieval, Step Functions is workflow orchestration, and raw EKS leaves every team to rebuild agent infrastructure.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A travel assistant agent must remember a user's preferences across separate conversations weeks apart, not just within one session. Which capability should be configured?
options: A larger context window on the foundation model
Agent memory (AgentCore Memory or Bedrock Agents session/long-term memory configuration) that persists user facts across sessions
Storing the whole chat history in the prompt on every call
Provisioned throughput so earlier messages are recalled faster
explain: Managed agent memory persists and retrieves user preferences across sessions. Context windows only hold the current session, replaying full history in prompts is costly and unbounded, and throughput does not create memory.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An agent must use a third-party weather API as a tool, with credentials kept out of prompts and model context. How should the integration be built?
options: Paste the API key into the agent's instructions so the model can call the API itself
Ask users to supply the API key at the start of each chat
Expose the API through an action group/gateway backed by Lambda that retrieves credentials from Secrets Manager and calls the API server-side
Store the key in an S3 object the model downloads during reasoning
explain: Tools execute in backend code; the Lambda/gateway holds secrets in Secrets Manager and the model only sees results. Placing keys in prompts, user input, or downloadable objects exposes them to leakage.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock agent answers questions from documents and also executes refunds; leadership wants document answers and transactional actions clearly separated and auditable. Which design supports this?
options: Merge refunds into the knowledge base as text instructions the model follows from memory
Let the model decide refunds conversationally with no action group
Disable logging for refund conversations to keep them private
Configure the agent with a knowledge base for retrieval and distinct action groups for refund operations, with invocation logging and guardrails, so each capability is governed separately
explain: Separating knowledge bases (read) from action groups (act) gives clear governance, testing, and audit per capability. Text-only refund instructions are unenforceable, unaudited conversational refunds are unsafe, and disabling logs destroys accountability.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Before launch, a team must verify an agent handles multi-step requests (check eligibility, then book, then confirm) reliably. Which testing approach is most appropriate?
options: Run scenario-based evaluations against the agent's test alias, tracing each reasoning step and tool call, and iterate on instructions and schemas before pointing the production alias at the version
Deploy directly to production and monitor complaints
Test only single-turn questions because multi-step behavior follows automatically
Increase guardrail strictness until all multi-step requests are blocked
explain: Alias-based testing with trace inspection validates the full reasoning and tool chain before release. Production experimentation risks users, single-turn tests miss orchestration failures, and blocking everything is not validation.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An agent built on Bedrock needs to browse an internal product catalog that changes hourly and answer with current prices. Which grounding approach keeps answers current?
options: Fine-tune the model nightly on the catalog
Connect the agent to a knowledge base (or a catalog API action group) that is synced/queried at request time rather than relying on model knowledge
Cache one day's catalog in the system prompt
Ask the model to estimate prices when unsure
explain: Request-time retrieval or live API calls reflect hourly changes. Nightly fine-tuning is stale within hours, prompt caching freezes data, and estimated prices are unacceptable for commerce.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Bedrock agent's responses must be restricted so it only discusses the company's products and politely declines other topics. Which layered controls achieve this?
options: A WAF rule blocking prompts that contain off-topic words at the network edge
Removing the agent's knowledge base so it knows nothing else
Agent instructions defining scope combined with Bedrock Guardrails denied topics for out-of-scope subjects
