explain: Network controls are per-protocol; IPv6 needs its own rules wherever dual-stack runs. Automatic inheritance does not exist, DNS changes do not disable routed IPv6, and Flow Logs do record IPv6 flows.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A dual-stack ALB serves global users, and the team wants IPv6 clients to get the same WAF protections and logging as IPv4 clients. Which fact should guide the design?
options: A separate WAF product is required for IPv6 requests
AWS WAF attached to the ALB inspects requests regardless of IP version, and ALB access logs/flow logs capture both families, so one web ACL covers dual-stack traffic
IPv6 requests bypass WAF because they arrive on AAAA records
Access logs omit IPv6 client addresses by design
explain: WAF operates at the HTTP layer after connection acceptance, covering both protocol families with one ACL, and logging includes the client IP in either family. There is no separate IPv6 WAF, and DNS record type does not bypass inspection.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A global application must send each user to the nearest healthy Region and automatically fail over when a Region's health check fails. Which Route 53 policy provides this?
options: Simple routing with all endpoints listed equally
Weighted routing fixed at 50/50 regardless of health
Latency-based routing (or Geoproximity) combined with Route 53 health checks so unhealthy endpoints are removed from answers
A single A record updated manually during incidents
explain: Latency-based routing with health checks directs users to the best healthy Region and withdraws failed ones automatically. Simple and fixed weighted routing ignore health and proximity, and manual updates are slow.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Users report high latency reaching an application hosted in one Region, even though content is dynamic and cannot be cached. Which service accelerates traffic over the AWS global network with static anycast IPs?
options: Amazon CloudFront with caching disabled as an accelerator
Route 53 latency records alone, which move packets onto the backbone
An NLB with cross-Region targets enabled by default
AWS Global Accelerator, which routes users to the nearest AWS edge and across the backbone to the healthy endpoint
explain: Global Accelerator improves dynamic traffic performance via anycast entry and the AWS backbone, with health-based endpoint failover. CloudFront is a CDN, DNS only chooses endpoints without changing the network path, and NLBs do not span Regions natively.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company is splitting traffic 90/10 between an old and a new platform during migration, and needs to shift weights gradually with the ability to roll back in minutes. Which Route 53 policy fits?
options: Weighted routing policy with health checks on both endpoints
Geolocation routing based on user country
Failover routing with one primary and one secondary
Multivalue answer routing returning all healthy records
explain: Weighted routing controls traffic percentages and adjusts in DNS quickly, with health checks removing failed endpoints. Geolocation routes by geography, failover is all-or-nothing, and multivalue returns multiple answers without percentage control.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Regulatory rules require EU users' requests to be served only from EU Regions and US users only from US Regions. Which Route 53 policy enforces this geographic steering?
options: Latency-based routing, which usually picks the closest Region
Geolocation routing policy mapping continents/countries to their regional endpoints
Weighted routing with equal weights for both Regions
Simple routing with separate subdomains per Region
explain: Geolocation routing deterministically maps user location to endpoints, meeting residency steering. Latency may cross borders, weights are proportional not geographic, and separate subdomains push the burden to users.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An active-active application runs in two Regions behind ALBs; clients should connect to whichever Region responds fastest, with instant withdrawal of a failed Region at the network entry layer. Which combination is strongest?
options: Route 53 records with 24-hour TTLs pointing at both ALBs
CloudFront origins in both Regions with origin failover for all dynamic APIs
AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups in both Regions and health checks, giving anycast IPs and fast failover independent of DNS TTLs
VPC peering between the Regions carrying user traffic
explain: Global Accelerator failover is driven by health checks at the edge and is not bound by client DNS caching. Long TTLs trap clients on failed endpoints, CloudFront origin failover suits cacheable content patterns, and VPC peering does not route public users.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A disaster-recovery design is active-passive: traffic must go to the secondary Region only when the primary fails health checks. Which Route 53 configuration expresses this?
options: Weighted routing at 100/0 adjusted manually after an outage
Latency routing with the secondary in a distant Region
Geoproximity routing with a bias toward the primary
Failover routing policy with a primary record and secondary record, each associated with health checks
explain: Failover routing is purpose-built for active-passive with health-driven switching. Manual weight changes are slow, latency routing may send traffic to the DR Region normally, and geoproximity bias is geographic, not health-based failover.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: During a Global Accelerator evaluation, the team needs to confirm which endpoint group receives traffic when one Region's endpoints all fail health checks. What is the expected behavior?
options: Traffic is directed to the next available healthy endpoint group (closest healthy) automatically, and clients keep using the same static anycast IPs
Clients must update their DNS to new IP addresses for the healthy Region
Traffic stops until the failed endpoints recover
The accelerator balances traffic equally including to failed endpoints
explain: Global Accelerator continuously health-checks endpoints and shifts traffic to healthy groups behind unchanged anycast IPs. No DNS change is needed, traffic does not halt, and failed endpoints are removed from rotation.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A company consolidates raw data from many systems into S3 and needs fine-grained access control, table discovery, and governance across accounts for analytics tools. Which services form the lake foundation?
options: RDS as the lake store with IAM policies for column access
S3 as storage with AWS Lake Formation for permissions and governance and the Glue Data Catalog for table metadata
EBS volumes shared to analytics accounts
Redshift alone holding both raw files and governance
explain: Lake Formation plus Glue Catalog over S3 is the standard governed data lake stack. RDS is a relational database, EBS is block storage, and Redshift is a warehouse consumer of the lake rather than its governance layer.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Analysts need to query curated data in S3 directly from Redshift without loading it, joining it with warehouse tables. Which feature enables this?
options: Redshift COPY jobs that duplicate the S3 data nightly
A Redshift materialized view over local tables only
Amazon Redshift Spectrum with external tables defined in the Glue Data Catalog (or Lake Formation-registered catalog)
Athena views copied into Redshift manually
explain: Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data in place via external tables. COPY loads data into Redshift (a valid pattern, but not querying in place), local views cannot see S3, and manual copying defeats the integration.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A data lake on S3 suffers from small-file problems and needs transactional upserts and time-travel queries from multiple engines. Which table format addresses this?
options: Plain CSV files with a nightly compaction script invented by the team
Parquet files with no table format, relying on folder naming for transactions
JSON dumps versioned by S3 object versioning as the transaction log
Apache Iceberg tables on S3, supported by Athena, Glue, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum
explain: Iceberg provides ACID transactions, upserts, schema evolution, and time travel over lake files across engines. CSV and bare Parquet lack transactional semantics, and object versioning is not a table transaction log.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A lakehouse design wants one copy of data in S3 serving both BI dashboards and ML feature queries with consistent tables. Which architecture reflects the lakehouse pattern?
options: Store data in S3 in an open table format (such as Iceberg) with a shared catalog, queried by Redshift/Athena/EMR/SageMaker tooling without duplicating the data per tool
Copy the data into each tool's proprietary storage nightly
Keep the only copy inside Redshift and export reports to S3
Use DynamoDB as the shared analytical store
explain: The lakehouse unifies lake storage with warehouse-style table management and multi-engine access to one copy. Per-tool copies drift, warehouse-only storage limits engine choice, and DynamoDB is a transactional store, not an analytical lakehouse.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Data owners in one account must grant analysts in another account access to specific tables and even specific columns without sharing whole buckets. Which Lake Formation mechanism supports this?
options: Copy the tables into the analysts' account every night
Cross-account grants in Lake Formation using resource shares (AWS RAM) with table- and column-level permissions for the consumer account's principals
Give analysts read access to the entire S3 bucket
Create IAM users for analysts inside the data owner's account
explain: Lake Formation governs cross-account table and column access centrally with RAM sharing. Copies duplicate governance, bucket-wide access over-shares, and creating foreign users breaks account boundaries and identity management.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A lake ingests change data from operational databases and must apply inserts, updates, and deletes to lake tables efficiently. Which combination handles CDC into the lake?
options: Reload the entire lake from source every hour
Store change files in S3 and let analysts mentally apply them at query time
Capture changes with a CDC-capable ingestion (such as DMS or AppFlow/Glue jobs) and apply them as merges into Apache Iceberg tables
Use S3 versioning to represent row updates
explain: CDC ingestion plus Iceberg MERGE semantics keeps lake tables current incrementally. Full reloads waste compute and delay freshness, unapplied change files return stale results, and versioning does not model row-level changes.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Query costs on Athena spike because tables are stored as many uncompressed CSVs scanned in full for every question. Which optimizations most directly cut cost and latency?
options: Increase the Athena workgroup's query timeout
Move the CSVs to S3 Intelligent-Tiering
Ask analysts to run queries less often
Convert to a columnar format (Parquet) with partitioning by common filter columns and appropriate file sizing/compaction
explain: Columnar storage, partitioning, and compaction reduce bytes scanned — the basis of Athena pricing and speed. Timeouts, storage class, and query frequency do not reduce per-query scan cost.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A central catalog must be shared so multiple accounts' Athena and EMR jobs use the same table definitions with Lake Formation permissions enforced. Which setup achieves this?
options: Share the Glue Data Catalog via Lake Formation cross-account grants so consumer accounts query the central catalog with fine-grained permissions
Export the catalog to CSV and import it into each account weekly
Give every account its own catalog and reconcile schemas in meetings
Store table definitions in a DynamoDB table each tool reads directly
explain: Lake Formation catalog sharing is the designed mechanism for governed cross-account metadata. Exports and parallel catalogs drift, and tools do not read arbitrary DynamoDB tables as their metastore.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A financial dataset requires auditors to reconstruct exactly what the data looked like at quarter-end, even after later corrections. Which lake capability provides this?
options: S3 MFA Delete on the bucket
Apache Iceberg time travel (snapshot queries) on the lake tables, or versioned snapshots retained per the audit policy
Redshift backups restored to a new cluster for each audit
Application logs describing each correction narratively
explain: Iceberg snapshots let queries target the table as of a prior snapshot or timestamp. MFA Delete protects objects, Redshift restores address warehouse data at cluster granularity, and narrative logs are not queryable data states.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Raw, cleansed, and curated zones in the lake need different retention and access: raw is append-only for data engineers, curated is analyst-facing. Which governance approach enforces this cleanly?
options: One bucket and one database where every principal has full access, documented in a wiki
Encrypt the raw zone and give everyone the key
Separate S3 prefixes/buckets per zone with Lake Formation permissions per database/table mapped to each zone, plus lifecycle policies per zone
Rely on file naming conventions to keep users out of raw data
explain: Zone separation with catalog-level permissions and lifecycle rules enforces access and retention mechanically. Shared full access, shared keys, and naming conventions are documentation, not controls.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A clickstream must be analyzed in near real time for fraud signals and also landed for long-term batch analysis. Which architecture serves both from one ingestion?
options: Write events only to Redshift and run both workloads there sequentially
Store events in RDS and poll for new rows every minute
Send events to SQS and analyze them after they expire
Ingest into Amazon MSK (or Kinesis), process the live stream for real-time analytics, and sink the same stream to S3 for batch analytics with EMR/Athena
explain: A streaming platform feeding both a stream processor and the lake is the lambda-style pattern for dual real-time and batch needs. Polling a database adds lag, a warehouse alone handles streaming poorly, and expiring queue messages lose the batch record.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A nightly job must join billions of historical records, run custom Spark transformations, and terminate when done to control cost. Which service fits?
options: Amazon EMR with transient clusters (or EMR Serverless) running Spark, reading and writing S3
Amazon Redshift running the Spark code as stored procedures
AWS Glue interactive sessions left running permanently
Lambda functions chained to process the dataset in 15-minute slices
explain: EMR is the managed big-data platform for large Spark jobs, and transient/serverless models control cost. Redshift does not run Spark jobs, permanent sessions waste money, and slicing a huge join across Lambdas is fragile.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Business users need fast, interactive dashboards over petabyte-scale structured data with complex joins and concurrency managed by AWS. Which service is the best fit?
options: Amazon EMR with Hive for dashboard queries
Amazon Redshift (RA3/Serverless) as the data warehouse for BI workloads
Amazon DynamoDB with scan-based reporting
Amazon S3 with browser-based file downloads
explain: Redshift is optimized for concurrent analytical SQL and BI tooling at scale. Hive on EMR is batch-oriented, DynamoDB scans are not warehouse queries, and raw downloads push analysis to desktops.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: SaaS application data from Salesforce and similar sources must flow into the lake daily without building custom API extraction code. Which service provides managed connectors for this?
options: Amazon MSK with producers the team writes for each SaaS API
AWS DataSync configured with Salesforce as a file location
AWS AppFlow with scheduled flows from SaaS sources into S3 or Redshift
Step Functions calling SaaS APIs from Lambda code the team maintains
explain: AppFlow offers built-in SaaS connectors and scheduled transfers. MSK and Lambda approaches require building and maintaining the extraction code AppFlow already provides, and DataSync moves files/storage, not SaaS application data.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Kafka-based streaming platform already exists on-premises and producers/consumers must move to AWS with minimal code change. Which service is the natural target?
options: Amazon Kinesis, requiring producer and consumer rewrites to its APIs
Amazon SQS FIFO, presented as a Kafka replacement
EventBridge with Kafka protocol emulation enabled
Amazon MSK (or MSK Serverless) as the managed Kafka-compatible streaming service
explain: MSK runs Apache Kafka, preserving Kafka APIs and tooling. Kinesis and SQS use different APIs requiring rewrites, and EventBridge does not emulate Kafka.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Streaming events in MSK must be transformed and loaded into Redshift continuously with exactly the team's SQL-based logic and minimal infrastructure. Which options are reasonable?
options: Use MSK Connect/Kafka Connect sink or stream processing (such as Flink via Kinesis Data Analytics/Managed Flink or EMR) writing to Redshift, chosen by latency and logic complexity
Load events into Redshift by manually exporting topic files weekly
Point Redshift Spectrum at the live Kafka topics directly
Have producers write each event twice, once to MSK and once as Redshift INSERT statements from the app tier
explain: Connectors and managed stream processors are the standard MSK-to-warehouse path. Manual exports break continuity, Spectrum queries files/catalogs not live topics, and dual writes in application code create consistency hazards.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A batch ETL job in Glue runs for six hours daily, but the business now needs the same transformations on data arriving every five minutes. Which redesign is most appropriate?
options: Run the six-hour batch job every five minutes in parallel copies
Move the transformation to a streaming architecture (Glue streaming ETL, Managed Flink, or EMR streaming) fed by Kinesis/MSK instead of shrinking the batch window indefinitely
Reduce the batch job's data by sampling 1 percent of records
Accept six-hour latency and rename the dashboard as real time
explain: Streaming ETL processes data continuously as it arrives; batch architectures cannot be compressed below their runtime. Parallel batch copies corrupt ordering and duplicate outputs, sampling destroys completeness, and relabeling misleads users.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Analysts need to combine historical S3 data with live MSK events in one investigation, seeing both in a SQL interface. Which pattern supports this?
options: Query the Kafka topics with Athena directly using no landing step
Keep live and historical data in separate tools permanently

Land streaming data continuously into the lake (Iceberg/Parquet on S3) with a short cadence and query the unified tables with Athena/Redshift Spectrum, or use a stream processor that joins live and reference data before landing curated results
Export historical data into Kafka and replay it for every investigation
explain: Unified SQL over continuously landed tables (or pre-joined curated streams) is the practical pattern. Athena does not query Kafka topics natively, permanent separation defeats the investigation, and replaying history per query is slow and costly.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An EMR cluster processing sensitive data must not store data on cluster local disks beyond the job, and results must persist in S3 with encryption and access logging. Which design choice supports this?
options: Use HDFS on the cluster as the permanent store and terminate the cluster nightly anyway
Store results on EBS volumes detached and shelved after each job
Disable logging to avoid recording sensitive access
Use EMR with EMRFS to S3 as the persistent store, transient cluster lifecycle, and S3 default encryption plus server access logging/CloudTrail data events
explain: EMRFS makes S3 the durable layer so clusters can terminate safely, with bucket encryption and logging providing controls. HDFS data dies with the cluster, shelved volumes are unmanageable, and disabling logs removes required evidence.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An application needs a relational database with complex joins, stored procedures, and strong consistency, managed by AWS with automated backups and failover. Which service should be selected?
options: Amazon RDS (or Aurora) with Multi-AZ deployment
Amazon DynamoDB with application-side joins
Amazon Redshift as the transactional database
Amazon S3 with SQL queries via Athena for transactions
explain: RDS/Aurora provide relational semantics with managed backups and Multi-AZ failover. DynamoDB lacks joins and procedures, Redshift is analytical, and Athena over S3 is not a transactional database.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A global mobile game needs a key-value store with multi-Region active-active writes and single-digit-millisecond latency in each Region. Which database fits?
options: Amazon Aurora Global Database with writes forwarded to one primary
Amazon DynamoDB with global tables
Amazon RDS with cross-Region read replicas promoted manually
Amazon Redshift with RA3 cross-Region sharing
explain: DynamoDB global tables provide active-active multi-Region writes at low latency. Aurora Global is single-writer (with forwarding), RDS replicas are read-only until promoted, and Redshift targets analytics.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A PostgreSQL workload outgrows its RDS instance: storage must scale independently, and the team wants faster failover and up to 15 read replicas with low replication lag. Which migration target fits?
options: Amazon DynamoDB with a SQL translation layer
Amazon Redshift with PostgreSQL drivers
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition
A larger RDS instance in a single AZ
explain: Aurora decouples storage from compute with a distributed storage layer, fast failover, and many low-lag replicas while staying PostgreSQL-compatible. The alternatives change the data model, target analytics, or remove availability.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An analytics team needs a columnar warehouse for complex aggregations over billions of rows, separate from the transactional system. Which service should be selected?
options: Amazon RDS MySQL with covering indexes
Amazon DynamoDB with global secondary indexes for reports
Amazon ElastiCache with data persisted for reporting
Amazon Redshift
explain: Redshift's columnar MPP design is built for large analytical aggregations. Transactional engines and caches are not substitutes for warehouse-scale analytics.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A session store needs sub-millisecond reads, automatic expiration of old sessions, and managed persistence as a cache rather than the primary database. Which service fits?
options: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis) with TTLs on session keys
Amazon RDS with a cron job deleting old sessions
Amazon Redshift with session tables vacuumed nightly
Amazon S3 with lifecycle expiration per session object
explain: ElastiCache provides in-memory speed with native TTL expiry, ideal for sessions. Scheduled deletions in RDS and nightly vacuuming cannot match latency or expiry semantics, and per-object S3 operations are too slow for session traffic.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A workload has unpredictable traffic that drops to near zero at night and the team wants the relational database itself to scale to zero and bill per use. Which option matches?
options: A provisioned RDS instance left at peak size permanently
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 (scaling within its configured range) or DynamoDB on-demand if the model is key-value; for a relational need, Aurora Serverless is the fit
Redshift provisioned concurrency for the application database
An EC2-hosted database the team patches and scales manually
explain: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with load for relational workloads with variable traffic. Permanently peak-sized instances waste money, Redshift concurrency is for warehouse queries, and self-hosting adds operations the requirement avoids.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A reporting workload is slowing the production RDS database because analysts run heavy scans against it all day. Which architectural change isolates them?
options: Add the analysts' queries to the primary with higher priority flags
Increase the primary's storage so scans run on the same instance faster
Offload reporting to a read replica dedicated to analytics (or replicate into Redshift/the lake for heavy analysis), keeping the primary for transactions
Schedule all transactions to pause during reporting hours
explain: Read replicas (or a downstream analytical store) isolate scan-heavy work from the transactional primary. Priority flags do not create separate resources, bigger primary storage does not isolate CPU/IO contention, and pausing transactions is not viable.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A product catalog has flexible attributes that differ per category, frequent single-item lookups by ID, and no cross-item joins. Which database model fits best?
options: Amazon Redshift with the catalog normalized into many tables
Amazon RDS with an EAV schema and joins per lookup
Amazon ElastiCache as the only catalog store
Amazon DynamoDB with the catalog keyed by product ID and attributes stored per item
explain: DynamoDB suits key-based access with flexible per-item attributes at scale. Warehouse normalization, EAV join storms, and cache-only storage all mismatch the access pattern or durability needs.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A financial ledger requires serializable transactions across multiple tables with relational integrity enforced by the database. Which choice is correct?
options: Amazon Aurora (or RDS) with its ACID relational engine and appropriate isolation levels
Amazon DynamoDB with transactions stretched across many items as the primary ledger design
Amazon S3 with Iceberg as the transactional ledger for the core banking flow
Amazon Redshift with nightly integrity checks
explain: Core ledgers belong on a relational ACID engine designed for multi-table transactions. DynamoDB transactions have item/scope limits unsuited as a general ledger, Iceberg targets analytical tables, and nightly checks detect rather than enforce integrity.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team must choose between ElastiCache and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for caching DynamoDB reads. When is DAX the better fit?
options: When the cache must also serve Redis data structures like sorted sets and pub/sub for non-DynamoDB data
When the workload is DynamoDB-centric and wants a managed, API-compatible in-memory cache with minimal application change (only DynamoDB items are cached)
When caching objects stored in S3
When the application uses ElastiCache for Redis already for all caching
explain: DAX accelerates DynamoDB specifically with the same API. Redis/ElastiCache is the choice for rich data structures and general caching beyond DynamoDB, and neither caches S3 objects in this pattern.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An RDS database must survive an Availability Zone failure with automatic failover and no application connection-string changes. Which configuration provides this?
options: A read replica in another AZ that the application promotes manually by editing connection strings
Nightly snapshots restored into the other AZ during an outage
RDS Multi-AZ deployment (DB instance or cluster) with its managed DNS failover endpoint
Two independent RDS instances kept in sync by application dual writes
explain: Multi-AZ gives synchronous standby and automatic DNS-based failover on the same endpoint. Manual replica promotion and snapshot restores are slower recovery procedures, and dual writes risk inconsistency.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A global application needs readers in three Regions with low-latency local reads and one writable primary, tolerating cross-Region replication lag under a second typically. Which Aurora feature fits?
options: Aurora Multi-AZ within one Region only
RDS read replicas in the same AZ as the primary
DynamoDB global tables fronting the Aurora data
Amazon Aurora Global Database with a primary cluster and secondary Region clusters for reads (and managed failover)
explain: Aurora Global Database spans Regions with fast replication for local reads and planned/unplanned cross-Region failover. Multi-AZ is intra-Region, same-AZ replicas add no regional resilience, and DynamoDB does not front Aurora.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Read traffic on Aurora overwhelms the writer even after adding replicas because the application sends all queries to the cluster endpoint for the writer. Which change distributes reads correctly?
options: Use the Aurora reader endpoint (or custom endpoints) for read-only queries so they load-balance across replicas
Increase the writer instance size indefinitely
Set all replicas to the same priority tier and stop adding them
Move reads into the application's in-memory cache permanently
explain: Aurora's reader endpoint distributes read connections across replicas. Scaling the writer alone ignores replica capacity, priority settings do not redirect application queries, and permanent in-memory caching is not a database scaling strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A DynamoDB table faces predictable seasonal spikes ten times baseline. Which capacity strategy avoids throttling while controlling off-season cost?
options: Provision for the peak all year with no scaling
Use on-demand capacity, or provisioned capacity with Application Auto Scaling and scheduled scaling for the known spike windows
Set provisioned capacity to the baseline and rely on retries
Switch the table to S3 tables for the season
explain: On-demand or auto-scaled provisioned capacity matches seasonal demand. Year-round peak provisioning wastes money, baseline-only provisioning throttles at peak, and changing storage systems is not a capacity strategy.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A DynamoDB global table deployment sees write conflicts when the same item is updated in two Regions simultaneously. Which statement describes the resolution model the architect must design around?
options: Global tables lock items globally so conflicts are impossible
Conflicts are resolved by asking the user which version to keep at read time

Global tables use last-writer-wins conflict resolution based on timestamps, so applications should avoid concurrent writes to the same item across Regions (for example, by routing a user's writes to a home Region)
Strongly consistent cross-Region writes are the default for global tables
explain: Multi-active replication resolves conflicts by last writer wins; design must minimize same-item cross-Region writes. There is no global locking or interactive resolution, and global tables are eventually consistent across Regions.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: An RDS read replica lags minutes behind during peak writes, and reports served from it are unacceptably stale. Which remedies are most effective?
options: Point reports at the Multi-AZ standby, which is readable during normal operation
Accept lag and disable report freshness requirements silently
Add more replicas of the same undersized type and expect lag to vanish
Reduce replica lag by right-sizing the replica, moving heavy reporting elsewhere (warehouse/lake), and checking write patterns; use synchronous Multi-AZ only for HA, not as a reporting source
explain: Replica lag is addressed by capacity, workload isolation, and write-pattern fixes. Multi-AZ standbys are not readable (for standard Multi-AZ DB instances), silently dropping requirements hides the problem, and more undersized replicas inherit the same bottleneck.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A mission-critical Aurora application must survive a full Region failure with an RTO of minutes and minimal data loss, rehearsed regularly. Which design and practice deliver this?
options: Aurora Global Database with secondary clusters in the DR Region, documented and rehearsed managed failover (or automatic cross-Region failover where supported), plus application connection updates via Route 53/endpoints
Nightly cross-Region snapshot copies with a restore runbook never tested
A second cluster in the same Region in a different AZ
Application-level exports to S3 in the same Region
explain: Global Database provides low-lag regional replicas and managed failover; rehearsal proves the RTO. Snapshot restores are slower and untested, same-Region copies share the failure, and same-Region exports do not survive regional loss.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Cache stampedes hit DynamoDB whenever a popular key expires in ElastiCache, spiking latency. Which caching strategies mitigate this?
options: Set all TTLs to the same exact second for predictability
Use techniques such as probabilistic early refresh, request coalescing/locking, jittered TTLs, or DAX for DynamoDB-integrated caching so expirations do not synchronize a thundering herd
Remove the cache so every request goes straight to DynamoDB
Increase DynamoDB capacity permanently to absorb every stampede
explain: Stampede protection spreads and coordinates refreshes instead of letting every request miss at once. Synchronized TTLs cause the problem, removing the cache worsens load, and permanent over-provisioning pays peak cost forever.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A video-editing workload needs a shared POSIX file system accessible concurrently from many EC2 instances across AZs with consistent performance. Which storage service fits?
options: Amazon EBS volumes attached to each instance with file copies synchronized manually
Amazon S3 mounted as the primary editing filesystem
Amazon EFS, providing a shared NFS file system across AZs
Instance store volumes shared over the network by one instance
explain: EFS is the managed shared file system for multi-instance POSIX access. EBS is single-instance block storage, S3 is object storage unsuited as a primary editing filesystem, and sharing instance store from one host creates a fragile bottleneck.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A database instance needs the lowest-latency block storage with high IOPS and persistence independent of the instance lifecycle. Which choice is correct?
options: Instance store volumes, which are lost when the instance stops
Amazon EFS mounted as the database's data directory for maximum IOPS
S3 Standard accessed through a gateway for data files
Amazon EBS (io2/gp3 volumes sized for the IOPS and throughput required)
explain: EBS provides persistent, low-latency block storage for databases. Instance store is ephemeral, EFS is a shared file system with different latency characteristics, and S3 is object storage, not database block storage.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Windows applications require a fully managed SMB file system with Active Directory integration and Windows ACLs. Which service should be selected?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EFS with SMB enabled
Amazon S3 with File Gateway in a Windows domain only
Amazon FSx for Lustre with Windows compatibility mode
explain: FSx for Windows File Server is the native SMB/AD-integrated managed file system. EFS is NFS-based, File Gateway is an on-premises access pattern rather than a managed Windows file system in AWS, and Lustre targets HPC scratch workloads.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A read-heavy application repeatedly computes the same expensive results; adding a cache must support data structures like sorted sets for leaderboards as well as simple key-value caching. Which service fits both?
options: Amazon DAX, which only accelerates DynamoDB item access
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, which provides rich data structures plus caching
CloudFront, which caches HTTP responses at the edge only
S3 Object Lambda transforming cached objects on read
explain: Redis in ElastiCache supports sorted sets and other structures alongside caching. DAX is DynamoDB-specific, CloudFront caches HTTP content, and Object Lambda transforms S3 reads rather than providing an in-memory data-structure store.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Product detail pages are read thousands of times per second from DynamoDB with occasional updates; the team wants microsecond-latency caching without rewriting queries. Which service is designed for exactly this?
options: ElastiCache for Memcached with manual cache-aside code for every query
A Lambda layer caching results in memory between invocations
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) as a write-through, DynamoDB-API-compatible cache
Read replicas for the DynamoDB table
explain: DAX caches DynamoDB items transparently behind the same API with write-through consistency to the table. Manual cache-aside adds code for what DAX manages, Lambda memory is not a shared cache, and DynamoDB does not use read replicas.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A team caches database query results in ElastiCache but serves stale data after updates because invalidation is ad hoc. Which strategy systematizes freshness?
options: Set TTL to zero so nothing is ever cached
Let each developer invalidate whichever keys they remember
Replicate the cache into a second Region to dilute staleness
Adopt a defined pattern such as write-through or cache-aside with explicit invalidation on writes plus sensible TTLs as a backstop, applied consistently in the data-access layer
explain: Consistent write-through/cache-aside with invalidation and TTL backstops is the disciplined approach. Zero TTL removes the cache's value, ad-hoc invalidation is the current failure, and replication spreads stale data further.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: Research teams in multiple accounts need to find and request access to curated datasets through a central catalog with governed sharing, including for ML collaboration with external parties on sensitive joins. Which services cover cataloging and privacy-safe collaboration?
options: Glue Data Catalog with Lake Formation for governed cross-account sharing, and AWS Clean Rooms for privacy-enhanced collaboration where parties join data without exposing raw records
A shared S3 bucket where every team lists objects to discover data
Emailing dataset extracts to external collaborators
A public Open Data registry entry for the internal datasets
explain: Catalog plus Lake Formation governs discovery and sharing, while Clean Rooms enable controlled multi-party analysis without raw data exchange. Shared buckets lack governance, emailed extracts lose control, and public registries expose internal data.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A Glue Data Catalog in a central account must serve as the single source of truth while workload accounts run their own Glue jobs against it. Which configuration enables this?
options: Copy the catalog into each workload account nightly with export jobs
Grant cross-account access to the central catalog via resource policies/Lake Formation so jobs in workload accounts use the shared catalog (catalog federation/sharing) rather than maintaining copies
Store a second catalog in each account and reconcile differences manually
Require all Glue jobs to run only in the central account
explain: Shared central catalogs via cross-account grants keep one metadata source of truth. Nightly copies and parallel catalogs drift, and forcing all jobs into one account breaks account isolation and scaling.
domain: Domain 1: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

q: A retailer is retiring local IAM users for its 400 engineers, whose accounts already live in Microsoft Entra ID. The engineers must sign in to AWS with their existing corporate credentials and be deprovisioned automatically when HR disables their Entra ID account. Which design best meets these requirements?
options: Federate IAM Identity Center with Entra ID using SAML 2.0 and provision users and groups with SCIM
Use an Amazon Cognito user pool as the corporate workforce directory and sync passwords to it
Store each engineer's long-term access keys in the corporate password vault for sign-in
Create an IAM user in each AWS account for every engineer and rotate their passwords quarterly
explain: Federate IAM Identity Center with Entra ID using SAML 2.0 and provision users and groups with SCIM. IAM Identity Center supports external IdPs over SAML 2.0, and SCIM provides automatic provisioning and deprovisioning driven by the IdP lifecycle. The main alternatives fail because local IAM users and stored access keys recreate the long-lived credential problem being retired, and Cognito user pools are for application end users, not the corporate workforce directory.

q: A software company's GitHub Actions workflows deploy to AWS several times a day, and an audit found AWS access keys stored as repository secrets. The team must eliminate the stored keys while ensuring only workflows in one named repository and branch can obtain AWS credentials. Which approach should they use?
options: Give the workflow the repository owner's personal access token so it can call AWS directly
Create a dedicated IAM user for CI and rotate its access key every 30 days instead of every 90 days
Configure GitHub as an OIDC provider in IAM and let the workflow assume a role whose trust policy restricts the sub and aud claims to that repository and branch
Store the access key in AWS Secrets Manager and have the workflow retrieve it with a second stored key
explain: Configure GitHub as an OIDC provider in IAM and let the workflow assume a role whose trust policy restricts the sub and aud claims to that repository and branch. OIDC federation exchanges a short-lived GitHub token for temporary role credentials, and claim conditions on the trust policy scope access to the exact repository and branch. The main alternatives fail because rotating or vaulting a long-term key still leaves a stored credential that can leak, and a GitHub personal token grants no AWS permissions at all.

q: A hospital group connects Okta to IAM Identity Center, but joiners and leavers are still being added and removed by hand a week after each HR change. Which change makes Identity Center membership track Okta automatically?
options: Ask administrators to create matching IAM users whenever Okta sends a welcome email
Schedule a weekly Lambda function that imports a CSV of Okta users into each account
Enable SCIM provisioning from Okta into IAM Identity Center for users and groups
Enable SAML just-in-time provisioning in each member account's IAM provider
explain: Enable SCIM provisioning from Okta into IAM Identity Center for users and groups. SCIM is the supported automatic provisioning protocol between an external IdP and Identity Center, so creates, updates, and disables flow without manual work. The main alternatives fail because CSV imports and manual user creation stay stale between runs, and IAM SAML providers do not perform Identity Center directory provisioning.

q: A bank assigns the same broad Identity Center permission set to developers, auditors, and operators across production and development accounts. A review requires each job function to get only the access its role needs in each account type. What should the architect implement?
options: Define separate least-privilege permission sets per job function and assign each set only to the matching groups and account types in IAM Identity Center
Attach a permissions boundary to the shared permission set and leave the assignments unchanged
Move all users to a single production account so only one permission set is needed
Keep one permission set but shorten its session duration to one hour for everyone
explain: Define separate least-privilege permission sets per job function and assign each set only to the matching groups and account types in IAM Identity Center. Permission sets are the unit of access in Identity Center, so scoping distinct sets by group and by account type is how least privilege is enforced per job function. The main alternatives fail because shorter sessions and boundaries limit duration or maximum permissions but do not differentiate what each job function can actually do, and consolidating accounts removes account isolation.

q: A manufacturer tags every resource with a department tag and wants engineers to administer only resources belonging to their own department, without writing a separate policy per team. Which IAM approach scales this access model?
options: Grant each engineer an IAM role per project and rely on role names to enforce separation
Create a dedicated IAM policy for each department and update all of them whenever a team forms
Use a permissions boundary per department and remove conditions from the identity policies
Use attribute-based access control with aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag conditions matching the department value in a single policy
explain: Use attribute-based access control with aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag conditions matching the department value in a single policy. ABAC compares principal tags to resource tags in one policy, so new teams are onboarded by tagging rather than by authoring new policies. The main alternatives fail because per-team policies and per-project roles multiply management work as teams grow, and a boundary only caps maximum permissions and cannot by itself grant tag-matched access.

q: A platform team delegates role creation to application teams but an incident showed a team creating a role with full administrator access and assuming it. The platform team must let teams keep creating their own roles while making privilege escalation of that kind impossible. Which control should they require?
options: Attach a session policy at sign-in that limits how long created roles can be assumed
Deny the teams the iam:CreateRole action and return all role creation to the platform team
Require a permissions boundary on every role the teams create so the role's effective permissions can never exceed the boundary
Require MFA for role creation so escalations need a second factor
explain: Require a permissions boundary on every role the teams create so the role's effective permissions can never exceed the boundary. A permissions boundary sets the maximum permissions an identity-based policy can grant a role, so a delegated creator cannot produce a role more powerful than the boundary allows. The main alternatives fail because removing CreateRole ends the delegation the team wants to keep, MFA authenticates the creator but does not cap the created role, and session policies limit a session rather than the role's permissions.

q: A SaaS vendor needs temporary access to a customer's AWS account to run diagnostics, and the customer is worried a second vendor customer could trick the vendor into acting in the wrong account. Which mechanism protects against this confused deputy problem?
options: Publish the role ARN only to the vendor so other customers cannot discover it
Ask the vendor to assume the role from a fixed IP address and check the address monthly
Give the vendor an IAM user in the account and audit its actions afterwards in CloudTrail
Require the vendor to pass a customer-assigned external ID when assuming the cross-account role, and validate it in the role trust policy
explain: Require the vendor to pass a customer-assigned external ID when assuming the cross-account role, and validate it in the role trust policy. An external ID is a secret the customer controls and the trust policy checks on AssumeRole, so the vendor cannot be tricked into using another customer's session. The main alternatives fail because an IP condition does not prove which customer the vendor intends to serve, an IAM user is a long-lived credential, and secrecy of an ARN is not an authorization control.

q: A consultant assumes a production support role for a migration weekend and the role itself legitimately allows broad read access across many services. For this one session, the customer's change board wants the consultant limited to Amazon EC2 and Amazon S3 read actions only. Which mechanism applies that limit only to this session?
options: Pass a session policy when assuming the role that allows only the approved EC2 and S3 read actions
Attach a new permissions boundary to the role for the weekend and detach it afterwards
Create a second consultant role and delete the original role until Monday
Edit the role's permission policy on Friday and restore it on Monday after the work
explain: Pass a session policy when assuming the role that allows only the approved EC2 and S3 read actions. Session policies are passed at role assumption and intersect with the role's permissions for that session only, leaving the role unchanged for other sessions. The main alternatives fail because editing the role or its boundary changes every session and risks not being restored, and deleting and recreating roles disrupts other users of the same role.

q: A security team receives a report that an Amazon S3 bucket in a member account can be read by an account outside the organization, but nobody remembers granting it. Which service gives them an authoritative view of this external access and similar findings across accounts?
options: AWS Config rules evaluating whether the bucket ACL is set to private
AWS CloudTrail Lake queries filtered to anonymous API calls against the bucket
IAM Access Analyzer external access findings generated from resource policies across the organization
Amazon GuardDuty findings filtered to public bucket alerts in the account
explain: IAM Access Analyzer external access findings generated from resource policies across the organization. Access Analyzer reasons over resource policies to report resources shared with principals outside the zone of trust, including cross-account S3 access. The main alternatives fail because CloudTrail records calls that happened rather than who could call, GuardDuty detects threats rather than policy exposure, and an ACL rule misses bucket-policy sharing entirely.

q: Before deploying a new IAM policy, a developer wants to know whether it introduces public or cross-account access that the current policy does not have. Which capability should be built into the deployment pipeline?
options: Run AWS Trusted Advisor IAM checks on the account after deployment completes
Deploy the policy to a sandbox account and watch CloudWatch alarms for a week
Use IAM Access Analyzer policy checks and custom policy checks against the existing policy during the pipeline run
Ask a reviewer to diff the policy JSON by eye in the pull request
explain: Use IAM Access Analyzer policy checks and custom policy checks against the existing policy during the pipeline run. Access Analyzer validates policies before deployment and its custom checks compare a new policy against a reference to flag new access being introduced. The main alternatives fail because post-deployment checks and manual review catch problems late or miss them, and sandbox observation cannot prove what access a policy grants.

q: An unused-access review shows dozens of IAM roles that have not been assumed in over a year and service permissions that no role has ever used. Which service produces this evidence so the team can safely remove the excess?
options: Amazon Macie reports listing roles that accessed sensitive data stores
AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations for downsizing IAM roles
IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings with last-accessed information for roles and services
Amazon Inspector findings for roles with old passwords
explain: IAM Access Analyzer unused access findings with last-accessed information for roles and services. Access Analyzer tracks when roles and services were last used and raises unused access findings, giving a defensible basis for removal. The main alternatives fail because Macie classifies data, Compute Optimizer sizes compute resources, and Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; none of them report unused IAM access.

q: A payments workload in a VPC may reach only two approved Amazon S3 buckets through its gateway endpoint, but today the endpoint allows every bucket. How should the architect restrict what the endpoint can be used to reach?
options: Create an S3 bucket policy on every other bucket denying this VPC by name
Add a route table entry that points the endpoint prefix list at the two bucket IP ranges
Attach a VPC endpoint policy to the gateway endpoint that allows actions only on the two approved bucket ARNs
Put a network ACL on the application subnets listing the two bucket addresses
explain: Attach a VPC endpoint policy to the gateway endpoint that allows actions only on the two approved bucket ARNs. Endpoint policies control which principals, actions, and resources are reachable through that endpoint, so scoping resource ARNs there enforces the restriction at the network path. The main alternatives fail because S3 addresses are not stable for route or ACL rules, and writing deny policies on every other bucket does not constrain this endpoint and cannot cover future buckets.

q: Contractors need browser access to an internal ticketing application in a private subnet, and the security team wants to remove the VPN and verify both user identity and device posture for every connection. Which service is designed for this access pattern?
options: An internet-facing Application Load Balancer protected only by a security group allow list
AWS Verified Access, evaluating identity from the IdP and device certificate status against a trust provider for each request
AWS Direct Connect from each contractor's home office to the VPC
A client VPN endpoint with split tunneling disabled for contractor accounts
explain: AWS Verified Access, evaluating identity from the IdP and device certificate status against a trust provider for each request. Verified Access provides VPN-less, per-request access to private applications using identity and device context from trust providers. The main alternatives fail because a VPN grants broad network reach after connection rather than per-application checks, an allow-listed load balancer checks addresses not device posture, and Direct Connect is a dedicated network link, not per-user application access.

q: An on-premises backup server must copy archives to Amazon S3 nightly, and policy forbids storing AWS access keys on any on-premises host. Which solution gives the server AWS credentials using its existing X.509 certificate?
options: Generate an access key for a backup IAM user and store it in the server's local keystore
Use an Amazon EC2 instance profile by registering the server as an instance in the VPC
IAM Roles Anywhere, with a trust anchor for the issuing CA so the server exchanges its certificate for temporary role credentials
Federate the server with SAML assertions issued by the backup application
explain: IAM Roles Anywhere, with a trust anchor for the issuing CA so the server exchanges its certificate for temporary role credentials. Roles Anywhere is built for workloads outside AWS to obtain temporary credentials by presenting X.509 certificates from a trusted CA. The main alternatives fail because a stored access key violates the policy directly, instance profiles only apply to EC2 instances, and SAML federation is for human identity federation rather than machine certificates.

q: A data platform runs transformation jobs on another cloud provider but must write results into an AWS data lake, and the team refuses to manage long-lived AWS keys in that environment. Which design provides the workload with AWS access?
options: IAM Roles Anywhere using the workload's X.509 certificate from the enterprise CA to obtain temporary credentials for a scoped role
Create one shared IAM user whose key is distributed to every transformation job
Replicate the data lake bucket to the other cloud so no AWS access is needed
Assume a role using a shared secret stored as an environment variable in the other cloud
explain: IAM Roles Anywhere using the workload's X.509 certificate from the enterprise CA to obtain temporary credentials for a scoped role. Roles Anywhere accepts certificates from a registered trust anchor regardless of where the workload runs, exchanging them for short-term role credentials. The main alternatives fail because replication changes the architecture rather than authorizing the writers, and both the shared key and the shared secret are long-lived credentials the team rejected.

q: A consumer mobile app needs users to register, sign in, reset passwords, and sign in with their social accounts, all managed rather than hand-built. Which service should provide this user directory and authentication?
options: IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to each app user
An Amazon Cognito identity pool configured with developer-authenticated identities
A custom user table in DynamoDB with passwords hashed by a Lambda function
An Amazon Cognito user pool with hosted UI and social identity provider federation
explain: An Amazon Cognito user pool with hosted UI and social identity provider federation. User pools are the managed user directory for app sign-up and sign-in, including social federation and hosted authentication flows. The main alternatives fail because identity pools exchange tokens for AWS credentials rather than managing users, Identity Center is for workforce access to AWS, and a hand-built credential store takes on password security the team wants managed.

q: After signing in to a shopping app through its Cognito user pool, users need temporary AWS credentials to upload their own photos directly to a private S3 prefix. Which component exchanges the user pool token for those credentials?
options: A pre-signed URL service that holds the bucket owner's access keys
A second Cognito user pool dedicated to storage permissions
An IAM user created automatically for each shopper at sign-up
An Amazon Cognito identity pool with authenticated roles scoped by the user's identity ID
explain: An Amazon Cognito identity pool with authenticated roles scoped by the user's identity ID. Identity pools federate an authenticated identity to an IAM role and return temporary AWS credentials, which can be scoped to a per-identity S3 prefix. The main alternatives fail because user pools authenticate users but do not vend AWS credentials, per-shopper IAM users do not scale, and holding owner keys in a signing service centralizes a long-lived secret.

q: A single-page application uses a Cognito user pool and currently relies on the OAuth implicit flow, which a security review has ordered the team to replace. Which flow should the application adopt for browser-based sign-in?
options: SAML 2.0 web browser SSO profile implemented by the single-page application itself
Authorization code flow with PKCE through the Cognito hosted UI
Resource owner password credentials flow with the user's password sent to the app
Client credentials flow using the app client secret embedded in the JavaScript bundle
explain: Authorization code flow with PKCE through the Cognito hosted UI. Authorization code with PKCE is the recommended flow for public browser clients because no secret is embedded and the code cannot be intercepted and reused. The main alternatives fail because the password flow exposes user credentials to the app, a client secret in a bundle is public by definition, and browsers cannot act as SAML relying parties in this pattern.

q: In a Cognito identity pool, members of the support group occasionally receive the customer role instead of the support role because role selection is ambiguous. How should the architect make group-based role selection deterministic?
options: Configure the identity pool to choose the role from the Cognito user pool group claim and set the support group's precedence so its role wins
Rename the support group so it sorts first alphabetically in the token
Disable group claims and map each user to a role manually in a DynamoDB table
Assign both roles' policies to a single merged role for all signed-in users
explain: Configure the identity pool to choose the role from the Cognito user pool group claim and set the support group's precedence so its role wins. Identity pools can resolve roles from the token's group claim, and group precedence decides which role applies when a user belongs to several groups. The main alternatives fail because group names do not control role resolution, merging roles grants customers support permissions, and manual per-user mapping abandons the group model that already exists.

q: Each microservice pod in an Amazon EKS cluster currently shares the worker node IAM role, so every pod can reach every team's DynamoDB tables. The platform team wants each pod to hold only its own service's permissions with a managed, per-pod association. Which feature should they adopt?
options: Annotate each pod with the node role ARN so kubelet can sort out access
EKS Pod Identity, associating a distinct IAM role with each Kubernetes service account
Run each microservice on its own EC2 instance with a separate instance profile
Store a different IAM access key in a Kubernetes secret for each deployment
explain: EKS Pod Identity, associating a distinct IAM role with each Kubernetes service account. Pod Identity binds an IAM role to a service account and delivers credentials to pods using it, removing the shared node role from the data path. The main alternatives fail because keys in secrets are long-lived credentials, per-instance isolation discards container density, and referencing the node role keeps the over-privileged shared role in place.

q: A team migrating from IRSA to EKS Pod Identity asks what operationally changes for credential delivery to pods. Which statement is accurate for the migration?
options: Pod Identity uses an EKS add-on agent and service account associations managed through the EKS API instead of an OIDC provider and annotated trust policies per role
Pod Identity requires each pod to store a web identity token file signed by the cluster administrator
Pod Identity works only for pods running on Fargate profiles
Pod Identity removes the need for IAM roles and grants permissions directly to namespaces
explain: Pod Identity uses an EKS add-on agent and service account associations managed through the EKS API instead of an OIDC provider and annotated trust policies per role. Pod Identity replaces the IRSA OIDC-and-annotation model with an EKS-managed add-on and association API while pods still assume IAM roles. The main alternatives fail because roles are still required, no administrator-signed token files are involved, and Pod Identity supports EC2-backed node groups as well as Fargate.

q: A Lambda function's code contains an access key that a developer copied from their own credentials, and the function needs S3 and DynamoDB access. What is the correct remediation?
options: Move the access key into the function's environment variables and enable encryption helpers
Rotate the developer's key and update the copy embedded in the code
Attach an execution role with least-privilege S3 and DynamoDB permissions to the function and remove the embedded key
Store the key in the deployment package but exclude it from source control
explain: Attach an execution role with least-privilege S3 and DynamoDB permissions to the function and remove the embedded key. Lambda assumes its execution role at runtime, giving the function temporary credentials with exactly the permissions it needs and no stored secret. The main alternatives fail because relocating or rotating the same long-lived key still leaves a credential in the function's configuration or code that anyone with read access can reuse.

q: A reporting account must read objects from a production account's bucket for nightly reconciliation, and the production team refuses to create IAM users for outsiders. Which pattern grants this access in the standard cross-account way?
options: Make the bucket public for the reconciliation window each night and private again after
Copy the production bucket owner's access keys into the reporting account's Secrets Manager
Create a role in the production account that the reporting account's role can assume, with a bucket-scoped read policy
Replicate the bucket and give the reporting account the replica's root credentials
explain: Create a role in the production account that the reporting account's role can assume, with a bucket-scoped read policy. Cross-account role assumption is the standard pattern: the resource account defines the role and its permissions, and the caller gets temporary credentials. The main alternatives fail because shared owner keys and public windows expose the whole account or bucket, and replication changes data flow rather than granting the reader controlled access.

q: An administrator role is used from both the office network and, during an incident, from responders' home connections, weakening the network-based control the auditors approved. How can sign-in policy require the corporate network or an approved exception path for this role?
options: Add an aws:SourceIp condition to the role's trust and permission policies, with the exception path federating through the corporate VPN egress addresses
Rely on the VPC endpoint policy of the management VPC to filter console sign-ins
Require the role name to include the office code so auditors can identify misuse
Shorten the role session to 15 minutes whenever the source address is unrecognized
explain: Add an aws:SourceIp condition to the role's trust and permission policies, with the exception path federating through the corporate VPN egress addresses. Aws:SourceIp conditions evaluate the caller's address on every request, so combining them with a VPN egress range enforces the approved network path. The main alternatives fail because endpoint policies govern traffic through an endpoint, not console federation, role names are labels, and session length does not restrict where a session originates.

q: A data science team keeps missing that an explicit deny in a sandbox boundary blocks experiments even though their identity policy allows the actions. Which explanation of policy evaluation should the architect give them?
options: A deny applies only when no allow exists anywhere in the account
Identity policies are evaluated last, so their allow wins over boundary denies
An explicit deny in any applicable policy, including a permissions boundary or SCP, overrides every allow for that request
Boundaries only warn in CloudTrail and never actually block API calls
explain: An explicit deny in any applicable policy, including a permissions boundary or SCP, overrides every allow for that request. Explicit deny takes precedence over all allows in AWS policy evaluation, regardless of which policy layer states the deny. The main alternatives fail because evaluation order does not let identity policies override denies, boundaries are enforced rather than advisory, and a deny blocks even when an allow also exists.

q: Developers federate into a sandbox account through Identity Center and need to test with a new AWS service before its permissions are added to their permission set. A security engineer wants to grant temporary broader access for one federated session without editing the shared permission set. Which mechanism fits?
options: Create duplicate user accounts in the sandbox with broader local policies
Attach an inline policy to the Identity Center instance itself
Temporarily promote the developers' group to the administrator permission set
Pass a session policy at federation that intersects with the permission set for that session only
explain: Pass a session policy at federation that intersects with the permission set for that session only. Session policies passed during role assumption narrow or further scope that one session's permissions without changing the underlying role or permission set. The main alternatives fail because promoting the whole group and creating shadow accounts affect other users and persist beyond the test, and Identity Center instances do not take inline permission policies.

q: A finance platform processes resources in ten AWS accounts and wants one policy that lets each account's automation touch only resources tagged with that account's cost center. Which design achieves this without duplicating the policy ten times?
options: Use session tags passed at role assumption and match them against resource tags with ABAC conditions in one shared policy
Encode the cost center in each role's name and parse it in a Lambda authorizer
Deploy ten copies of the policy, each hard-coding one cost center value
Grant the automation administrator access and filter its actions in a nightly report
explain: Use session tags passed at role assumption and match them against resource tags with ABAC conditions in one shared policy. Passing the cost center as a session tag lets a single ABAC policy compare principal and resource tags at request time for every account. The main alternatives fail because hard-coded copies drift as accounts are added, after-the-fact reporting does not prevent cross-cost-center access, and role names are not an authorization input.

q: An auditor asks how the company proves that no resource in its organization is shared with external accounts except through a small allow list. Which combination provides continuous evidence for that claim?
options: CloudWatch dashboards counting AssumeRole calls from unknown account IDs
Amazon GuardDuty threat detections exported to the audit data lake
A quarterly export of every IAM policy reviewed in a spreadsheet by the audit team
IAM Access Analyzer organization external access findings plus analyzer rules that archive findings for the allow-listed principals
explain: IAM Access Analyzer organization external access findings plus analyzer rules that archive findings for the allow-listed principals. Access Analyzer continuously evaluates resource policies organization-wide and reports external access, and its archive rules document the approved exceptions. The main alternatives fail because manual quarterly reviews miss changes between audits, counting role assumptions misses resource-policy sharing entirely, and GuardDuty reports threats rather than policy-based exposure.

q: A private REST API in a VPC must be invocable only through one specific VPC endpoint by one partner account's role, with defense in depth on both sides. Which pair of controls enforces this?
options: An API resource policy allowing only that principal and endpoint, together with a VPC endpoint policy allowing only that API and action
An ACM certificate for mutual TLS and a CloudFront distribution in front of the API
A Network Firewall rule for the partner CIDR and an S3-style bucket policy on the API stage
A security group on the API's load balancer and a WAF rule for the partner's user agent
explain: An API resource policy allowing only that principal and endpoint, together with a VPC endpoint policy allowing only that API and action. Resource policies and endpoint policies are evaluated together for private APIs, so constraining both the API side and the endpoint side gives the required two-sided control. The main alternatives fail because private APIs have no load balancer security group to configure in this pattern, CloudFront makes the API edge-optimized rather than private, and firewall CIDR rules cannot express the partner role principal.

q: A genomics platform defines a data perimeter so that only identities from its organization can access its buckets and only its identities can reach external storage it approves. Which condition keys are central to expressing the identity side of that perimeter in resource policies?
options: aws:SourceVpc conditions listing the research VPC on every bucket policy
aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:PrincipalOrgIDs conditions requiring the calling principal to belong to the organization
aws:RequestedRegion conditions naming the regions where the lab operates
aws:MultiFactorAuthAge conditions limiting how old an MFA authentication can be
explain: aws:PrincipalOrgID and aws:PrincipalOrgIDs conditions requiring the calling principal to belong to the organization. Organization conditions in resource policies are the data-perimeter primitive that restricts access to principals from the trusted organization. The main alternatives fail because VPC conditions cover only network-originated calls, MFA age governs session freshness, and region conditions govern where resources are created rather than who may access them.

q: Engineers keep pasting production database credentials into chat tools, and leadership wants human workforce access to AWS to leave no long-term credentials anywhere. Which target state should the architect commit to?
options: Require engineers to memorize new passwords every week for their IAM users
All human access federated through IAM Identity Center with temporary credentials and MFA, and local IAM users for humans disabled by SCP
Move credentials into a shared team vault with checkout logging
Issue each engineer two access keys so one can be rotated while the other is in use
explain: All human access federated through IAM Identity Center with temporary credentials and MFA, and local IAM users for humans disabled by SCP. Federation through Identity Center issues short-lived credentials tied to the corporate identity lifecycle, and an SCP can prevent new long-lived human credentials from being created. The main alternatives fail because dual keys, weekly passwords, and vaulted shared credentials all preserve long-lived secrets whose lifecycle is the problem being solved.

q: A support platform's Cognito user pool must challenge suspicious sign-ins with an additional factor while letting normal sign-ins through unchanged. Which user pool capability provides this risk-based behavior?
options: Compromising credential checks run nightly against the user pool by a cron job
Adaptive authentication in the user pool's threat protection features, applying MFA or blocking based on risk signals
Requiring every user to complete MFA on every sign-in regardless of risk
A pre sign-up Lambda trigger that checks the user's IP address against a list
explain: Adaptive authentication in the user pool's threat protection features, applying MFA or blocking based on risk signals. Cognito threat protection evaluates sign-in risk and can step up to MFA or block only when signals warrant it, matching the risk-based requirement. The main alternatives fail because pre sign-up triggers run before sign-in risk exists, nightly checks do not protect live sign-ins, and universal MFA ignores the requirement to leave normal sign-ins unchanged.

q: A healthcare app's Cognito user pool issues ID tokens, access tokens, and refresh tokens, and a new API team is unsure which token its API Gateway authorizer should validate. Which token is correct for authorizing API calls?
options: The ID token, because it contains the user's profile attributes for the API
The access token, validated by the Cognito authorizer for scope and client before the API is invoked
Any of the three, because the user pool signs all of them identically
The refresh token, because it proves the session is still renewable
explain: The access token, validated by the Cognito authorizer for scope and client before the API is invoked. Access tokens carry the scopes and client identity intended for resource servers, and Cognito authorizers for API Gateway validate access tokens for API authorization. The main alternatives fail because ID tokens are for the client application to establish who signed in, refresh tokens are only for obtaining new tokens from the pool, and the three token types have different audiences and purposes despite sharing a signer.

q: A fintech's API Gateway APIs accept Cognito access tokens, but one API is letting any authenticated app user invoke an admin-only endpoint. Which fix enforces the finer-grained authorization?
options: Require the admin endpoint to be called only during business hours using a WAF rule
Define OAuth scopes on the user pool resource server and require the admin scope on that method's Cognito authorizer
Check the user's email domain in each Lambda integration before running admin logic
Move the admin endpoint to a separate API and rely on its obscurity for protection
explain: Define OAuth scopes on the user pool resource server and require the admin scope on that method's Cognito authorizer. Cognito authorizers can require specific OAuth scopes per method, so the admin method can demand a scope only admin clients are granted.
