The main alternatives fail because node passwords are not a Redshift encryption mechanism, exporting reports leaves the underlying warehouse data unencrypted, and TLS protects the connection rather than data at rest.

q: A SaaS analytics job generates a fresh data key for every record and is hitting KMS request limits and latency targets. Which envelope-encryption refinement preserves security while cutting calls?
options: Disable envelope encryption and call KMS Encrypt on every record instead
Reuse one data key for the lifetime of the job with no limits
Store data keys in plaintext beside the records to avoid re-requesting them
Cache data keys briefly with strict reuse limits (bytes, messages, and time) using the AWS Encryption SDK's data key caching
explain: Cache data keys briefly with strict reuse limits (bytes, messages, and time) using the AWS Encryption SDK's data key caching. Bounded data key caching is the sanctioned middle ground: limited reuse under cryptographic limits reduces KMS calls without creating an unbounded shared key. The main alternatives fail because unbounded reuse makes one key compromise expose the whole dataset, per-record KMS calls are the bottleneck being escaped, and plaintext key storage defeats the encryption entirely.

q: An organization wants every new backup, volume, and file system in a Region encrypted under keys it controls, without relying on each service team's choices. Which layered approach comes closest to guaranteeing this?
options: Encrypt data only at the central analytics platform after ingestion
Combine service defaults (such as EBS encryption by default and S3 default encryption with CMKs) with SCP and Config enforcement that denies or flags unencrypted resource creation
Publish an encryption standard document and review compliance annually
Give every team administrator access so they can fix encryption quickly
explain: Combine service defaults (such as EBS encryption by default and S3 default encryption with CMKs) with SCP and Config enforcement that denies or flags unencrypted resource creation. Defaults make the secure path automatic while preventive and detective controls catch the exceptions, which is the only way to cover services with different creation models. The main alternatives fail because documents and annual reviews do not change creation-time behavior, broad admin access spreads risk, and encrypting after ingestion leaves source data exposed at rest.

q: A key used to encrypt regulated data must have its material generated outside AWS and imported, with an expiration the compliance team sets. Which KMS origin and process supports this?
options: Use an AWS_KMS origin key and download its material for safekeeping
Generate the key in CloudHSM and reference it from KMS by ARN
Request an ACM key with import enabled and attach it to the services
Create a KMS key with EXTERNAL origin, import the externally generated material wrapped for import, and set its expiration as required
explain: Create a KMS key with EXTERNAL origin, import the externally generated material wrapped for import, and set its expiration as required. Imported key material is a first-class KMS feature for EXTERNAL-origin keys, including wrapping requirements and optional expiration of the imported material. The main alternatives fail because AWS-generated material cannot be downloaded, CloudHSM keys are not KMS keys by reference, and ACM manages certificates rather than importable encryption keys for services.

q: Verifiers outside AWS must check signatures produced by an application's KMS asymmetric key, without calling AWS for each verification. Which property of KMS asymmetric keys makes this possible?
options: Verification must always occur inside the account that owns the key
KMS symmetric keys expose a public half for verification
The private key can be exported to verifiers under an NDA
The public key of a KMS asymmetric key pair can be downloaded and used to verify signatures externally
explain: The public key of a KMS asymmetric key pair can be downloaded and used to verify signatures externally. KMS asymmetric keys are designed so the public component is shareable for verification while the private component never leaves KMS. The main alternatives fail because private keys are never exported from KMS, symmetric keys have no public half, and external verification with the downloaded public key is an intended use case.

q: A disaster-recovery design copies encrypted RDS snapshots to a second Region, and restores there fail because the target cannot use the source key. Which key strategy should have been chosen for the source database?
options: Share the source key's ARN with the DR account so it can borrow the key
Encrypt with a key whose policy names the DR Region as a principal
Encrypt the source with a multi-Region KMS key so a replica key in the DR Region can decrypt copied snapshots
Disable encryption for snapshots that will be copied across Regions
explain: Encrypt the source with a multi-Region KMS key so a replica key in the DR Region can decrypt copied snapshots. KMS keys are Regional resources; only multi-Region keys provide a same-material replica in the target Region for copied ciphertext. The main alternatives fail because policies cannot make a key operate outside its Region, an ARN reference does not move the key, and dropping encryption for DR copies sacrifices protection exactly where oversight is weakest.

q: A security team wants to be alerted the moment anyone schedules deletion of a production KMS key, before the waiting period expires. Which detection should they wire to paging?
options: An S3 event notification on buckets encrypted by the key
A CloudWatch alarm on the key's enabled metric in the KMS console
An EventBridge rule on the CloudTrail ScheduleKeyDeletion event for production key IDs, routed to SNS
A daily report of key policies exported to the team wiki
explain: An EventBridge rule on the CloudTrail ScheduleKeyDeletion event for production key IDs, routed to SNS. Key deletion scheduling is an API event recorded in CloudTrail, so event-driven detection catches it at the moment it happens and leaves the waiting period to respond. The main alternatives fail because there is no console metric that pages on this action, daily reports can miss the start of a short waiting period, and bucket notifications do not observe KMS control-plane events.

q: A genomics pipeline in FIPS-regulated accounts must use FIPS-validated cryptographic endpoints for its KMS calls. Which endpoint choice satisfies the requirement?
options: Route KMS calls through a CloudHSM cluster in the same VPC
Direct the SDK to the KMS FIPS endpoint for the Region (for example kms-fips.<region>.amazonaws.com)
Enable TLS 1.3 on the standard endpoint to make it FIPS-validated
Use the standard KMS endpoint but request FIPS mode in the call headers
explain: Direct the SDK to the KMS FIPS endpoint for the Region (for example kms-fips.<region>.amazonaws.com). AWS publishes distinct FIPS endpoints for KMS whose modules are FIPS-validated, and clients must address those endpoints explicitly. The main alternatives fail because no header upgrades the standard endpoint's validation status, TLS version and FIPS module validation are different properties, and CloudHSM changes key storage rather than the KMS endpoint's certification.

q: A team wants to temporarily let an external auditor decrypt a sample dataset under a production key, with access that self-expires and is auditable. Which mechanism fits better than editing the key policy?
options: Add the auditor as a permanent key administrator in the key policy
Create a KMS grant for the auditor's principal with the needed operations and a retirement schedule, then retire the grant after the review
Disable the key for all other users during the audit window
Give the auditor a copy of an internal user's credentials
explain: Create a KMS grant for the auditor's principal with the needed operations and a retirement schedule, then retire the grant after the review. Grants are the delegated, constrained, and revocable way to share key usage temporarily without rewriting the key's standing policy. The main alternatives fail because permanent admin rights outlive the engagement, disabling the key halts production, and sharing credentials breaks attribution and policy alike.

q: A mobile banking backend in a regulated market must keep its KMS keys' material in HSMs located in that market's Region while using standard AWS service integrations. Which design respects the residency of the key material itself?
options: Store a copy of the key material in the on-premises vault as a backup
Replicate the key to three Regions for durability of the material
Create the customer managed keys (or a custom key store) in that Region only, and avoid multi-Region replicas that would copy material elsewhere
Create one global key and rely on its alias being Regional
explain: Create the customer managed keys (or a custom key store) in that Region only, and avoid multi-Region replicas that would copy material elsewhere. Key material lives where the key is created; single-Region creation (or an in-Region custom key store) keeps material resident, while replicas deliberately copy it to other Regions. The main alternatives fail because aliases do not relocate material, replication is exactly the cross-Region copying being avoided, and exporting AWS key material to a vault is not possible for AWS-generated keys.

q: An API team terminates TLS at API Gateway and wants to require TLS 1.3-capable clients for a new high-security API without breaking its other APIs. Which per-API control applies the requirement?
options: Set the API's security policy (TLS_1_3) on its custom domain so only that domain enforces the modern floor
Add a resource policy denying clients by user agent string
Change the account-wide ACM default so all certificates require TLS 1.3
Enable WAF TLS inspection on the API stage
explain: Set the API's security policy (TLS_1_3) on its custom domain so only that domain enforces the modern floor. API Gateway custom domains carry a security policy that selects the minimum TLS version per domain, so the strict floor can apply to one API only. The main alternatives fail because ACM does not set protocol floors account-wide, user agents are spoofable and unrelated to negotiated TLS, and WAF does not negotiate the TLS version for the API.

q: A workload's certificates from Private CA are being rejected because clients cannot build a chain to a trusted root after a CA restructure. Which Private CA concept most likely needs repair?
options: The CA hierarchy and certificate chain: reissue or correctly install the subordinate CA certificate signed by the root so clients can chain to the trusted root
Each client must import every leaf certificate individually
The KMS key encrypting the CA's private key
The S3 bucket storing the CRL must be made public to all clients
explain: The CA hierarchy and certificate chain: reissue or correctly install the subordinate CA certificate signed by the root so clients can chain to the trusted root. Chain building depends on a correctly issued and installed intermediate certificate linking leaves to the root; a broken hierarchy breaks every certificate under it. The main alternatives fail because the CA's key encryption does not affect client chain building, CRL distribution is about revocation checking rather than chain construction, and importing leaves individually abandons PKI's trust model.

q: A company wants encryption at rest for a new Amazon OpenSearch domain with a key it controls, chosen before the domain takes data. Which decision must be made at domain creation?
options: Use node-to-node encryption as a substitute for at-rest encryption
Select the customer managed KMS key for the domain's encryption at rest at creation time, since it cannot be changed afterward
Decide the key later once the data classification is known
Rely on index-level passwords for stored-data protection
explain: Select the customer managed KMS key for the domain's encryption at rest at creation time, since it cannot be changed afterward. OpenSearch encryption at rest and its key are creation-time choices that cannot be modified later, so the controlled key must be selected up front. The main alternatives fail because deferring the choice forfeits it, node-to-node encryption protects traffic between nodes rather than stored data, and passwords do not encrypt data at rest.

q: A platform team needs a single statement they can give developers about when to choose CloudHSM over KMS. Which statement is accurate?
options: Choose CloudHSM when regulation or contract demands dedicated single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control or direct PKCS#11 access; otherwise KMS's managed, integrated model fits most workloads
Choose KMS only for non-production because it lacks FIPS-validated modules
Choose CloudHSM whenever a workload is described as sensitive
Choose CloudHSM because KMS cannot use customer managed keys
explain: Choose CloudHSM when regulation or contract demands dedicated single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control or direct PKCS#11 access; otherwise KMS's managed, integrated model fits most workloads. The differentiator is control and interface: dedicated HSM tenancy and standard HSM APIs versus KMS's shared, AWS-integrated key service with customer managed keys. The main alternatives fail because sensitivity alone does not mandate dedicated hardware, KMS does offer customer managed keys, and KMS uses FIPS-validated modules in production widely.

q: A checkout service's TLS certificates for an internal ALB keep being issued for the wrong DNS name because requests are manual. Which automation removes this class of error?
options: Request certificates through ACM (public or Private CA as appropriate) with DNS validation so issuance and renewal are programmatic and verified against DNS
Issue one wildcard self-signed certificate for all internal names
Keep a spreadsheet of certificate names reviewed at each sprint
Let each developer generate certificates on their laptop for their services
explain: Request certificates through ACM (public or Private CA as appropriate) with DNS validation so issuance and renewal are programmatic and verified against DNS. ACM's DNS-validated issuance ties the certificate exactly to verified DNS names and automates renewal, removing manual name handling. The main alternatives fail because spreadsheets preserve the manual process, laptop-generated certificates are unauditable, and self-signed wildcards are untrusted and over-broad.

q: A growing company still runs production, development, and sandbox workloads in one AWS account, and a development accident recently took down a production database. Which organizational change is the foundation for fixing this class of problem?
options: Move workloads into separate accounts grouped in AWS Organizations OUs by function and environment, so account boundaries isolate blast radius
Tag every resource with its environment and review tags weekly
Create separate VPCs in the same account for each environment
Add more IAM policies in the single account naming each environment
explain: Move workloads into separate accounts grouped in AWS Organizations OUs by function and environment, so account boundaries isolate blast radius. Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary in AWS for permissions, limits, and billing, and Organizations OUs let policy be applied per environment group. The main alternatives fail because policies, tags, and VPCs inside one account cannot contain an account-level compromise or administrative error the way separate accounts do.

q: A regulated firm wants a landing zone where every new account arrives with logging, guardrails, and identity already configured to company standard. Which service provides this governed starting point?
options: A wiki page describing how teams should configure new accounts
Amazon GuardDuty deployed first so accounts inherit its settings
AWS Organizations alone, creating bare accounts for teams to configure
AWS Control Tower to set up the landing zone with mandatory guardrails, a log archive, and an audit account
explain: AWS Control Tower to set up the landing zone with mandatory guardrails, a log archive, and an audit account. Control Tower builds the multi-account landing zone with preventive and detective guardrails and centralized logging accounts out of the box. The main alternatives fail because Organizations provides the hierarchy but not the configured baselines, GuardDuty is one security service rather than a landing zone, and documentation does not enforce anything.

q: Account requests are handled by ticket and take two weeks, each needing the same baseline of trails, config, and network settings applied by hand. Which capability automates compliant account creation?
options: Manually scripting the console steps and sharing the script with requesters
Amazon WorkSpaces images preloaded with account settings
A Lambda function that creates IAM users in the management account for requesters
AWS Control Tower Account Factory (or Account Factory for Terraform) to vend accounts with the standard baseline applied automatically
explain: AWS Control Tower Account Factory (or Account Factory for Terraform) to vend accounts with the standard baseline applied automatically. Account Factory exists to provision standardized accounts through a self-service, automated pipeline with baselines baked in. The main alternatives fail because IAM users in the management account are not new accounts, desktop images do not configure accounts, and a shared manual script keeps the process hand-driven and inconsistent.

q: An account is being moved from the development OU to the production OU after a product launch, and the team is surprised its effective permissions shrink overnight. Which mechanism explains the change?
options: Control Tower randomly reassigns guardrails when accounts move
The account's billing method changes and limits its API calls
Moving an account deletes its IAM roles and recreates them with defaults
SCPs inherited from the new OU replace those from the old OU, so the account's maximum permissions now follow production OU policy
explain: SCPs inherited from the new OU replace those from the old OU, so the account's maximum permissions now follow production OU policy. An account's applicable SCPs come from its position in the hierarchy, so moving OUs changes the permission ceiling even though nothing inside the account changed. The main alternatives fail because roles are untouched by OU moves, billing does not gate permissions this way, and guardrail application follows the OU structure deterministically, not randomly.

q: Member account administrators must be unable to stop or alter the record of their own account's API activity, even with full in-account admin rights. Which logging design guarantees this?
options: CloudWatch Logs in each account with a retention policy set by its admins
An organization CloudTrail trail created from the management or delegated account, delivered to a central log archive account's bucket that member admins cannot modify
Asking administrators to export their logs to the security team monthly
A trail in each member account whose settings only that account controls
explain: An organization CloudTrail trail created from the management or delegated account, delivered to a central log archive account's bucket that member admins cannot modify. Organization trails are managed outside member accounts and write to a bucket in a separate log archive account, putting both configuration and evidence beyond member admin reach. The main alternatives fail because account-local trails and logs remain under the control of the very administrators being watched, and monthly exports can be filtered before sending.

q: A security team wants one place to query whether encryption and logging rules are being met across 200 accounts and all Regions. Which Config deployment provides that single view?
options: CloudTrail Lake queries joining each account's trails by hand
A Config recorder in the management account only, since it sees all accounts
An AWS Config aggregator in the security account collecting configuration and rule results from all accounts and Regions
Separate Config consoles per account reviewed in a weekly rotation
explain: An AWS Config aggregator in the security account collecting configuration and rule results from all accounts and Regions. Aggregators are Config's cross-account, cross-Region collection mechanism, rolling recorders' data and compliance results into one queryable view. The main alternatives fail because the management account's recorder sees only its own resources, per-account review does not scale or centralize, and trails record API calls rather than resource configuration state.

q: Threat detection must be switched on for every current and future account without each team remembering to enable it, and findings must roll up centrally. Which GuardDuty deployment pattern achieves this?
options: Email each account owner instructions to enable GuardDuty themselves
Designate a delegated administrator account and configure GuardDuty organization-wide auto-enable for all existing and new member accounts
Enable GuardDuty only in the management account and rely on its visibility
Install a GuardDuty agent on every EC2 instance in the organization
explain: Designate a delegated administrator account and configure GuardDuty organization-wide auto-enable for all existing and new member accounts. GuardDuty's organization support with a delegated admin and auto-enable turns the detector on everywhere, including future accounts, with findings aggregated centrally. The main alternatives fail because manual enablement drifts and misses new accounts, the management account sees only its own detector's findings, and GuardDuty is agentless, so there is no per-instance agent to install.

q: The SOC wants to store security logs from many AWS services in one normalized format it can query for years and share selectively with analytics tools. Which service is purpose-built for this?
options: Amazon Security Lake, centralizing logs in OCSF format in S3 with subscriber access for analytics tools
Amazon OpenSearch domains per account holding raw logs
AWS CloudTrail event history retained in each account
Amazon Macie repositories organized by log source
explain: Amazon Security Lake, centralizing logs in OCSF format in S3 with subscriber access for analytics tools. Security Lake collects, normalizes to OCSF, and centrally stores security data with managed subscriber access, which matches the long-term queryable lake requirement. The main alternatives fail because Macie discovers sensitive data, event history is short-lived per-account API records, and per-account search domains fragment the central lake the SOC asked for.

q: Security findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config arrive in different consoles per account, and leadership wants one prioritized cross-account security posture view. Which service provides it?
options: Amazon Detective graphs linked manually by analysts
AWS Security Hub CSPM aggregating findings across accounts and Regions against enabled security standards
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards plotting finding counts per service
AWS Trusted Advisor checks exported nightly to a spreadsheet
explain: AWS Security Hub CSPM aggregating findings across accounts and Regions against enabled security standards. Security Hub CSPM is the central findings and posture service, ingesting partner and AWS findings and scoring them against standards like CIS and the Foundational Security Best Practices. The main alternatives fail because dashboards and spreadsheets count findings without posture scoring or workflow, and Detective investigates entities rather than aggregating organization posture.

q: Application logs from forty member accounts must be searchable in the security account within minutes without giving the security team login access to each account. Which CloudWatch Logs pattern delivers this?
options: Grant the security team root access to each member account for log viewing
Replicate each account's log groups manually after incidents
Cross-account log sharing with subscription filters in member accounts streaming to a destination (such as Kinesis or a central log group) owned by the security account
Schedule nightly exports of each account's log groups to the owners' email
explain: Cross-account log sharing with subscription filters in member accounts streaming to a destination (such as Kinesis or a central log group) owned by the security account. CloudWatch Logs supports cross-account subscriptions and sharing, streaming member-account logs to a central destination in near real time. The main alternatives fail because root access violates least privilege and account isolation, nightly email exports are neither timely nor searchable, and manual replication after incidents loses the live view required.

q: A central network account owns a Transit Gateway that twenty application accounts must attach their VPCs to, without the network team creating resources in each account. Which sharing mechanism distributes the gateway?
options: Use VPC peering exports to publish the gateway route tables
AWS Resource Access Manager sharing the Transit Gateway to the organization or specific accounts, which can then create attachments
Create the gateway in the management account where sharing is automatic
Email the Transit Gateway ID to teams so they can reference it in their policies
explain: AWS Resource Access Manager sharing the Transit Gateway to the organization or specific accounts, which can then create attachments. RAM is the service for sharing resources like Transit Gateways across accounts, after which recipient accounts manage their own attachments. The main alternatives fail because an ID alone does not authorize use of another account's resource, management-account placement does not auto-share resources, and peering is a different connectivity construct.

q: A shared services VPC's subnets must host workloads from several application accounts while IP addressing stays centrally managed. Which pattern is designed for this?
options: Share the VPC subnets with the application accounts using AWS RAM so they launch resources into centrally owned subnets
Create duplicate subnets with the same CIDRs in each account
Peer each application VPC and renumber them to match the shared ranges
Give each application account the network admin's access keys for the shared VPC
explain: Share the VPC subnets with the application accounts using AWS RAM so they launch resources into centrally owned subnets. RAM subnet sharing lets other accounts run resources in subnets the network account owns, preserving central IP management. The main alternatives fail because shared admin keys break account boundaries, peering does not share subnets, and duplicate CIDRs create overlapping, unroutable designs.

q: A company operating in the US and EU wants to technically prevent any account from creating resources in Asian Regions, not just discourage it. Which preventive control enforces this?
options: An SCP denying actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not one of the approved US and EU Regions, applied at the organization root or OU
A tag policy requiring a region-purpose tag on every resource
A Config rule that reports resources created in unapproved Regions
A CloudWatch alarm that fires when an API call names an Asian Region
explain: An SCP denying actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not one of the approved US and EU Regions, applied at the organization root or OU. SCPs are preventive: the region condition denies the creation call itself, organization-wide, before any resource exists. The main alternatives fail because Config rules and alarms are detective and react after creation, and tag policies govern tag consistency rather than where resources may be created.

q: An attacker with stolen member-account admin credentials disabled CloudTrail and GuardDuty before acting, in an account where the security team believed this was impossible. Which guardrail should have prevented the disabling itself?
options: A Config rule checking hourly whether trails are still enabled
An IAM policy in the account asking administrators not to disable logging
A CloudWatch alarm on the absence of GuardDuty findings
An SCP denying cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and GuardDuty detector deletion/disable actions for member accounts
explain: An SCP denying cloudtrail:StopLogging, cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, and GuardDuty detector deletion/disable actions for member accounts. Only a preventive SCP sits above the member account's own administrators and can deny the disabling actions outright. The main alternatives fail because hourly checks and absence alarms detect the gap after it opens, and an in-account policy can be edited by the same compromised administrator.

q: A developer with an administrator policy in a sandbox account still cannot call certain services, and suspects their IAM policy is broken. Their policy is fine. Which layer is actually capping them?
options: The organization's root account has MFA enabled, filtering API calls
The account's service quotas for those services are set to zero
A permissions boundary on the developer role that nobody documented
The SCP applied to the sandbox OU sets the maximum permissions for the account, and IAM allows cannot exceed it
explain: The SCP applied to the sandbox OU sets the maximum permissions for the account, and IAM allows cannot exceed it. Effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP ceiling and identity policies, so an SCP that omits a service blocks it despite a full in-account allow. The main alternatives fail because quotas limit usage volumes rather than authorization, a boundary is possible but the scenario states the policy layer in question is organizational, and MFA on the root does not filter member API calls.

q: Leadership wants a guardrail that applies to resources in member accounts even against principals coming from outside the organization, expressing what resources may allow rather than what internal identities may do. Which policy type serves this resource-side purpose?
options: Tag policies, which standardize tags on resources across accounts
Session policies passed when external principals assume roles
Service control policies, which filter what member-account principals can request
Resource control policies (RCPs), which set the maximum permissions resources in member accounts can grant, including to external principals
explain: Resource control policies (RCPs), which set the maximum permissions resources in member accounts can grant, including to external principals. RCPs are the resource-side counterpart to SCPs: they cap what resource policies in member accounts can permit, which is exactly the external-access perimeter leadership described. The main alternatives fail because SCPs govern internal principals' requests and do not bind external ones, tag policies govern tags, and session policies belong to sessions the organization does not control for external callers.

q: A compliance standard requires every S3 bucket to have server-side encryption, and the team wants violations fixed automatically, not just reported. Which Config pattern delivers remediation?
options: A managed Config rule for S3 default encryption with automatic remediation using an SSM Automation document that enables encryption
A GuardDuty finding routed to a chat channel for manual fixing
A weekly Lambda that lists buckets and emails their owners
A Security Hub custom action that an analyst clicks per finding
explain: A managed Config rule for S3 default encryption with automatic remediation using an SSM Automation document that enables encryption. Config rules support attaching remediation actions, including automatic execution of SSM documents when a resource is noncompliant. The main alternatives fail because chat notifications and emails depend on humans for every fix, and Security Hub custom actions are analyst-triggered rather than automatic on evaluation.

q: The CISO wants CIS AWS Foundations and the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices evaluated continuously in every account from one console. Which Security Hub capability should be enabled organization-wide?
options: CloudWatch Synthetics canaries probing each control hourly
Security Hub CSPM standards with organization configuration from the delegated administrator, aggregating control results centrally
Amazon Inspector benchmark scans run on the management account
AWS Audit Manager assessments scheduled quarterly per account
explain: Security Hub CSPM standards with organization configuration from the delegated administrator, aggregating control results centrally. Security Hub standards are its continuous control-evaluation framework, and organization configuration deploys them consistently with central aggregation. The main alternatives fail because the scope names Security Hub CSPM for this function rather than periodic assessments, Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities rather than account configuration controls, and canaries test application endpoints.

q: Container images pushed to ECR and Lambda functions deployed across accounts must be vulnerability-scanned continuously without each team configuring scanners. Which Inspector deployment achieves this?
options: A third-party scanner appliance deployed in the shared services VPC
Amazon Inspector with a delegated administrator auto-enabling EC2, ECR, and Lambda scanning for all organization accounts
GuardDuty Malware Protection scheduled scans of ECR repositories
Developers running image scans locally before every push as a manual step
explain: Amazon Inspector with a delegated administrator auto-enabling EC2, ECR, and Lambda scanning for all organization accounts. Inspector's organization support auto-enables its scan types across accounts from a delegated admin, covering instances, container images, and Lambda functions continuously. The main alternatives fail because appliances and manual local scans leave coverage to individual teams, and GuardDuty malware scanning is a different detection purpose from Inspector's vulnerability management.

q: Servers across sixty accounts miss critical OS patches for months because each team patches on its own schedule, and auditors want one compliance view. Which Systems Manager design centralizes this?
options: Distributing patch files from a central S3 bucket for teams to apply manually
Amazon Inspector findings alone, exported to each team's backlog
A wiki schedule assigning each team a patching weekend per quarter
Patch Manager with organization-wide patch baselines and maintenance windows via Quick Setup or delegated administration, reporting compliance centrally
explain: Patch Manager with organization-wide patch baselines and maintenance windows via Quick Setup or delegated administration, reporting compliance centrally. Patch Manager defines baselines, approval rules, and maintenance windows and rolls compliance up across accounts, replacing per-team improvisation. The main alternatives fail because schedules and file shares keep execution manual and unverifiable, and Inspector identifies missing patches but does not apply or orchestrate them.

q: Generative AI usage is expanding and governance requires records of which models were invoked, by whom, with prompts and responses retained centrally for review. Which logging arrangement meets this AI governance requirement?
options: Record model names only in monthly billing reports
Ask users to save transcripts of sensitive AI sessions themselves
Rely on each application team's own debug logs of their prompts
Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs and S3, centralized in the log archive account with the organization's retention policy
explain: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs and S3, centralized in the log archive account with the organization's retention policy. Bedrock invocation logging is the service-native audit trail for model usage, and routing it to central log storage puts AI evidence under the same governance as other logs. The main alternatives fail because application debug logs are inconsistent and outside central control, billing shows cost rather than invocation content, and self-saved transcripts are unverifiable.

q: After an incident, an account is quarantined: it must keep its data for forensics but be unable to run workloads, change network settings, or reach other accounts. Which immediate OU-level action enforces quarantine?
options: Change the account's root password and wait for sessions to expire
Move the account to a quarantine OU whose SCP denies nearly all actions except those the forensic role needs
Remove the account from the organization so it is unmanaged
Delete the account's VPCs from the management account console
explain: Move the account to a quarantine OU whose SCP denies nearly all actions except those the forensic role needs. A deny-heavy SCP on a quarantine OU instantly caps everything the account's principals can do while preserving the account and its evidence. The main alternatives fail because the management account cannot reach into member VPCs directly, password changes do not stop existing role sessions or service activity, and removing the account surrenders the very controls needed to govern it.

q: A company wants new accounts to arrive with not just logging but also its standard VPC, baseline IAM, and Identity Center assignments ready on day one. Which Account Factory feature assembles these extras?
options: The Organizations console's notes field documenting the extras
CloudTrail organization trails, which create VPCs when accounts join
GuardDuty auto-enable, which provisions network resources for new accounts
Account Factory account customizations (blueprints/provisioned products) that deploy the standard VPC, roles, and assignments as part of vending
explain: Account Factory account customizations (blueprints/provisioned products) that deploy the standard VPC, roles, and assignments as part of vending. Account Factory supports customization blueprints that layer the organization's standard resources onto each vended account automatically. The main alternatives fail because notes document nothing enforceable, GuardDuty only enables threat detection, and trails record activity rather than provisioning network or identity resources.

q: Control Tower reports drift in a member account after a team manually changed a guardrail-managed setting. What does drift detection give the governance team?
options: Proof that the change was malicious rather than accidental
Visibility that the account's configuration no longer matches the landing zone baseline, so they can investigate and remediate or reapply controls
A bill credit for the period the account was drifted
Automatic deletion of the account to restore compliance
explain: Visibility that the account's configuration no longer matches the landing zone baseline, so they can investigate and remediate or reapply controls. Control Tower detects and reports drift from its managed baseline, surfacing accounts whose guardrails or configurations were altered out of band. The main alternatives fail because drift is reported, not punished by deletion or compensated, and detection alone does not establish the intent behind a change.

q: Policy requires that no one, including developers with local admin rights, can create long-lived IAM users in workload accounts; all human access must be federated. Which preventive control enforces this organization-wide?
options: An SCP denying iam:CreateUser and iam:CreateAccessKey in workload OUs
An IAM password policy with maximum complexity requirements
A Security Hub control that scores accounts with IAM users lower
A Config rule that deletes IAM users it discovers each hour
explain: An SCP denying iam:CreateUser and iam:CreateAccessKey in workload OUs. An SCP blocks the creation actions themselves for every principal in scope, including local administrators, which detective controls cannot do. The main alternatives fail because hourly deletion leaves windows of usable credentials, password policy governs the users once created rather than preventing them, and scoring reports posture without blocking creation.

q: Findings in Security Hub repeat for months on accepted risks, drowning out new issues, and analysts want those specific findings suppressed with an expiry and a reason. Which Security Hub mechanism handles accepted-risk findings properly?
options: Deleting the findings from the underlying services so they stop arriving
Asking GuardDuty and Inspector to lower their severity for the account
Exporting findings to S3 and filtering them in the reporting spreadsheet only
Automation rules or suppression via workflow status that mark matching findings as suppressed with documented justification
explain: Automation rules or suppression via workflow status that mark matching findings as suppressed with documented justification. Security Hub supports suppressing findings matching criteria with a documented reason, keeping them out of active views while preserving the record. The main alternatives fail because deleting source findings destroys evidence and they regenerate, source severities are not customer-tunable that way, and spreadsheet filtering leaves the operational console still flooded.

q: GuardDuty findings must also be retained as raw evidence in the security account's S3 bucket for seven years, beyond the console's retention. Which GuardDuty feature provides this export?
options: Enable CloudTrail data events for the GuardDuty console
Configure the detector's finding export (publishing destination) to the central S3 bucket from the delegated administrator design
Copy findings manually from each member account's console
Screenshot high-severity findings into the evidence folder weekly
explain: Configure the detector's finding export (publishing destination) to the central S3 bucket from the delegated administrator design. GuardDuty supports exporting findings to an S3 publishing destination, which the delegated admin arrangement centralizes for the organization. The main alternatives fail because screenshots and manual copying are incomplete and unscalable, and CloudTrail records API calls, not the findings content needing retention.

q: The central trail bucket must accept writes only from the organization's trails and resist tampering by any single account's administrators. Which bucket design enforces this?
options: A bucket in the log archive account whose policy allows writes only from the organization trail's service principal and account set, combined with restrictive ownership of the archive account
A bucket per member account cross-replicated to the archive account nightly
A bucket in the management account with public-read disabled as the only control
A bucket protected only by enabling versioning and MFA Delete
explain: A bucket in the log archive account whose policy allows writes only from the organization trail's service principal and account set, combined with restrictive ownership of the archive account. Putting the bucket in a dedicated archive account under a policy scoped to the organization trail keeps both the data and its controls outside member accounts' reach. The main alternatives fail because the management account should not host workload-adjacent data stores, replication from member-controlled buckets lets tampering happen at the source, and versioning alone does not restrict who may write.

q: All VPC flow logs across the organization must land in one place for network forensics without each account inventing its own format and destination. Which centralized design should be standardized?
options: Let each team choose any destination and reconcile during incidents
Enable flow logs only on the Transit Gateway and skip VPC-level logging
Store flow logs on the instances themselves in local files
Deliver flow logs to the central log archive (S3 or Security Lake via its log collection) from every account under an organization-standard configuration
explain: Deliver flow logs to the central log archive (S3 or Security Lake via its log collection) from every account under an organization-standard configuration. Organization-standard delivery to the central archive (directly or through Security Lake) gives forensics one complete, consistently formatted source. The main alternatives fail because Transit Gateway logs do not replace per-VPC visibility, per-team choices recreate fragmentation, and instance-local files disappear with instances and are unreachable centrally.

q: Config remediation for a failed encryption rule must run in member accounts from a central design, including assuming an execution role in each account. Which pattern makes central remediation work?
options: Run remediation from the management account's own credentials directly in member accounts
Deploy a remediation role in each member account (via StackSets or Account Factory baseline) that the central SSM Automation configuration is authorized to assume
Give the Config service the member accounts' root credentials
Disable remediation in member accounts and fix findings from the aggregator console
explain: Deploy a remediation role in each member account (via StackSets or Account Factory baseline) that the central SSM Automation configuration is authorized to assume. Cross-account automation requires a target-account role to assume; baselining that role into every account is what makes organization-wide remediation possible. The main alternatives fail because management credentials do not automatically operate inside member accounts, root credentials must never be distributed, and the aggregator is a read view that cannot itself change member resources.

q: Patch compliance for hybrid on-premises servers must appear in the same Patch Manager view as EC2 instances. Which Systems Manager capability brings hybrid machines under management?
options: Give the servers IAM users so Patch Manager can see them
Register the servers as managed hybrid instances (activations) so Patch Manager baselines and compliance apply to them
Add the servers as targets in a Config rule for patching
Install the CloudWatch agent and treat log data as patch compliance
explain: Register the servers as managed hybrid instances (activations) so Patch Manager baselines and compliance apply to them. SSM hybrid activations enroll non-EC2 machines as managed instances, after which patch baselines, windows, and compliance reporting treat them like instances. The main alternatives fail because log collection is not patch management, Config rules evaluate AWS resources rather than enrolling machines, and IAM users are identities for people or applications, not managed-node enrollment.

q: A new Region's findings never appear in the security team's Security Hub view even though member accounts there show findings locally. Which aggregation setting is the likely gap?
options: Security Hub only aggregates the home Region by design
Member accounts must email findings from new Regions to the admin
The new Region needs its own separate Security Hub organization
Finding aggregation must include that Region in the aggregation configuration (linked Regions) for the administrator account
explain: Finding aggregation must include that Region in the aggregation configuration (linked Regions) for the administrator account. Cross-Region aggregation is configurable: Regions must be linked into the aggregation region before their findings roll up. The main alternatives fail because aggregation is automatic once configured, not email-based, multi-Region aggregation is a core feature rather than a home-Region limit, and one organization uses one administrator aggregation design.

q: An organization wants its Transit Gateway route design to enforce that development VPCs can never route to production VPCs, while both reach shared services. Which central network design enforces this segmentation?
options: Separate Transit Gateway route tables: associate development and production attachments with different route tables that propagate only the routes each segment is allowed
A single route table for all attachments with careful engineer discipline
Security groups in each VPC referencing the other segment's groups
NACLs on the shared services subnets listing every VPC CIDR
explain: Separate Transit Gateway route tables: associate development and production attachments with different route tables that propagate only the routes each segment is allowed. Transit Gateway route tables are the segmentation control for TGW routing domains, isolating segments by which routes their attachments can learn. The main alternatives fail because security groups filter traffic instance-to-instance but do not define TGW routing domains, one shared table with discipline is the unenforced design being replaced, and NACLs cannot substitute for route separation across dozens of VPCs.

q: RAM sharing with the whole organization is desired for shared resources, but a newly created account's resources were shared outside unexpectedly because sharing defaults were misunderstood. Which RAM organization setting governs this behavior?
options: The organization's SCP named ram:EnableSharing must be edited per share
CloudFormation StackSets automatically share every created resource
Enabling sharing with AWS Organizations in RAM settings, which should be deliberate and paired with SCPs, since it allows resource shares with the organization without per-account acceptance
RAM shares always require the management account's password approval
explain: Enabling sharing with AWS Organizations in RAM settings, which should be deliberate and paired with SCPs, since it allows resource shares with the organization without per-account acceptance. RAM's organization-sharing setting is the switch that lets shares target the organization; governance comes from enabling it intentionally and constraining it with policy. The main alternatives fail because no per-share SCP edit or password approval exists in RAM's model, and StackSets deploy resources but do not share them by themselves.

q: A subordinate Private CA in the security account must be usable by workload accounts to issue their own service certificates without accessing the CA account. Which sharing mechanism distributes certificate authority usage?
options: Give workload teams the CA account's console credentials for issuance days
Create a separate root CA in every workload account
Share the subordinate CA with the workload accounts using AWS RAM so their ACM can issue certificates from it
Export the CA's private key to each workload account's KMS
explain: Share the subordinate CA with the workload accounts using AWS RAM so their ACM can issue certificates from it. ACM Private CA supports RAM sharing of a CA, letting other accounts issue certificates through ACM while the CA and its key stay in the owning account. The main alternatives fail because shared console credentials and exported CA keys both surrender the central control the design protects, and per-account roots fragment the trust hierarchy.

q: An RCP is written to cap S3 resource policies, but the team is puzzled that it has no effect on activity in the management account. Which fact explains this?
options: The management account needs an SCP with the same name to activate the RCP
RCPs apply to member accounts only; they do not apply to resources in the management account
RCPs apply only after the next billing cycle closes
RCPs must be attached twice before they take effect anywhere
explain: RCPs apply to member accounts only; they do not apply to resources in the management account. By design, resource control policies govern member accounts and exclude the management account, which is one reason workloads should not run there. The main alternatives fail because attachment count, naming, and billing cycles have no role in RCP applicability; the management-account exclusion is structural.

q: A bank's sandbox OU should be experimental but must never reach production data or spend without limit, and its SCP is being drafted. Which SCP posture fits a sandbox OU?
options: Allow broad service experimentation but deny access to production accounts' resources and deny the most expensive or risky actions, with the account isolated from production networks
Apply the production OU's SCP unchanged so behavior is identical
Deny every action except console sign-in for safety
Give the sandbox no SCP at all so experiments are unconstrained
explain: Allow broad service experimentation but deny access to production accounts' resources and deny the most expensive or risky actions, with the account isolated from production networks. Sandbox governance balances freedom inside the boundary with hard denies at the boundary: production data, production reachability, and runaway actions. The main alternatives fail because identical-to-production policy defeats the sandbox's purpose, no policy leaves production exposed through a weak account, and deny-all makes the sandbox useless.

q: Security Lake subscribers in the SOC's analytics platform need query access to the lake's S3 data without the platform team handing out bucket credentials. Which Security Lake mechanism grants subscriber access?
options: Give the analytics platform the log archive account's root access
Copy the lake data nightly into the analytics account's own bucket
Make the Security Lake bucket public to authenticated AWS users
Register the analytics tool as a Security Lake subscriber, which provisions managed access (via Lake Formation) to the specified data sources
explain: Register the analytics tool as a Security Lake subscriber, which provisions managed access (via Lake Formation) to the specified data sources. Subscribers are Security Lake's governed access path, receiving scoped, managed permissions to the log types they are entitled to query. The main alternatives fail because public buckets and root access abandon access control, and nightly copies fork the data and its governance away from the lake.

q: GuardDuty's newer protections must cover S3 buckets being used as malware staging and EBS volumes on compromised instances, organization-wide. Which enablement covers these?
options: Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 and EBS (and related protection plans) from the delegated administrator for all accounts
Schedule Inspector scans of the S3 buckets weekly
Turn on Macie sensitive data discovery for the staging buckets
Enable Security Hub's malware standard and wait for findings
explain: Enable GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 and EBS (and related protection plans) from the delegated administrator for all accounts. GuardDuty's malware protection plans are the service's mechanism for scanning S3 objects and EBS volumes for malware across the organization. The main alternatives fail because Macie classifies sensitive data rather than malware, Inspector does not scan S3 buckets for malware, and Security Hub aggregates findings but provides no scanning itself.

q: A compliance dashboard must answer, for any control, which accounts are noncompliant right now, using Config data rather than screenshots. Which capability should the dashboard query?
options: CloudTrail event history filtered to configuration change events
Each account's Trusted Advisor PDF exports merged by a script
The Config aggregator's compliance data (aggregate rule compliance and advanced queries) in the security account
Billing reports tagged by compliance status
explain: The Config aggregator's compliance data (aggregate rule compliance and advanced queries) in the security account. Aggregators exist precisely to answer cross-account compliance questions centrally, exposing rule results and resource configuration for query. The main alternatives fail because event history shows changes rather than current compliance state, PDF merging is the screenshot-era process being replaced, and billing data carries no compliance signal.

q: Audit logs must be provably untampered for seven years, with even the archive account's administrators unable to rewrite history during the retention period. Which storage control provides this guarantee?
options: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log archive bucket with a seven-year retention period
A lifecycle rule moving logs to Glacier after ninety days
SSE-KMS encryption with a customer managed key on the bucket
Bucket versioning with MFA Delete enabled by the administrators
explain: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on the log archive bucket with a seven-year retention period. Object Lock compliance mode prevents modification or deletion by anyone, including root, until retention expires, which is the tamper-proof property required. The main alternatives fail because MFA Delete can be changed by those same administrators and versions can still be managed, encryption protects confidentiality not immutability, and lifecycle tiering changes storage class, not writability.

q: A team keeps creating accounts directly in Organizations, bypassing Account Factory, so the accounts miss baselines and show up in audits as unmanaged. Which governance response closes the bypass?
options: Delete stray accounts immediately without investigating their contents
Rename the bypassed accounts so auditors overlook them
Restrict account creation to the Account Factory pipeline by denying organizations:CreateAccount outside the factory's role/principal, and detect strays with Control Tower and Config
Move stray accounts into the production OU to inherit its controls
explain: Restrict account creation to the Account Factory pipeline by denying organizations:CreateAccount outside the factory's role/principal, and detect strays with Control Tower and Config. Preventing creation outside the vending path is the only durable fix; detection handles the transition period and any exceptions. The main alternatives fail because renaming hides rather than fixes the gap, blind deletion can destroy evidence or workloads, and an OU move applies SCPs but not the missing logging and baseline resources.

q: Patch Manager baselines differ per OS and criticality, and a web server fleet keeps receiving a database fleet's patch approvals. Which Patch Manager construct was likely misassigned?
options: The S3 output bucket for patch logs is shared between fleets
The Patch Manager service role has both fleets' permissions
The maintenance window's time zone differs between the fleets
Patch groups and their baseline associations: the fleets' instances carry the wrong patch group tag, so they evaluate against the wrong baseline
explain: Patch groups and their baseline associations: the fleets' instances carry the wrong patch group tag, so they evaluate against the wrong baseline. Instances select baselines through patch group tags, so a wrong group assignment directly explains a fleet receiving another fleet's approvals. The main alternatives fail because time zones shift timing not baseline selection, shared log buckets do not change approvals, and the service role's breadth does not decide which baseline an instance evaluates.

q: Accepted vulnerabilities in a legacy image need to stop paging the team while a migration completes, without hiding genuinely new findings. Which Inspector feature handles this?
options: Inspector suppression rules matching the specific finding criteria, with the accepted risk documented
Lowering the image's scan frequency to monthly
Asking the registry to mark the image as compliant
Turning off Inspector for the account until migration finishes
explain: Inspector suppression rules matching the specific finding criteria, with the accepted risk documented. Suppression rules filter defined findings from active views while scanning continues, so new findings still surface. The main alternatives fail because disabling scanning blinds the account entirely, slower scans delay new findings rather than filtering known ones, and registries do not decide compliance status.

q: Before a new workload deploys, governance wants its CloudFormation templates checked so resources violating encryption and logging standards never launch. Which Control Tower capability provides this pre-provision check?
options: A post-deployment Lambda that deletes noncompliant resources
An SCP that inspects template contents at deploy time
Proactive guardrails in Control Tower, evaluating templates with rules (CloudFormation Guard) before resources are provisioned
Detective guardrails that report violations in the console weekly
explain: Proactive guardrails in Control Tower, evaluating templates with rules (CloudFormation Guard) before resources are provisioned. Proactive controls evaluate infrastructure code before provisioning, blocking noncompliant resources at deployment time rather than after. The main alternatives fail because detective guardrails and post-deployment cleanup both act after resources exist, and SCPs evaluate API actions and parameters, not template semantics.

q: The management account currently hosts a reporting application because it was convenient when the organization was small. Which governance principle does this violate, and what is the fix?
options: Organizations require the management account to run at least one workload for billing
The management account should host no workloads; move the application to a member account and reserve the management account for organization management
The application is safe because the management account cannot be suspended
The fix is to add an SCP to the management account restricting the application
explain: The management account should host no workloads; move the application to a member account and reserve the management account for organization management. The management account holds organization-wide power, so running workloads there exposes that power to application risk; workloads belong in member accounts. The main alternatives fail because no workload is required for billing, SCPs do not apply to the management account in the way the fix assumes, and its unsuspendable nature increases rather than decreases the stakes.

q: Findings from a new account take days to reach the central Security Hub view because the account joined the organization before delegated administration was configured. Which step enrolls such existing accounts centrally?
options: From the Security Hub administrator account, invite or auto-associate existing member accounts (organization configuration with auto-enable and member association) so their findings aggregate
Create a second Security Hub administrator in the new account
Wait for the next monthly organization sync to include them
Ask the new account to forward findings by email until then
explain: From the Security Hub administrator account, invite or auto-associate existing member accounts (organization configuration with auto-enable and member association) so their findings aggregate. Security Hub organization configuration can auto-enable and associate member accounts, including existing ones, from the delegated administrator. The main alternatives fail because there is no monthly sync that fixes unassociated accounts, email forwarding is not aggregation, and each organization designates its administrator centrally rather than per new account.

q: A central logging design must include CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, and Bedrock invocation logs under one retention and access regime. Which destination strategy unifies them?
options: Send all logs to the management account's default event history
Print monthly log summaries to PDF for the compliance library
Route all three log types to the log archive account (S3 and/or Security Lake and central CloudWatch Logs) with common retention, encryption, and access policies
Keep each log type in the account that produced it under local policies
explain: Route all three log types to the log archive account (S3 and/or Security Lake and central CloudWatch Logs) with common retention, encryption, and access policies. Centralizing the destinations in the archive account is what allows one retention, encryption, and access regime to govern every log type. The main alternatives fail because local retention fragments the regime by account, event history is short-term and not an archive, and PDF summaries are derivatives, not the logs themselves.

q: An SCP intended to deny a dangerous action works in most OUs but not in one OU where a child OU shows unexpected allows. Which SCP evaluation fact explains how to fix the layering?
options: SCPs stop applying after three levels of OU nesting

SCPs from every level of the hierarchy (root, parent OU, child OU, account) combine, and the action must be allowed at every level; a deny or missing allow at any level blocks it, so the fix is to align the filters at each level
Only the SCP closest to the account matters, so edit that one alone
Child OU SCPs override parent SCPs like CSS rules
explain: SCPs from every level of the hierarchy (root, parent OU, child OU, account) combine, and the action must be allowed at every level; a deny or missing allow at any level blocks it, so the fix is to align the filters at each level. SCP evaluation is cumulative down the hierarchy: every level acts as a filter, and the effective ceiling is their intersection. The main alternatives fail because no single level decides on its own, there is no override semantics between levels, and nesting depth does not switch SCPs off.

q: A shared Transit Gateway design must let a new application account create its VPC attachment without the network team performing each attachment manually. After RAM sharing, what else must the design include?
options: RAM sharing alone creates attachments automatically in every account
The application account must be given the network account's admin role
The gateway must be recreated each time an account joins
The Transit Gateway's auto-accept setting for shared attachments (or an approval workflow in the network account) plus route table association guidance for the new attachment
explain: The Transit Gateway's auto-accept setting for shared attachments (or an approval workflow in the network account) plus route table association guidance for the new attachment. RAM sharing authorizes use, but attachments from other accounts still need acceptance, which auto-accept provides for trusted organization shares. The main alternatives fail because handing out the network admin role defeats the self-service boundary, sharing does not create attachments by itself, and gateways are long-lived shared resources, not per-account recreations.

q: A detective control must catch any public S3 bucket in any account within minutes and open a ticket with the owning team's queue. Which event-driven design delivers this?
options: A monthly Access Analyzer report reviewed by the governance board
A CloudWatch alarm on total bucket count in the organization
An annual survey asking teams whether they own public buckets
Config rule or Security Hub finding events routed through EventBridge to the ticketing integration, filtered to the owning account's team
explain: Config rule or Security Hub finding events routed through EventBridge to the ticketing integration, filtered to the owning account's team. Config and Security Hub emit findings as events, and EventBridge routing turns a new public-bucket finding into a ticket in near real time. The main alternatives fail because monthly reports and annual surveys are far slower than the minutes required, and bucket-count alarms cannot identify which bucket became public.

q: A firm enables Security Hub in a new aggregation Region and finds duplicate findings for the same issue arriving from two Regions. Which aggregation behavior should be configured to consolidate them?
options: Export both Regions' findings to separate spreadsheets
Disable Security Hub in one of the Regions permanently
Use Security Hub finding aggregation with linked Regions so duplicate findings across Regions are consolidated in the aggregation Region view
Accept duplicates and double the team's triage staffing
explain: Use Security Hub finding aggregation with linked Regions so duplicate findings across Regions are consolidated in the aggregation Region view. Finding aggregation is designed to link Regions and present consolidated findings centrally instead of per-Region duplicates. The main alternatives fail because disabling a Region loses its coverage, spreadsheet exports abandon the console workflow, and staffing around duplicates treats a configuration feature as a people problem.

q: Patch operations for instances without internet access fail because Patch Manager cannot reach Systems Manager endpoints from private subnets. Which network fix aligns with the shared-network design?
options: Store patches on a USB-attached EBS volume for each instance
Give the instances public IP addresses during patch windows
Disable Patch Manager and patch from local administrator laptops
Create VPC interface endpoints for Systems Manager (ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages) in the shared or local VPC so patch operations stay on private connectivity
explain: Create VPC interface endpoints for Systems Manager (ssm, ssmmessages, ec2messages) in the shared or local VPC so patch operations stay on private connectivity. Systems Manager operations from private subnets require the relevant VPC endpoints, which is the standard private-connectivity pattern for patching. The main alternatives fail because public IPs during windows expose the fleet, physical media does not scale to a fleet, and laptop patching abandons central baselines and compliance reporting.

q: An organization wants evidence that its Detective controls are actually running in every account, not merely intended in the landing zone design. Which report best provides this evidence?
options: A survey of account owners attesting their controls are on
Screenshots of one sample account's GuardDuty console
Security Hub CSPM control results and Config aggregator compliance for the logging and monitoring rules, exported from the delegated security account
The landing zone's design document signed by the architects
explain: Security Hub CSPM control results and Config aggregator compliance for the logging and monitoring rules, exported from the delegated security account. Aggregated control results are live evidence from every account's actual configuration, unlike design intent or sampled spot checks. The main alternatives fail because documents state intent, one account's screenshot says nothing about the other accounts, and attestations are claims rather than measured state.

q: A new compliance requirement forces the organization trail to also capture data events for sensitive S3 buckets and Lambda invocations, centrally. Which trail change implements this without losing management-event coverage?
options: Edit the organization trail's event selectors to add the specified data event types while keeping management events enabled, so all accounts inherit the change
Create a second trail in each member account for data events
Enable data events only in the management account's own trail
Turn on S3 server access logging and treat it as the trail
explain: Edit the organization trail's event selectors to add the specified data event types while keeping management events enabled, so all accounts inherit the change. Organization trail settings propagate to all member accounts, so changing its selectors centrally extends data-event capture everywhere at once. The main alternatives fail because per-account trails fragment the central design, management-only capture misses member activity, and S3 access logs are a separate, less complete record than CloudTrail data events.

q: A team wants GuardDuty, Security Hub, and Inspector all governed from the security account rather than the management account. Which delegation pattern is correct?
options: Register the security account as the delegated administrator for each service from the management account, then configure organization settings from there
Move the organization management role into the security account permanently
Give the security team the management account's root credentials
Create duplicate organizations administered by each team
explain: Register the security account as the delegated administrator for each service from the management account, then configure organization settings from there. Delegated administration is the supported pattern: the management account designates the security account, which then runs each service's organization features. The main alternatives fail because management responsibilities cannot be transferred wholesale to a member account, root credential sharing is prohibited practice, and duplicate organizations split the estate being governed.

q: CloudWatch Logs from member accounts contain customer identifiers that must not be visible to the central operations team, yet the logs must still be centralized. Which design reconciles centralization with data minimization?
options: Apply data protection/redaction at the source log groups (such as CloudWatch Logs data protection policies) before cross-account subscription delivers them centrally
Encrypt the central logs with a key the operations team also holds
Stop centralizing logs from any account that handles customers
Give the operations team access but ask them not to look at identifiers
explain: Apply data protection/redaction at the source log groups (such as CloudWatch Logs data protection policies) before cross-account subscription delivers them centrally. Redacting sensitive data at the source lets the central stream remain useful for operations without carrying identifiers the central team has no need to see. The main alternatives fail because abandoning centralization loses the governance benefit, requests are not controls, and encryption the readers can decrypt does not hide content from them.

q: An SCP blocks a needed deployment action in production, and the team proposes editing the production OU's SCP during the incident and reverting it later. Which safer governance pattern should replace this habit?
options: Route the exception through a break-glass change: a time-boxed SCP change approved and logged as an exception, or a dedicated deployment OU/role design that anticipates the action
Let each account opt out of SCPs by tag during incidents
Disable all SCPs organization-wide during incidents
Give the incident commander the management account root login
explain: Route the exception through a break-glass change: a time-boxed SCP change approved and logged as an exception, or a dedicated deployment OU/role design that anticipates the action. SCP changes are organization-risk events; treating exceptions as approved, time-boxed, and recorded preserves the guardrail's integrity under pressure. The main alternatives fail because root logins and organization-wide disabling remove every protection at the moment of highest risk, and SCPs have no per-account tag opt-out mechanism.

q: A multinational's Config aggregator shows a rule as noncompliant in accounts where the underlying resource type does not exist in some Regions. Which Config behavior should the team use to keep the compliance view meaningful?
options: Delete the rule in every account to clean the dashboard

Scope rules and aggregation appropriately (resource types and Regions where they apply) and use the aggregator's compliance states rather than raw counts, so not-applicable results do not masquerade as violations
Disable Config recorders in Regions without the resource type
Count every not-applicable result as a violation for safety
explain: Scope rules and aggregation appropriately (resource types and Regions where they apply) and use the aggregator's compliance states rather than raw counts, so not-applicable results do not masquerade as violations. Meaningful compliance views come from correct rule scoping and interpreting aggregated states, not from inflating or deleting results. The main alternatives fail because deleting rules removes the control, inflating violations destroys trust in the dashboard, and disabling recorders blinds those Regions to everything else.

q: A platform team wants one Terraform-driven pipeline to vend accounts identically to the console Account Factory. Which offering is that pipeline?
options: Organizations' CreateAccount API called from a laptop script
Account Factory for Terraform (AFT), which vends and customizes accounts through Terraform with the landing zone's baselines
Control Tower drift detection run on a schedule
AWS Proton templates for account creation
explain: Account Factory for Terraform (AFT), which vends and customizes accounts through Terraform with the landing zone's baselines. AFT is the Terraform-native account vending framework integrated with Control Tower, providing the pipeline-driven equivalent of Account Factory. The main alternatives fail because raw API calls from a laptop skip baselines and governance, drift detection observes existing accounts, and Proton provisions application environments, not organization accounts.

q: A security team wants to know which member accounts have not enabled a newly required GuardDuty protection plan, without logging into each account. Which delegated-admin view answers this?
options: The GuardDuty administrator account's organization configuration and account status pages, which show detector and protection-plan status for every member account
A Macie coverage report listing unprotected accounts
The billing console's GuardDuty line items per account
Each account's CloudTrail history searched for GuardDuty calls
explain: The GuardDuty administrator account's organization configuration and account status pages, which show detector and protection-plan status for every member account. The delegated administrator sees organization-wide detector status centrally, which is the operational point of delegation. The main alternatives fail because billing shows spend rather than enablement detail, per-account trail searches abandon centralization, and Macie reports on data discovery, not GuardDuty status.

q: An organization shares a central NAT and inspection VPC, and new application accounts must route egress through it by default when vended. Which vending-time mechanism bakes this routing in?
options: An SCP that denies VPC creation so teams request networking by ticket
An Account Factory customization or StackSet baseline that creates the TGW attachment and route tables pointing egress to the central inspection VPC in every new account
A note in the runbook asking network engineers to update routes after vending
GuardDuty findings that flag accounts with direct internet egress
explain: An Account Factory customization or StackSet baseline that creates the TGW attachment and route tables pointing egress to the central inspection VPC in every new account. Baselines applied at vending time are how standard network posture is guaranteed from an account's first day.
