q: A payment platform executes two million short AWS Step Functions workflows per day, and each execution completes in under 30 seconds with no need for an auditable step-by-step history. Which change most reduces workflow cost?
options: Duplicate each execution across two Regions for durability
Replace the workflow with a single long-running EC2 instance
Switch to Standard Workflows and enable X-Ray tracing on every transition
Switch the workflow to Express Workflows and price it by number of requests and duration
explain: Express Workflows are designed for high-volume, short-duration event processing and charge by requests and duration, which is far cheaper at millions of daily executions than Standard per-transition billing at that scale. Adding tracing or multi-Region duplication raises cost, and an EC2 rewrite abandons the managed workflow benefits.

q: A data team can move a large fleet of x86 Amazon EC2 and AWS Lambda workloads to a new processor family with minimal code change and wants better price performance. Which option should the architect evaluate first?
options: Burstable instances throttled to baseline CPU at all times
Dedicated Instances on x86 hardware in a single Availability Zone
AWS Graviton-based instances and arm64 Lambda functions, which typically deliver better price performance than comparable x86 options
High-memory x86 instances sized for peak load year-round
explain: Graviton processors are AWS-designed Arm chips that commonly provide better price performance for EC2, Lambda (arm64), RDS, and other services when the software supports Arm. The other choices keep x86 pricing or add tenancy and sizing premiums without the Graviton efficiency gain.

q: An AWS Lambda function uses 1,024 MB of memory, finishes in 800 ms, and profiling shows it would finish in 200 ms at 2,048 MB because it is CPU-bound. Why might doubling memory lower total cost for this function?
options: Lambda billing depends on memory multiplied by duration, so a sufficiently large duration reduction can offset the higher memory price
Lambda charges a flat fee per invocation regardless of memory or duration
Lambda on Graviton removes all duration charges
Doubling memory always halves duration for every workload
explain: Lambda cost is proportional to allocated memory times billed duration (GB-seconds). For a CPU-bound function, more memory adds CPU proportionally and can cut duration enough to lower GB-seconds overall. The effect is workload-dependent, not automatic, and neither Graviton nor any tier makes duration free.

q: A company wants to reserve Amazon Bedrock throughput for a latency-sensitive production chatbot so inference cost and performance are predictable during peak hours. Which Bedrock purchase option fits this need?
options: Prompt caching with no throughput reservation
Provisioned Throughput for the selected foundation model, purchased for a fixed term and number of model units
On-Demand inference with no commitment and variable throttling limits
Batch inference jobs submitted once per day
explain: Provisioned Throughput reserves model units for a chosen foundation model, giving predictable throughput and term-based pricing for steady, latency-sensitive demand. On-Demand suits variable traffic, Batch suits offline jobs at a discount, and prompt caching reduces repeated-prefix cost but reserves no capacity.

q: A research team needs Amazon Bedrock to summarize 500,000 stored documents overnight, with no interactive latency requirement. Which inference mode offers the lowest cost for this job?
options: Provisioned Throughput purchased for a six-month term
Cross-Region inference routing to the busiest Region
Amazon Bedrock batch inference, which processes prompts asynchronously at a discount to On-Demand pricing
On-Demand inference called synchronously document by document
explain: Bedrock batch inference is built for large offline jobs and is priced below On-Demand because AWS can schedule the work efficiently. Provisioned Throughput pays for reserved capacity the one-off job does not need, and synchronous On-Demand calls forfeit the batch discount.

q: A support chatbot repeatedly sends the same long system prompt and product manual prefix to Amazon Bedrock before each short user question. Which feature most directly reduces the cost of that repeated prefix?
options: Prompt caching, which reuses the cached prompt prefix at a lower cost than reprocessing it on every request
Batch inference run after the conversation has ended
Provisioned Throughput sized for maximum concurrent users
Increasing the maximum output tokens on every request
explain: Prompt caching stores a reusable prompt prefix so subsequent requests pay less to process it again, which fits a long shared preamble with short variable suffixes. Provisioned Throughput buys capacity, batch inference adds latency a live chat cannot accept, and larger output limits raise rather than lower cost.

q: A team trains models intermittently on Amazon SageMaker AI and leaves training instances running between experiments. Which practice most reduces their SageMaker cost without changing model quality?
options: Store every intermediate checkpoint in Amazon S3 Standard indefinitely
Move all training to the largest GPU instance in the catalog
Keep a real-time endpoint running at peak instance size at all times
Stop or delete training instances and endpoints when idle, and use managed spot training for fault-tolerant jobs
explain: SageMaker charges for running instances, so shutting down idle notebooks, training jobs, and endpoints — plus using managed spot training with checkpointing — cuts cost without affecting model quality. Oversized always-on endpoints and indefinite Standard storage for checkpoints add avoidable spend.

q: A company deploys a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint that receives most requests in short bursts and sits idle 80 percent of the day. Which deployment change best aligns inference cost with that traffic pattern?
options: Keep two provisioned GPU instances running across three Availability Zones
Move the workload to a serverless inference endpoint or asynchronous inference that scales capacity toward zero when idle
Enable multi-model endpoints that still require full-time hosts
Purchase a three-year Reserved Instance for the endpoint instance
explain: Serverless and asynchronous SageMaker inference options scale with demand and avoid paying for idle provisioned hosts, suiting bursty, mostly idle traffic. Always-on multi-AZ GPU hosts and long commitments lock in peak cost for a workload that is usually idle.

q: A finance workload runs unchanged on Amazon EC2 for at least one year, and the team can commit to a consistent instance configuration but needs the option to change instance size within the same family. Which Reserved Instance attributes fit this need?
options: Zonal Reserved Instances, which allow family changes at any time
Spot Instances with a one-year duration block
Standard Reserved Instances in a Region, which allow size flexibility within the same instance family for Linux instances
Convertible Reserved Instances, which are required for any size change
explain: Regional Standard Reserved Instances automatically apply size flexibility within a family (for Linux/Unix), so the team can change sizes without a new purchase. Convertible Reserved Instances are needed to change family or other attributes, not merely size, and zonal reservations trade that flexibility for capacity assurance.

q: After a merger, a company must move its committed Amazon EC2 workload from one instance family to a completely different family while keeping a discount commitment. Which purchase change supports that move?
options: Modify the instance family attribute of Standard Reserved Instances in the console
Convert a Compute Savings Plan into EC2 Instance Savings Plans
Cancel Spot Instance requests and re-request them in the new family
Exchange Convertible Reserved Instances for new ones of equal or greater value in the target family
explain: Convertible Reserved Instances can be exchanged for other families and configurations as long as the new reservation is of equal or greater value. Standard Reserved Instances cannot change family, and neither Spot requests nor Savings Plan conversions perform that exchange.

q: A seasonal analytics job runs for three weeks each quarter on Amazon EC2 and is idle for the rest of the year. Which purchase model avoids paying for idle commitment while still controlling cost during the run?
options: On-Demand or Spot Instances only during the three-week run, with no one-year or three-year commitment
A Compute Savings Plan sized for the seasonal peak all year
EC2 Instance Savings Plans with a three-year hourly commitment
Three-year All Upfront Standard Reserved Instances for the full fleet
explain: A short seasonal burst should not carry a year-long hourly commitment, because Savings Plans and Reserved Instances charge for the committed amount whether or not it is used. On-Demand and Spot confine spending to the weeks the job actually runs.

q: A platform team wants to lower Amazon Lambda costs for a high-volume image-processing function that currently runs on x86 with default settings. Which combination offers the best price performance?
options: Attach the function to a VPC in three Availability Zones
Migrate the function to the arm64 (Graviton) architecture and right-size its memory using measured duration data
Enable Lambda provisioned concurrency at peak level around the clock
Increase the function timeout to the maximum value
explain: Arm64 Lambda functions on Graviton provide better price performance for many workloads, and tuning memory to the point where GB-second cost is lowest compounds the saving. A longer timeout does not change per-invocation price, and always-on provisioned concurrency adds a standing charge.

q: A product team notices its AWS bill is dominated by a few oversized Amazon RDS instances that average 15 percent CPU. Which service provides rightsizing recommendations that account for both performance and cost for these databases?
options: Amazon CloudWatch billing alarms on estimated charges
AWS Budgets alerts that fire when spend exceeds a threshold
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection findings grouped by service
AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations for RDS, reviewed alongside performance metrics before resizing
explain: Compute Optimizer analyzes RDS utilization and performance data to recommend instance changes that preserve performance at lower cost. Budgets, billing alarms, and anomaly detection report on spend patterns but do not model database performance headroom for rightsizing.

q: A batch pipeline built on Amazon ECS can tolerate tasks being stopped with two minutes of warning, and the team wants cheaper compute than standard Fargate pricing. Which capacity choice should the architect select?
options: On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the ECS service
EC2 Dedicated Hosts registered to the ECS cluster
Fargate Spot capacity for the interruptible ECS tasks
Fargate capacity with provisioned concurrency enabled
explain: Fargate Spot offers discounted spare capacity for ECS tasks that handle interruption gracefully, which matches a checkpointable batch pipeline. Dedicated Hosts and capacity reservations target licensing or assurance needs and cost more, not less.

q: A company commits to a Compute Savings Plan based on current usage, then six months later migrates many workloads from Amazon EC2 to AWS Lambda. What happens to the plan's benefit?
options: The Compute Savings Plan continues to apply automatically to the eligible Lambda usage up to the hourly commitment
The plan is cancelled automatically and the remaining commitment is refunded
The commitment must be converted into Standard Reserved Instances
The plan applies only if the team files a support case to retarget it
explain: Compute Savings Plans float across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, so a service migration within those families does not strand the commitment. No support case or conversion is needed, and commitments are not refunded on a workload change.

q: An architect must choose between Step Functions Standard and Express Workflows for an order-processing flow that can run for up to 20 days while waiting for human approvals and external shipments. Which type is required regardless of cost?
options: A Lambda function with the maximum 15-minute timeout, chained manually
Either type, because both support executions lasting 20 days
Standard Workflows, because Express Workflows are limited to five-minute executions
Express Workflows, because they support unlimited execution duration
explain: Express Workflows cap a single execution at five minutes, so a 20-day approval flow can only run as a Standard Workflow. Duration limits are a hard eligibility constraint that overrides any per-execution price comparison.

q: A generative-AI application sends many small, similar classification prompts to Amazon Bedrock and pays per input and output token. Which strategy most directly reduces token spend without reducing answer quality for repeated questions?
options: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for every user Region
Cache responses for identical or near-identical prompts so repeat questions are answered without a new model invocation
Route every request through cross-Region inference to the cheapest Region
Raise the temperature so the model answers in fewer tokens
explain: Response caching (for example with Amazon ElastiCache or an application cache) avoids paying for inference at all on repeated prompts. Temperature does not reliably cut tokens, Provisioned Throughput buys capacity rather than eliminating calls, and cross-Region routing changes where inference runs, not how often.

q: A machine-learning team wants to reduce inference costs in Amazon Bedrock by batching work that does not need an immediate answer, such as nightly document classification. Which statement best describes the benefit of that approach?
options: Batch inference processes many prompts asynchronously and is priced lower than equivalent On-Demand inference
Batch inference requires Provisioned Throughput for every model
Batching converts all token charges into a flat monthly fee
Batch inference guarantees lower latency than On-Demand inference
explain: Bedrock batch inference trades immediacy for price: jobs run asynchronously in bulk at a discount. It does not promise lower latency, a flat fee, or a Provisioned Throughput prerequisite.

q: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances for a web application that is busy only during business hours in one time zone and nearly idle overnight. Which rightsizing action yields the largest saving with the least risk?
options: Buy three-year Reserved Instances sized for the daytime peak
Move the application to Dedicated Hosts for licensing savings
Replace all instances with the largest Graviton instance type
Schedule the Auto Scaling group to scale in overnight and scale out before business hours, based on observed traffic
explain: Matching provisioned capacity to the diurnal traffic curve with scheduled scaling removes the overnight idle spend, which is the dominant waste here. Reserved capacity sized to the peak still charges for the commitment, and larger instances or Dedicated Hosts move cost in the wrong direction.

q: An architect reviews AWS Compute Optimizer and finds several Amazon EBS volumes and EC2 instances flagged as underutilized. What is the most appropriate next step before acting on every recommendation?
options: Terminate every flagged resource immediately to maximize savings
Validate the recommendations against application performance requirements and peak-period utilization, then resize in stages
Purchase Savings Plans to cover the current oversized footprint
Ignore Compute Optimizer because it only reports billing data
explain: Compute Optimizer recommendations are based on historical utilization windows and should be checked against peaks and application needs before staged resizing. Terminating flagged resources risks outages, and buying commitments for an oversized footprint locks in the waste.

q: A startup wants a discount on a predictable Amazon EC2 baseline but expects to change Regions and instance families as it expands internationally next year. Which commitment best preserves flexibility?
options: EC2 Instance Savings Plans tied to one family in one Region
Zonal Reserved Instances purchased in the launch Region
Standard Reserved Instances with Dedicated tenancy
Compute Savings Plans, which apply across Regions, families, and EC2, Fargate, and Lambda
explain: Compute Savings Plans are the most flexible commitment instrument: they follow usage across Regions, families, sizes, and supported compute services. Family- and Region-locked plans and zonal reservations sacrifice exactly the flexibility this startup needs.

q: A workload on AWS Lambda invokes a function 50 million times per month, and each invocation transfers a large payload that forces high memory allocation. Which change most reduces Lambda cost while keeping the same business logic?
options: Store large payloads in Amazon S3 and pass only a reference through Lambda, then right-size memory to the measured need
Move the function into a VPC with NAT gateways in every subnet
Enable provisioned concurrency equal to peak concurrency all day
Increase memory to the maximum so every invocation finishes sooner
explain: Passing S3 references instead of large payloads and right-sizing memory attack the GB-second driver of Lambda cost directly. Maximum memory, always-on provisioned concurrency, and unnecessary NAT paths all add cost without addressing payload-driven allocation.

q: A company uses Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints for three models whose request rates differ widely, and the highest-traffic model subsidizes idle capacity for the others. Which SageMaker feature helps match inference cost to each model's actual demand?
options: Provisioned Throughput purchased for all models in all Regions
A single largest-class endpoint shared by all three models
Appropriate service tiers and deployment options per model, such as serverless inference for low-traffic models and provisioned endpoints only where volume justifies them
Batch Transform jobs used to answer live user requests
explain: Matching the deployment tier to each model's traffic — serverless or asynchronous for sparse models, provisioned capacity only for sustained volume — aligns cost with demand. One oversized shared endpoint and live use of offline batch jobs both mismatch the requirement.

q: An e-commerce company can commit to an hourly spend amount for compute over one year but cannot predict which instance families it will need after a planned replatforming. Which purchase option should it choose?
options: A one-year Compute Savings Plan sized to the stable baseline spend, with On-Demand capacity above the baseline
A three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the current families
Dedicated Hosts purchased for the replatforming year
Spot Instances for the entire production storefront
explain: An hourly-commit Compute Savings Plan preserves family and service flexibility through a replatform while still discounting the stable baseline, with On-Demand absorbing uncertainty above it. Family-locked three-year plans risk being stranded, and Spot or Dedicated Hosts do not fit a production storefront baseline.

q: A team runs GPU training jobs on Amazon EC2 that checkpoint every 10 minutes and can resume on different hardware. Which purchase option gives the lowest cost for these jobs?
options: Three-year Partial Upfront Reserved Instances for one GPU family
On-Demand GPU instances with no commitment
Spot Instances with capacity-optimized allocation across multiple GPU instance pools
Dedicated Hosts with hourly billing for the training cluster
explain: Checkpointable training that can resume elsewhere is the canonical Spot use case, and diversifying across pools with capacity-optimized allocation reduces interruption impact while keeping the Spot discount. Reserved and Dedicated options pay a premium for assurance this workload does not need.

q: A company wants to lower the cost of a long-running Amazon ECS service on EC2 without changing application code. The service runs continuously at a predictable baseline. Which combination is most cost-effective?
options: Double the task count and halve each task's CPU allocation
Cover the baseline with a Compute Savings Plan and use target tracking scaling so capacity follows demand above the baseline
Place the service behind a Network Load Balancer in every Region
Run the entire service on Spot Instances with no baseline commitment
explain: A Savings Plan discounts the predictable baseline while target tracking prevents over-provisioning above it — savings on both the committed and the elastic portions. Spot-only risks the production baseline, and multi-Region load balancing adds cost unrelated to compute efficiency.

q: An architect is asked to cut costs for AWS Step Functions executions that invoke AWS Lambda for a few milliseconds per step across hundreds of millions of monthly executions. Which redesign offers the largest saving?
options: Add a Standard Workflow wrapper around every existing workflow
Enable detailed CloudWatch logging on every state transition
Insert wait states between every pair of steps
Consolidate trivial steps and use Express Workflows, or implement short high-volume steps directly in fewer Lambda invocations where the orchestration allows
explain: At hundreds of millions of short executions, per-transition and per-request pricing dominates, so reducing state transitions and using Express pricing attacks the main cost driver. Extra wrappers, detailed logging, and artificial waits add transitions or charges without reducing work.

q: A firm wants predictable pricing for Amazon Bedrock inference for a model it uses heavily, and it is willing to commit for one year in exchange for a discount on reserved throughput. Which option should it evaluate?
options: Spot Instances hosting a self-managed copy of the model
On-Demand inference with Cost Explorer recommendations enabled
Provisioned Throughput with a one-year or six-month term commitment for that model
Batch inference with a service quota increase
explain: Term-based Provisioned Throughput trades a commitment for discounted, reserved model units on Bedrock. On-Demand has no commitment discount, batch inference addresses offline latency-tolerant work, and self-hosting on Spot reintroduces operational and interruption risk the managed option avoids.

q: A DevOps team keeps Amazon EC2 instances running for a CI system that is used only when developers push code, roughly 30 hours per week. Which approach most reduces compute cost for this pattern?
options: Keep the fleet running so builds never wait for an instance to start
Migrate the CI fleet to Dedicated Instances for a volume discount
Purchase All Upfront Reserved Instances for the full CI fleet
Automatically stop or scale to zero the CI fleet outside working and build windows, and restart it on demand
explain: CI capacity that is needed only about 30 hours a week should not be paid for during the other 138 hours; automated start/stop or scale-to-zero removes that idle spend. Long commitments priced on full-time use waste money on a part-time workload.

q: A company evaluates AWS Graviton for its Amazon RDS databases and Amazon ElastiCache clusters in addition to its compute fleet. What is the primary cost reason for this evaluation?
options: Graviton-based database and cache instance families often provide better price performance than comparable x86 families
Graviton instances are free when combined with Savings Plans
Graviton eliminates data transfer charges between services
Graviton removes the need for backups and Multi-AZ deployments
explain: Graviton families extend beyond EC2 to RDS, ElastiCache, and other services and are chosen for price performance, not for removing resilience, backup, or transfer charges. Savings Plans change billing discounts; they do not make Graviton capacity free.

q: A product team runs a Lambda-based API whose cost rose after a release doubled the average function duration without changing invocation count or memory. Which investigation best explains and addresses the increase?
options: Assume the Savings Plan expired and purchase a larger commitment
Profile the new code path for added latency, because Lambda charges scale with billed duration at the allocated memory level
Check whether the account exceeded the free tier for API Gateway
Move the function to a larger memory size without measuring the effect
explain: With invocations and memory unchanged, a duration doubling directly increases GB-second charges, so profiling the regression is the cost fix. Blindly raising memory or buying commitments treats the symptom without confirming whether duration or allocation is the efficient lever.

q: A company wants to commit to Amazon SageMaker AI usage for its steady inference and training baseline to reduce AI/ML spend over the next year. Which instrument is designed for that purpose?
options: Database Savings Plans applied to SageMaker notebooks
EC2 Instance Savings Plans applied to SageMaker endpoints
SageMaker Savings Plans, which commit to an hourly SageMaker usage amount in exchange for discounted rates
Spot Instances used for production inference endpoints
explain: SageMaker Savings Plans are the commitment instrument scoped to eligible SageMaker usage such as training and inference instances. EC2 and Database Savings Plans do not cover SageMaker, and Spot is unsuitable for production endpoints that cannot be interrupted.

q: An operations team wants Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling to remove capacity quickly when a nightly batch job finishes, rather than paying for a slow cooldown tail. Which configuration best supports cost-efficient scale-in?
options: Disabling scale-in so instances are reused for the next night's job
Target tracking or step scaling with appropriately tuned scale-in policies and termination of excess instances once the metric falls
A minimum capacity equal to the nightly peak at all times
Scheduled scaling that adds capacity every hour regardless of load
explain: Cost-efficient scale-in requires policies that actually release capacity when demand falls. A peak-sized minimum, hourly additions, or disabled scale-in all keep the fleet paying for the peak long after the batch ends.

q: A media company stores user uploads and serves them through compute that scales to zero between campaigns. Leadership asks why the team chose AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate instead of a fixed EC2 fleet. Which answer best captures the cost principle?
options: EC2 cannot be used with Auto Scaling to reduce idle capacity
Lambda removes all data transfer and request charges
Lambda and Fargate are always cheaper than EC2 for every workload at any scale
Serverless and container-on-demand services charge for resources only while work runs, avoiding payment for idle provisioned capacity
explain: The cost principle is paying only for consumed compute instead of an always-provisioned fleet, which wins when demand is sparse or spiky. At sustained high scale the comparison can reverse, and neither service eliminates request or transfer charges.

q: A team must run a stateful legacy application that cannot be interrupted, needs predictable performance, and will run at a constant size for two years. Spot Instances have been proposed purely for their discount. Why should the architect reject Spot for this workload?
options: Spot Instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a two-minute warning, which violates the application's no-interruption requirement
Spot Instances cost more than On-Demand Instances for long-running work
Spot Instances cannot run for more than one hour at a time
Spot Instances require the application to be stateless by law
explain: Spot capacity is spare capacity that AWS can reclaim, so it is fundamentally incompatible with a stateful workload that cannot be interrupted, regardless of the discount. Spot has no one-hour runtime cap, and its unsuitability here is about interruption, not price or a legal statelessness rule.

q: A company runs a portfolio of Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate, and Amazon RDS workloads and wants one rightsizing review that covers compute, containers, and databases together. Which tool provides cross-service rightsizing recommendations from utilization data?
options: Amazon CloudFront reports filtered by edge location
AWS Budgets, with one budget per service
AWS Cost and Usage Reports, queried manually in Amazon Athena
AWS Compute Optimizer, which covers EC2, ECS on Fargate, Lambda, EBS, and RDS recommendations in one place
explain: Compute Optimizer is the single AWS service that generates rightsizing recommendations across those compute, container, serverless, storage, and database resources from utilization history. Cost reports and budgets expose spend, and CloudFront reports cover content delivery, not rightsizing.

q: A website serves the same product images and downloadable files to a global audience from Amazon S3 in one Region, and origin egress and request costs keep rising. Which design most reduces those costs?
options: Add a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone for image traffic
Copy the bucket to every AWS Region and serve users from the nearest copy
Deliver the content through Amazon CloudFront so edge caches serve repeat requests instead of the origin
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for all viewer downloads
explain: CloudFront caching at edge locations absorbs repeat requests, cutting origin requests and S3 egress while also lowering latency. Multi-Region copies multiply storage and replication cost, NAT gateways are for private-subnet egress, and Transfer Acceleration optimizes uploads into S3 rather than viewer delivery.

q: A company uses Amazon CloudFront but still sees high origin traffic because cache misses from many edge locations each fetch the same objects from Amazon S3. Which CloudFront feature consolidates those origin fetches?
options: CloudFront Functions executed at the origin on every request
Origin Shield, which adds a central caching layer between edge locations and the origin
AWS Global Accelerator endpoints placed in front of S3
S3 Cross-Region Replication to a second origin bucket
explain: Origin Shield funnels edge cache misses through a single regional shield cache, raising the effective cache-hit ratio and reducing origin load and cost. The other options add replication or routing without consolidating origin fetches in the same way.

q: Applications in private subnets make millions of requests per month to Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB, all currently routed through NAT gateways that incur hourly and per-GB processing charges. Which change removes most of that NAT cost for this traffic?
options: Add gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB and update the route tables so that traffic bypasses the NAT gateways
Replace the NAT gateways with a self-managed NAT instance fleet
Route S3 traffic through an internet gateway attached to the private subnets
Add a second NAT gateway in each Availability Zone for redundancy
explain: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and keep that traffic on the AWS network, eliminating NAT data-processing charges for it. More NAT gateways increase hourly cost, and private subnets should not be given direct internet routes to solve an AWS-service access pattern.

q: A workload in a VPC generates heavy traffic to an interface-endpoint-only AWS service, and the team is surprised by hourly endpoint charges multiplied across many subnets. Which review best controls interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) cost?
options: Create a separate interface endpoint in every subnet of every VPC
Disable PrivateLink and route all service traffic over the public internet
Replace interface endpoints with NAT gateways for all AWS services
Consolidate interface endpoints into fewer Availability Zones and subnets where the architecture allows, because each endpoint ENI is billed hourly per AZ
explain: Interface endpoints are priced per endpoint per Availability Zone per hour plus data processed, so endpoint sprawl across subnets and AZs multiplies the hourly bill. Consolidation where resilience allows is the cost lever; NAT gateways cannot reach services that require interface endpoints in the same way, and public routing sacrifices the private path.

q: Two application tiers in the same VPC but different Availability Zones exchange several terabytes per month, and the bill shows growing inter-AZ data transfer charges. Which redesign most directly reduces those charges?
options: Move one tier to a different AWS Region to use replication pricing
Co-locate tightly coupled, high-volume tiers in the same Availability Zone or redesign communication to reduce cross-AZ chatter, while preserving required resilience
Route the traffic through AWS Transit Gateway so it is billed once
Send the traffic through a NAT gateway in a third Availability Zone
explain: Inter-AZ transfer is charged per GB, so reducing cross-AZ volume or co-locating chatty tiers attacks the charge directly. Cross-Region moves, Transit Gateway hops, and NAT detours add their own processing or transfer fees rather than removing the underlying chatter.

q: A company replicates an Amazon S3 bucket with S3 Cross-Region Replication to three destination Regions, but only one Region is actually required for disaster recovery. What is the main cost consequence of the current design?
options: The company pays replication data transfer and destination storage charges in all three Regions, including two Regions that provide no required recovery benefit
Replication itself is free and only storage in the source bucket is billed
Each destination bucket reduces the price of the source bucket's storage
Cross-Region Replication automatically deletes the source objects to save cost
explain: S3 CRR incurs inter-Region data transfer charges plus storage (and request) costs in every destination bucket. Replicating to Regions the recovery plan does not need multiplies both charges with no benefit, so pruning destinations is a direct saving.

q: A product uses Amazon DynamoDB global tables across four Regions, but analytics show that two Regions serve almost no local users and exist only because they were in an early template. Which action best controls the global table's ongoing cost?
options: Convert the table to provisioned capacity in all four Regions
Add S3 Cross-Region Replication for the table's backups
Remove the low-value replica Regions, because every global table replica incurs replicated write and storage charges for the data it holds
Enable DynamoDB auto scaling in the unused Regions
explain: Each global table replica Region adds replicated write units and replica storage costs for the full dataset, so unused replicas are pure overhead. Capacity-mode or scaling changes do not remove the per-replica replication cost of Regions that serve no users.

q: A hub-and-spoke network connects 40 VPCs through AWS Transit Gateway, and the finance team asks why the network bill includes charges beyond VPC attachment fees. Which explanation is correct?
options: Transit Gateway data processing is free when traffic stays in one Region
Transit Gateway replaces all NAT gateway and endpoint charges at no extra cost
Transit Gateway also charges per GB of data processed through the gateway, so high-volume east-west traffic adds a data processing component on top of hourly attachment charges
Transit Gateway charges only a flat monthly fee per account
explain: Transit Gateway pricing combines an hourly charge per attachment with a per-GB data processing charge. High east-west volume therefore scales the bill, and architects must weigh centralised inspection against processing cost for chatty flows.

q: A team routes all traffic between its VPCs through AWS Transit Gateway, including a nightly multi-terabyte backup flow between two VPCs in the same Availability Zone. Which alternative most reduces cost for that specific flow?
options: Add a second Transit Gateway and split the backup flow across both
Route the backups through a NAT gateway to obtain NAT pricing
Enable Transit Gateway multicast for the backup traffic
Use VPC peering or a direct same-AZ path for the high-volume point-to-point backup flow and keep Transit Gateway for the broader hub-and-spoke traffic
explain: Transit Gateway data processing is charged per GB, so a predictable multi-terabyte two-VPC flow is cheaper on a peering-style path that avoids that processing charge, while Transit Gateway remains valuable for many-to-many routing. Splitting or rerouting through NAT does not remove a per-GB gateway charge.

q: Static assets are served through Amazon CloudFront, but the cache hit ratio is only 30 percent because cache keys include dozens of query string parameters and cookies that do not change the content. Which fix most improves cost-effectiveness?
options: Disable compression so edge caches store a single object version
Narrow the cache key to only the parameters and headers that actually vary the response, raising the cache hit ratio
Forward all cookies to the origin on every request
Shorten the default TTL to one minute so objects refresh more often
explain: An over-broad cache key fragments the cache into near-duplicate objects and forces origin fetches; trimming it to what truly varies content raises hit ratio and cuts origin cost. Short TTLs, disabled compression, and forwarding everything all push traffic back to the origin.

q: A SaaS provider's Amazon S3 data transfer bill spikes whenever EU customers download reports generated in a US Region. Which architecture change most reduces that recurring transfer cost?
options: Serve the reports through Amazon CloudFront with caching, or generate and store the reports in a Region closer to the customers
Enable S3 Versioning so older report versions are retained
Route downloads through the VPC's NAT gateway for a volume discount
Increase the S3 bucket's request rate by adding random key prefixes
explain: Repeated cross-continent downloads from a distant origin incur both transfer cost and latency; CloudFront caching or regional placement serves bytes closer to users and reduces origin egress. Versioning retains more data, and NAT gateways add processing charges rather than discounts.

q: Developers in a private subnet pull container images and call AWS APIs through a single NAT gateway in another Availability Zone, creating both a resilience risk and cross-AZ transfer charges. Which design corrects both problems at the lowest reasonable cost?
options: Place a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone that hosts private subnets and use gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and ECR image layers where possible
Replace all NAT gateways with interface endpoints for internet access
Move the private subnets into the public subnet tier
Keep the single NAT gateway and accept cross-AZ charges as unavoidable
explain: One NAT gateway per AZ removes cross-AZ NAT traffic and the single point of failure, while gateway endpoints offload S3-based image and storage traffic for free. Interface endpoints do not provide general internet egress, and making subnets public sacrifices the private design.

q: A company uses AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints for a partner service in every Availability Zone of three VPCs, but utilization reports show most endpoints carry almost no traffic. What is the most cost-effective action?
options: Convert each interface endpoint into a NAT gateway
Remove or consolidate the idle interface endpoints, retaining endpoints only in the AZs and VPCs that actively use the service
Add hourly CloudWatch alarms to each idle endpoint
Replicate the endpoints to additional Regions for symmetry
explain: Idle interface endpoints still incur hourly per-AZ charges, so consolidation is the saving. Alarms only observe the waste, and NAT gateways or extra Regions do not substitute for, or cheapen, an unused PrivateLink endpoint.

q: An architect compares keeping microservices in one VPC versus splitting them across many VPCs connected by AWS Transit Gateway. Which cost factor must be included in that comparison?
options: Amazon CloudFront distribution charges per VPC
Amazon S3 storage charges for every VPC created
AWS Lambda invocation charges for each route table entry
Transit Gateway per-GB data processing charges for inter-VPC traffic, plus hourly attachment charges for each attached VPC
explain: Cross-VPC designs pay Transit Gateway attachment and data processing charges that a single-VPC design avoids for local traffic. VPC creation itself and route entries do not incur the listed S3, Lambda, or CloudFront charges.

q: A gaming company wants to reduce Amazon CloudFront costs for a popular download that is requested millions of times with the same URL each release day. Which setting most ensures the object is served from cache rather than the origin?
options: Require signed URLs that expire every 60 seconds
Disable the distribution's cache and use Lambda@Edge for every request
Set a long cache TTL with appropriate cache-control headers and a cache key that does not fragment on irrelevant parameters
Set the TTL to zero so CloudFront always checks the origin
explain: A long TTL and a clean cache key keep the hot object resident at the edge, minimising origin fetches on release day. Zero TTL, per-minute expiry, and bypassing the cache all force origin or per-request compute work.

q: A finance team discovers large data transfer charges between an application in one Region and Amazon Bedrock inference endpoints in another Region, because the preferred foundation model is not available locally. Which strategy best balances availability and transfer cost?
options: Disable cross-Region inference even if the model is unavailable locally
Send every prompt multiple times to compare Regional prices
Copy all application data to every Region preemptively

Use cross-Region inference profiles deliberately for the models that need them, and keep data-heavy preprocessing and storage in the inference Region to minimise repeated cross-Region payload movement
explain: Cross-Region inference routing solves model availability but moves payloads across Regions; co-locating the data-heavy stages with inference limits repeated transfer. Blanket data copies multiply storage cost, and disabling the profile removes access to the required model.

q: A multi-Region active-active application writes to Amazon DynamoDB global tables, and leadership asks why write costs are higher than in the previous single-Region design. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Every write is replicated to the other replica Regions and billed as replicated write capacity in each, in addition to storage held in every Region
Global tables charge only for reads; writes remain single-Region priced
Global tables remove the need to pay for storage in replica Regions
The increase comes solely from CloudFront caching of table data
explain: DynamoDB global tables replicate writes across all replicas and charge replicated write units plus per-Region storage, so active-active convenience carries an inherent multi-Region write premium. That premium is a core input to any cost-aware replication decision.

q: An analytics platform in a VPC reads terabytes per day from Amazon S3 through an internet gateway via a public subnet, and the team wants a private, lower-cost path. Which endpoint choice fits S3 access from a VPC at no hourly charge?
options: A NAT gateway dedicated exclusively to S3 traffic
An AWS PrivateLink endpoint billed per GB processed
A gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 associated with the VPC's route tables
An interface VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in every subnet
explain: S3 supports gateway VPC endpoints, which have no hourly or per-GB endpoint charge and keep traffic private. Interface endpoints and PrivateLink-style billing apply to other services (and an S3 interface option exists for specific cases), but the gateway endpoint is the no-charge default for in-VPC S3 access.

q: A company centralises internet egress for 30 VPCs through inspection VPCs attached to AWS Transit Gateway to simplify security. Which cost trade-off should the architect surface to leadership?
options: Transit Gateway inspection removes all data transfer charges
Centralised egress adds Transit Gateway data processing and NAT or appliance costs on the inspected path, which may outweigh the savings from fewer per-VPC NAT gateways for very high-volume flows
Per-VPC NAT gateways are prohibited when Transit Gateway is used
Centralised egress is always cheaper regardless of traffic volume
explain: Hub-and-spoke inspection centralises control but routes bytes through chargeable gateway and egress components, so volume determines whether it saves or costs more than distributed NAT gateways. The correct answer is a volume-dependent trade-off analysis, not an absolute claim.

q: A video platform stores masters in Amazon S3 in one Region and transcodes them in another Region because GPU capacity is cheaper there, moving terabytes daily between Regions. Which review should happen first?
options: Add CloudFront Origin Shield between the two Regions
Compare the inter-Region data transfer cost of moving the masters against the compute saving, and consider moving the transcode stage to the storage Region instead
Purchase Reserved Instances for the NAT gateways on the path
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication so two copies can be transferred daily
explain: Cross-Region architecture must be cost-aware: per-GB inter-Region transfer on terabytes per day can erase a compute discount, so co-location economics come first. Replication, shielding, and NAT reservations do not change that fundamental transfer bill.

q: A team enables Amazon CloudFront for a new API whose responses are unique per user and explicitly marked non-cacheable, expecting a large cost saving. Why will the expected saving not materialise?
options: APIs behind CloudFront are billed as Lambda invocations
CloudFront cannot be used in front of any API
Non-cacheable responses are stored permanently at the edge at extra cost

CloudFront primarily saves cost by caching repeatable responses; unique non-cacheable API responses still travel to the origin on nearly every request, while the distribution adds its own request and transfer pricing
explain: Content delivery economics depend on cacheability. For per-user, non-cacheable responses, CloudFront may still help with connection optimisation, but it cannot absorb origin requests the way it does for shared static content, so a caching-based saving projection is invalid.

q: A retailer's Amazon S3 bucket replicates order archives to a second Region for compliance, and the archives are rarely read. Which companion setting keeps the replication design cost-effective?
options: Replicate the archives onward to a third Region for redundancy
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the destination bucket
Apply S3 Lifecycle rules in the destination bucket to transition replicated archives to a cheaper Glacier storage class after a defined period
Store the replicated archives in S3 Standard in perpetuity
explain: Replication satisfies the compliance copy requirement, and lifecycle tiering in the destination controls the long-term storage price of rarely read archives. Holding everything in Standard or adding Regions only grows the replicated footprint's cost.

q: An architect must explain the cost of AWS PrivateLink to a team that assumes private connectivity is free once an endpoint exists. Which statement is correct?
options: Interface endpoints incur an hourly charge for each endpoint in each Availability Zone plus a per-GB data processing charge, so both endpoint count and traffic volume matter
Gateway endpoints and interface endpoints are priced identically per hour
PrivateLink data processing is free for all AWS services
PrivateLink charges a single one-time setup fee per endpoint
explain: PrivateLink interface endpoint pricing is hourly per AZ plus per-GB processed, unlike free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB. Endpoint sprawl and high volume both raise the bill, which is why placement and consolidation are cost decisions.

q: A logistics app runs in two Availability Zones, but its database clients all connect to a writer in one AZ while application servers in the other AZ generate constant cross-AZ traffic. Which change reduces transfer cost without weakening the database design?
options: Move the entire application into a single Availability Zone
Prefer local-AZ endpoints and read replicas for reads where the service supports them, so routine traffic stays within the AZ and only necessary writes cross AZs
Disable Multi-AZ and accept the availability risk for the savings
Route application traffic through Transit Gateway within the VPC
explain: AZ-aware client routing — using local endpoints and local read replicas — trims avoidable cross-AZ bytes while keeping the resilient database topology. Collapsing to one AZ or disabling Multi-AZ trades away the resilience the design requires.

q: A startup serves images from Amazon S3 directly to the public internet, and S3 data transfer out dominates its bill as traffic grows. Which migration offers the most durable cost relief?
options: Move the images to EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances
Rename bucket keys with random prefixes to spread request pricing
Enable S3 Object Lock so images cannot be overwritten
Put Amazon CloudFront in front of the bucket, because CloudFront data transfer out is priced favourably and caching reduces S3 egress volume
explain: CloudFront is the standard cost lever for public S3 delivery: edge caching cuts origin egress and CloudFront transfer pricing is designed for internet delivery at scale. Key naming, Object Lock, and EBS hosting do not address internet egress economics.

q: A company pays for three NAT gateways per VPC across many VPCs, yet traffic analysis shows several VPCs send almost all of their private-subnet traffic to Amazon S3, DynamoDB, and ECR. Which optimisation should come first?
options: Add free gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB (and use interface endpoints for ECR where justified) so AWS-service traffic bypasses the NAT gateways
Route AWS-service traffic over a Direct Connect public VIF
Add a fourth NAT gateway to each VPC for headroom
Replace NAT gateways with t3.micro NAT instances in every subnet
explain: When private traffic is mostly to AWS services, endpoints divert that traffic off the NAT path, cutting per-GB NAT processing and sometimes allowing NAT consolidation. Adding NAT capacity treats the symptom while the endpoint offload removes the chargeable flow.

q: A global SaaS product replicates user files with S3 Cross-Region Replication to meet data-residency rules in two Regions only, but an audit finds replication also enabled to a third Region by mistake. What should the architect do and why?
options: Enable versioning in the third Region to offset the cost
Convert the third bucket to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and leave replication on
Disable replication to the third Region, because each CRR destination adds inter-Region transfer and destination storage charges with no residency requirement to justify them
Keep the third copy because replication destinations are not billed
explain: CRR is billed per destination through transfer and stored bytes, so an unjustified replica is ongoing waste. Tiering lowers but does not eliminate an unnecessary copy's cost; removing the unneeded replication is the correct fix.

q: A team uses AWS Transit Gateway Connect and multiple attachments, and its bill grows faster than traffic. Which cost review is most relevant to Transit Gateway architecture?
options: Audit the number of DNS queries resolved by Route 53
Review CloudFront price class settings for the account
Count the S3 buckets in each attached VPC
Audit the number of Transit Gateway attachments and the volume of data processed, because both the hourly attachment count and per-GB processing drive the total
explain: Transit Gateway cost scales with attachments (hourly) and data processed (per GB), so those are the two levers an architecture review can actually move. DNS, bucket counts, and CloudFront price class belong to different services' bills.

q: An application calls Amazon Bedrock in a distant Region for every request because cross-Region inference profiles route automatically, and prompt payloads include large retrieved documents. Which cost-aware redesign is best?
options: Store all retrieval data in the application's home Region indefinitely
Increase the retrieved document set so each request is more complete
Retrieve and assemble context in the inference Region or reduce the retrieved payload size, and evaluate a locally available smaller model where quality allows
Duplicate inference calls in two Regions and keep the cheaper answer
explain: Cross-Region inference moves the full prompt — including retrieved context — across Regions on every call, so payload discipline and data placement determine transfer cost. Larger payloads and duplicate calls increase the very charges the redesign must cut.

q: A publisher uses Amazon CloudFront with Origin Shield enabled in a Region far from its S3 origin, and origin fetches still cross long distances on shield misses. Which adjustment improves the design?
options: Disable Origin Shield so every edge location contacts the origin directly
Place Origin Shield in the Region closest to the origin so the shield-to-origin leg is short and the shield cache absorbs edge misses efficiently
Add a second origin in every CloudFront edge location
Set the origin protocol policy to match viewer on all requests
explain: Origin Shield works best near the origin: edge requests converge on the shield, and only shield misses make the short hop to the origin. A distant shield preserves a long, chargeable origin leg on every miss, and disabling the shield multiplies origin fetches.

q: A company notices NAT gateway charges are its second-largest network cost. Traffic logs show a data pipeline in a private subnet downloads public datasets over the internet for hours each day. Which options should the architect present for this specific flow?
options: Move dataset downloads to instances in a public subnet with an internet gateway, or stage the datasets in Amazon S3, so bulk internet downloads do not incur NAT per-GB processing charges
Replace the NAT gateway with an interface VPC endpoint for the internet
Add more NAT gateways to spread the download cost
Enable NAT gateway detailed billing and continue unchanged
explain: Bulk internet downloads through a NAT gateway pay per-GB processing on every byte; a public-subnet path or S3 staging removes that processing charge for a workload that does not need a private subnet for this flow. Interface endpoints do not provide general internet access.

q: A microservices platform in one VPC uses an Amazon API Gateway VPC link and interface endpoints in three AZs for a low-traffic internal admin service. Which statement captures the cost issue?
options: The interface endpoints charge hourly in each of the three AZs around the clock, which can dwarf the cost of a genuinely low-traffic service and may justify fewer AZs for that endpoint
Three-AZ endpoints reduce the hourly charge per endpoint
Interface endpoints are billed only when requests succeed
Low-traffic services are exempt from PrivateLink hourly charges
explain: PrivateLink hourly charges accrue per endpoint per AZ whether or not traffic flows, so multi-AZ endpoint footprints for trivial internal services deserve explicit justification. There is no low-traffic exemption and no volume discount for adding AZs.

q: A team replicates a DynamoDB table globally for latency, but most Regions only read data that changes in the home Region. Which cost-aware alternative should be evaluated before committing to global tables everywhere?
options: Add more replica Regions to dilute the per-Region write cost
Evaluate whether read replicas via a caching layer or a single-Region table with CloudFront or DAX-style caching meets latency goals at lower cost than paying replicated write charges in every Region
Accept global tables because replicated writes are not billed
Convert the table to provisioned capacity with a very high write ceiling
explain: Global tables charge replicated writes and storage in every replica, so for read-heavy, single-writer patterns a cheaper caching or single-Region design may meet the goal. Adding replicas raises, rather than dilutes, total replicated write cost.

q: A content site enables Amazon CloudFront but leaves the price class set to use all edge locations worldwide, while 98 percent of its audience is in North America. Which cost setting should be reviewed?
options: Increase the minimum TTL so objects never expire
Add a second distribution for the same content
Select a CloudFront price class limited to the Regions where the audience actually is, trading unused global edge coverage for a lower delivery price
Enable Origin Shield in every Region to offset the price class
explain: CloudFront price classes let a distribution use only the edge locations in chosen geographies at a lower price, which fits a regionally concentrated audience. Keeping worldwide coverage the audience never uses pays for reach that delivers no value.

q: A company has 200 AWS accounts and cannot tell which product team owns thousands of untagged Amazon EC2 and Amazon S3 resources. Which tagging approach should be implemented first to enable reliable cost allocation?
options: Allow each team to invent its own tag keys and values without a standard
Tag only the AWS account root user and rely on account names
Use resource names instead of tags for all cost reporting
Define a mandatory tag schema (such as team, application, and environment), activate those cost allocation tags, and apply them consistently to new and existing resources
explain: Cost allocation only works when the same tag keys and values are applied consistently and then activated as cost allocation tags so they appear in billing data. Free-form tagging fragments reporting, and names or account labels cannot allocate shared resources inside an account.

q: Finance needs a monthly report that shows AWS spend by service, Region, and cost allocation tag, with the ability to filter, group, and forecast future spend interactively. Which tool is designed for that analysis?
options: AWS Cost Explorer, which provides interactive filtering, grouping, and forecasting over billing data
AWS Cost and Usage Reports delivered as raw files to Amazon S3
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection findings in the console
AWS Budgets alerts sent to an SNS topic
explain: Cost Explorer is the interactive analysis and forecasting interface over cost data. Cost and Usage Reports provide the raw underlying detail for custom processing, while Budgets and Anomaly Detection monitor thresholds and unusual spend rather than serving as general analysis tools.

q: A data team wants line-item-level billing records, including resource IDs, pricing, and tags, delivered regularly so it can build custom cost analytics in Amazon Athena and Amazon QuickSight. Which source should it use?
options: AWS Cost Explorer saved reports exported manually each month
Amazon CloudWatch billing metrics at one-hour resolution
AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) delivered to Amazon S3 at hourly or daily granularity
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimisation checks
explain: CUR is the most detailed billing dataset AWS publishes, with line items per resource, charge, and tag, designed for Athena and QuickSight analysis. Cost Explorer is a summarised UI, and Trusted Advisor or CloudWatch billing metrics cannot supply line-item detail.

q: A company wants to prevent any user from launching Amazon EC2 instances without a required CostCenter tag, blocking non-compliant requests rather than only reporting them later. Which control provides that preventive enforcement?
options: A tag policy that only defines the allowed tag values
An AWS Budgets action that emails the account owner
An AWS Config rule that records non-compliant instances after launch
A Service Control Policy or an IAM policy condition that denies the launch action when the required tag is absent, using tag condition keys
explain: Preventive enforcement requires a deny at request time, which SCPs and IAM policies with aws:RequestTag conditions provide. Config rules and tag policies are detective or definitional controls that detect or standardise tags after the fact, and a budget email blocks nothing.

q: An organisation defines allowed values for its Environment tag (prod, staging, dev) in AWS Organizations and wants member accounts to see guidance that keeps tagging consistent. Which feature provides that standardisation?
options: IAM Access Analyzer findings for unused tags
Tag policies in AWS Organizations, which define allowed tag keys, values, and enforcement options for supported resources
S3 Lifecycle rules applied to tagged objects
AWS Cost Categories, which rename tags automatically
explain: Tag policies are the Organizations feature for standardising tag keys and allowed values (and optionally preventing non-compliant tagging operations). Cost Categories group costs for reporting but do not define or enforce tag values.

q: Several teams keep creating resources with misspelled or missing Owner tags, and the platform team wants continuous detective checks with automatic remediation where possible. Which combination fits best?
options: AWS Config rules that evaluate the required-tags rule, with remediation actions that notify owners or apply the correction workflow
Manual spreadsheet audits performed at year end
AWS Cost Explorer forecasts reviewed once per quarter
CloudFront access logs analysed for missing tags
explain: Config's required-tags rule continuously evaluates resources for mandatory tags and supports remediation, making it the detective complement to preventive SCPs. Quarterly forecasts and manual audits are too infrequent and cannot remediate automatically.

q: A business wants to group its AWS costs by product line even though the underlying accounts and tags do not map one-to-one to products, by combining account, tag, and service rules into virtual reporting dimensions. Which feature provides those dimensions?
options: Cost allocation tags renamed at the account level
S3 storage classes named after each product line
Reserved Instance utilisation reports filtered by Region
AWS Cost Categories, which build custom cost groupings from accounts, tags, services, and other dimensions for use in Cost Explorer and CUR
explain: Cost Categories create rule-based virtual dimensions on top of billing data without retagging history, and they flow into Cost Explorer, Budgets, and CUR. Renaming tags or storage classes does not create a reporting dimension.

q: Two Amazon Bedrock applications share one AWS account, and finance needs each application's token usage and inference cost reported separately for internal chargeback. Which approach provides that separation?
options: Rely on the account total because Bedrock usage cannot be separated
Move both applications to On-Demand Capacity Reservations
Tag the Bedrock resources and application invocations consistently, monitor token usage per application, and use cost allocation tags with Cost Categories or CUR queries to split the charges
Enable CloudFront logging for the Bedrock endpoints
explain: Bedrock cost attribution depends on disciplined tagging, per-application usage monitoring (input/output tokens), and billing breakdowns via cost allocation tags, Cost Categories, and CUR. An account total alone cannot support chargeback between two applications sharing the account.

q: A platform team shares a central NAT and networking account across 30 application teams and needs to divide those shared costs fairly instead of assigning them all to the network team. Which billing feature supports that division?
options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering applied to the network account's logs
Split cost allocation and Cost Categories in the billing data, so shared container, networking, or support costs can be apportioned across the consuming teams
Spot Instance rebates applied to the network account
Tag policies that force every team to create its own NAT gateway
explain: Split cost allocation (for supported shared services) and Cost Categories let finance apportion shared costs by defined proportions or usage drivers for showback and chargeback. Forcing duplicate infrastructure or tiering logs does not allocate a shared bill.

q: Leadership wants each department to see its AWS spend (showback) before the company moves to full chargeback against departmental budgets. Which reporting setup best supports that first step?
options: Block department accounts when they exceed the account average
Use cost allocation tags and Cost Categories to produce per-department views in Cost Explorer and scheduled CUR-based reports, without yet changing internal accounting
Purchase Savings Plans centrally and hide the resulting bill detail
Delete department tags so only the total bill is visible
explain: Showback is visibility without financial transfer: tagged, categorised per-department reports deliver exactly that. Blocking accounts is an enforcement action, and hiding or deleting the attribution data defeats the purpose of showback.

q: A team sets an AWS Budget at 100 percent of forecast monthly spend but only learns about overruns two weeks after the month ends. Which improvement gives earlier, actionable cost control?
options: Increase the budget to 200 percent so alerts stop firing
Disable Cost Explorer forecasting for the account
Review the Cost and Usage Report once per quarter
Configure AWS Budgets with forecast-based alerts at thresholds such as 80 and 100 percent of forecast, plus budget actions that can notify or apply a restrictive policy when a threshold is crossed
explain: Forecast-based budget alerts fire before the overrun completes, and budget actions can automate notification or guardrails. Raising the budget, quarterly reviews, and disabling forecasts all delay or remove the early warning.

q: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection flags a sudden spike in Amazon EC2 spend in one account, but the team cannot tell which workload caused it. Which next step best isolates the cause?
options: Enable S3 Versioning on the billing bucket
Close the anomaly because anomaly detection is always a false positive
Open the anomaly in Cost Explorer or CUR filtered by account, service, Region, and cost allocation tags for the anomaly window to identify the driving usage type and resources
Purchase additional Reserved Instances to cover the spike
explain: An anomaly alert identifies unusual spend; root-cause work requires slicing the same window by account, service, usage type, Region, and tags in Cost Explorer or CUR. Buying commitments or changing the billing bucket does not diagnose the spike.

q: A company wants machine-learning-based monitoring that learns each service's normal spending pattern and alerts when spend deviates significantly, without the team hand-tuning a threshold for every service. Which service provides that capability?
options: AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, which uses machine learning to detect unusual spend and identify its likely root causes
Amazon CloudWatch alarms on the EstimatedCharges metric only
AWS Budgets with a fixed dollar threshold per service
AWS Config rules evaluated on billing records
explain: Cost Anomaly Detection builds per-service and per-account baselines with ML and surfaces anomalies with root-cause context. Fixed budgets and single-metric alarms require manual thresholds and cannot learn normal seasonal patterns per dimension.

q: New cost allocation tags were applied to resources yesterday, but the tags do not yet appear as dimensions in AWS Cost Explorer. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Tags never appear in Cost Explorer under any circumstances
The resources must be terminated and relaunched for tags to register
Cost allocation tags must be activated in the Billing console and then take time to appear in cost management products; tags applied but not activated are not available for reporting
Cost Explorer only supports account names as dimensions
explain: User-defined cost allocation tags require explicit activation and a propagation delay (often up to a day or more) before they become reportable dimensions. Relaunching resources is unnecessary, and activated tags are a standard Cost Explorer dimension.

q: An organisation wants a single payer account to receive the consolidated bill while each member account's usage, discounts, and tags remain separately visible for chargeback. Which structure provides that outcome?
options: Separate standalone accounts with no organisation relationship
A single S3 bucket that stores every team's invoices as PDFs
One shared root login used by every team
AWS Organizations with consolidated billing, reviewed through CUR and Cost Explorer grouped by linked account and cost allocation tags
explain: Consolidated billing in Organizations centralises payment while preserving per-account and per-tag visibility in CUR and Cost Explorer — the foundation for chargeback. Standalone accounts lose the consolidated view, and shared credentials destroy attribution entirely.

q: A team shares an Amazon ECS cluster and an Application Load Balancer across five products, and per-product cost reports currently assign the entire shared bill to whichever product was tagged first. Which capability most improves fairness?
options: Split cost allocation for supported shared resources, combined with per-product tags and Cost Categories, so shared costs are distributed by defined usage proportions
Tag the load balancer with all five product names in one tag value
Move every product to its own AWS account immediately
Disable cost allocation tags for shared resources
explain: Split cost allocation was built for shared container and load-balancing-style costs, distributing them by CPU, memory, or other defined shares instead of a single owner tag. A multi-name tag value cannot be split by billing, and account-per-product is a much larger migration than the reporting fix.

q: Finance asks for an hourly-granularity billing export that includes amortised costs for Reserved Instances and Savings Plans so internal dashboards match the invoices teams are charged against. Which configuration should the billing team choose?
options: An AWS Budgets email that lists the monthly total
A Cost and Usage Report with hourly granularity and the amortised cost view enabled for sharing with the analytics pipeline
A Trusted Advisor PDF attached to a support case
A Cost Explorer chart saved as a PNG image each morning
explain: CUR supports hourly line items and amortised cost columns that spread upfront and commitment fees across the usage they cover, which chargeback dashboards require. Screenshots, budget emails, and advisor PDFs cannot feed a reconciled analytics pipeline.

q: A department consistently exceeds its cloud budget mid-month, and leadership wants an automated guardrail rather than another email. Which AWS Budgets capability can act automatically when a threshold is breached?
options: Cost Anomaly Detection, which terminates the most expensive resource automatically
Tag policies, which delete untagged resources at month end
Budget actions, which can send SNS notifications, apply an IAM or SCP policy, or stop specified EC2 or RDS resources when the budget threshold is crossed
Cost Categories, which move charges to a different department
explain: Budget actions are the automated response mechanism attached to AWS Budgets: notifications, restrictive policies, or stopping targeted instances. Anomaly Detection only alerts, and tag policies or Cost Categories neither stop resources nor reassign charges automatically.

q: A company migrates to a new tagging standard and needs historical cost reports to reflect the new product groupings without waiting for a full year of newly tagged data. Which feature can regroup historical billing data by rule?
options: AWS Cost Categories, whose rules can be applied retroactively to historical months within the supported lookback period
S3 Lifecycle rules, which rename billing objects by month
Cost allocation tags, which rewrite resource tags in the past
Reserved Instance modification requests for past terms
explain: Cost Categories can recategorise up to the supported historical window when rules change, which suits a reporting restructure. Resource tags themselves cannot be backdated, and lifecycle or reservation tools do not regroup billing history.

q: An auditor asks how the company ensures that the Project tag uses only approved project codes and that deviations are visible centrally across all accounts. Which combination answers the auditor most completely?
options: An S3 bucket policy that stores the approved code list
Tag policies in AWS Organizations to define the approved codes, plus AWS Config required-tags and compliance reporting to detect resources that deviate
Cost Explorer filters saved by each account owner
A wiki page listing the approved codes, with voluntary compliance
explain: Governance needs both a defined standard (tag policies) and continuous detection (Config rules with organisation-wide reporting). Documentation alone does not enforce or detect, and saved filters or a stored list provide neither control.

q: A team wants to track Amazon Bedrock spending by counting input and output tokens per feature, not just total inference dollars, so it can price its AI features accurately. Which practice enables that unit-cost view?
options: Purchase Provisioned Throughput and treat its price as the per-feature cost
Rely solely on the monthly AWS invoice total for Bedrock
Disable Bedrock logging so token counts stay private
Emit per-feature token usage metrics and logs from the application, tag Bedrock usage by feature, and join that telemetry with CUR cost data to compute cost per feature and per thousand tokens
explain: Unit economics for AI features require application-level token telemetry joined to billing data by tag or feature dimension. The invoice total has no feature granularity, and a Provisioned Throughput commitment is a capacity price, not a per-feature token cost.

q: A multi-account organisation discovers that a Service Control Policy denies a required tagging API call, so automated tagging fails silently in member accounts. How should the platform team respond?
options: Disable the tagging automation and tag resources manually once a year
Update the SCP to allow the tagging actions the automation needs while keeping the deny rule that blocks resource creation without the required tags
Move all resources into the management account to bypass SCPs
Remove all SCPs so tagging automation can run without restriction
explain: The fix is a scoped SCP correction: permit the tag operations the automation performs while preserving the preventive deny on untagged creation. Removing all guardrails or abandoning automation sacrifices both enforcement and consistency.

q: A product's AWS costs are visible in Cost Explorer, but the support and shared platform fees are missing from the product's internal cost report. Which step completes the product's true cost picture?
options: Exclude shared costs permanently because they are not taggable
Convert shared costs into Spot Instance credits
Charge all shared costs to the newest product each month
Include allocated shared costs — such as support plans, management-account, and shared platform charges — through Cost Categories or split allocation rules in the internal report
explain: Full product cost includes an allocated share of untaggable and shared charges; Cost Categories and split allocation provide the mechanism to apportion them transparently. Excluding them understates product cost, and arbitrary assignment is not an allocation method.

q: A team receives AWS Cost Anomaly Detection alerts every day for normal weekend batch spikes and begins ignoring all alerts. Which tuning action restores the alerts' usefulness?
options: Configure anomaly monitors and alert subscriptions with appropriate dimensions and thresholds so predictable batch patterns are baselined and only genuine deviations alert the team
Turn off Cost Anomaly Detection for the entire organisation
Raise every AWS Budget by 50 percent
Delete the batch workload to stop the alerts
explain: Anomaly Detection learns baselines per monitor dimension; scoping monitors to the right accounts and services and setting sensible alert thresholds reduces noise from known patterns without disabling detection. Turning the service off loses protection against real anomalies.

q: An engineering manager wants a weekly view of Reserved Instance and Savings Plans coverage and utilisation to confirm the company's commitments are actually being used. Where should that review be performed?
options: In Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights queries over API calls
In S3 access logs for the billing bucket
In AWS Cost Explorer's Reserved Instances and Savings Plans utilisation and coverage reports, which show how much eligible usage the commitments covered
In the AWS Config timeline for each instance
explain: Cost Explorer hosts the commitment utilisation and coverage reporting that shows wasted or uncovered commitment. API logs, Config timelines, and bucket access logs do not aggregate commitment effectiveness.

q: A company enforces tagging through AWS Config and tag policies, yet each month a small set of resources still appears untagged in the CUR. Which additional preventive measure closes the remaining gap?
options: Increase the Config evaluation frequency to every minute
Ask teams to tag resources before the monthly invoice closes
Export the CUR more often so untagged resources appear sooner
Add IAM and SCP deny conditions on resource-creation APIs that require the mandatory tags at request time, covering the services Config can only detect after creation
explain: Detective controls inevitably leave a window between creation and detection; request-time deny conditions in IAM and SCPs close that window for supported creation APIs. Faster detection or export still leaves resources briefly untagged.

q: A SaaS company wants to bill its largest customers a cloud surcharge proportional to the AWS resources each customer actually consumed. Which data foundation makes that defensible?
options: A Cost Explorer screenshot of the monthly service totals
Spot Instance prices published on the AWS website
Consistent per-customer tagging (or per-customer accounts) joined to CUR line items, so each customer's resource usage and amortised cost can be evidenced line by line
The company's total AWS bill divided equally among all customers
explain: Defensible customer chargeback needs resource-level attribution — per-customer tags or accounts reconciled to CUR line items including amortisation. Equal splits and service totals cannot evidence what a specific customer consumed.

q: A team wants to be alerted when forecast spend for the month will exceed the approved amount, even though actual spend is still below it today. Which AWS Budgets setting provides that early warning?
options: An actual-cost alert set at 100 percent of the budget
