A forecasted budget alert that triggers when predicted month-end spend exceeds the budgeted amount
A tag policy that warns at resource creation time
A Cost Anomaly Detection monitor with no subscribers
explain: Forecasted budget notifications evaluate AWS's spend prediction against the budget and fire before the money is spent, enabling corrective action. Actual-cost alerts at 100 percent only confirm an overrun that has already occurred.

q: Different teams use inconsistent values for the same tag — for example 'prod', 'Production', and 'PROD' for the Environment tag — and cost reports fragment into three groups. Which governance tools directly address this inconsistency?
options: Tag policies that define the single allowed value set, combined with Config rules and reporting that surface resources using non-standard values
S3 Versioning, which keeps every value variant
Cost Explorer grouping, which automatically merges similar values
CloudFront field-level encryption for tag values
explain: Only tag governance — a defined value list in tag policies plus Config detection of deviations — standardises values at the source. Cost Explorer groups exactly what billing contains and cannot merge misspellings or case variants on its own.

q: A platform team needs to prove to finance that tagging compliance rose from 60 percent to 95 percent over two quarters. Which evidence source best supports that claim?
options: Anecdotal confirmation from each team lead
AWS Config compliance history for the required-tags rule across accounts, trended over the two quarters
The number of tag policies created during the period
A single Cost Explorer report from the final month
explain: Config records rule compliance over time per resource and account, providing auditable trend evidence for a tagging programme. A point-in-time cost report or a count of policies shows neither coverage nor improvement.

q: A company wants finance, not engineering, to own the definitions that map accounts, tags, and services into business reporting units, while engineering keeps owning resource tags. Which division of responsibility matches AWS tooling?
options: Finance purchases all Reserved Instances without usage data
Engineering maintains Cost Categories and finance applies resource tags manually
Both teams edit the same tag policies with no change control
Finance maintains AWS Cost Categories and the CUR analytics, while engineering maintains tagging standards enforced through tag policies, Config rules, and SCPs
explain: Cost Categories are a billing-side, rule-based reporting construct suited to finance ownership, whereas tags live on engineering-created resources and need engineering-side enforcement. Swapping the ownership puts each control furthest from the team that can operate it.

q: An organisation enables AWS Cost Anomaly Detection but routes every alert to a general inbox that no team monitors. Which change makes anomaly detection operationally effective?
options: Create per-service or per-account anomaly monitors with subscriptions that route alerts to the owning teams' SNS topics or email lists, with a defined triage process
Disable anomaly detection in member accounts
Increase the anomaly threshold so almost nothing alerts
Export anomalies to S3 once per year for review
explain: Detection only creates value when alerts reach an owner who can act; scoped monitors plus routed subscriptions and triage close that loop. Suppressing, archiving annually, or disabling detection discards the signal.

q: A workload's costs are correctly tagged, but the team is charged for data transfer between two of its own components and wants that transfer broken out separately in its cost review. Which data source gives transfer charges at the required detail?
options: A CloudWatch graph of network bytes with no pricing data
Tag policies that list transfer types as tag values
The Cost and Usage Report, filtered by usage type for the relevant data transfer categories and by the resources' cost allocation tags
The AWS pricing page for the two services involved
explain: CUR line items encode usage type (including the distinct data transfer categories) alongside tags and pricing, enabling a precise transfer breakout. Byte graphs lack pricing, and the public pricing page lacks the account's actual usage.

q: A company plans to move from showback to chargeback next quarter and wants departments to trust the numbers before money moves. Which practice most builds that trust?
options: Exclude Reserved Instance and Savings Plans effects from department totals
Start chargeback immediately with unpublished allocation rules
Round every department's total to the nearest thousand dollars
Publish the allocation methodology — tags, Cost Categories, split rules, and amortised commitment treatment — and reconcile the department totals to the AWS invoice for several showback cycles first
explain: Trust comes from a transparent, invoice-reconciled methodology proven over showback cycles, including how commitment discounts are amortised and allocated. Hidden rules, rounding, and omitted commitment effects all create disputes once real budgets are debited.

q: A team tags all new resources correctly, but a legacy application creates Amazon S3 buckets through an API path that does not support tagging on creation. How should governance handle this exception?
options: Block all bucket creation across the organisation with an SCP
Use AWS Config rules to detect the untagged buckets promptly and trigger automated remediation that applies the required tags after creation
Delete any bucket that is untagged for more than one hour
Exempt all S3 buckets from the tagging standard permanently
explain: Where creation-time tagging is unsupported, fast detective control plus automated remediation is the proportionate pattern. Blanket exemptions weaken the standard, blocking all creation breaks the business, and automatic deletion risks data loss.

q: An executive dashboard must show AWS cost per business transaction so the company can spot unit-cost creep even when total spend grows with the business. Which inputs are required to build that metric?
options: Tagged AWS cost data from CUR or Cost Explorer divided by a business volume metric (such as orders or active users) supplied from the company's own systems
The total AWS invoice alone, trended month over month
AWS Budgets thresholds expressed as percentages
Spot Instance price history for the account's Regions
explain: Unit cost is cost divided by business output; AWS supplies the numerator through tagged billing data, but the transaction denominator exists only in company systems. Total spend alone cannot distinguish healthy growth from efficiency loss.

q: A company stores millions of Amazon S3 objects whose access patterns are unpredictable — some are hot for a week, then untouched for a year. Which storage class automatically balances access cost and storage cost for this pattern?
options: Amazon S3 Standard for every object regardless of age
S3 Standard-IA with a one-day minimum billing duration ignored
Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects between access tiers based on observed access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive applied on the day objects are created
explain: Intelligent-Tiering was designed for unknown or changing access patterns, automatically tiering objects between frequent, infrequent, and archive tiers for a small monitoring fee. Glacier Deep Archive on day one would impose slow retrieval on hot objects, and Standard forever overpays for cold data.

q: Log files in Amazon S3 are accessed daily for 30 days, rarely for the next 60 days, and must be retained for seven years for compliance but are almost never read after day 90. Which lifecycle design is most cost-effective?
options: An S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, then to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive for the long retention period, expiring them after seven years
Keep all logs in S3 Standard for the full seven years
Delete the logs after 90 days to end storage charges
Move logs to EBS volumes attached to a logging instance
explain: Lifecycle tiering matches each age band to its cheapest suitable class — Standard-IA for infrequent access, Glacier classes for cheap long-term retention — then expires objects at the retention limit. Seven years in Standard wastes money, and deleting at 90 days violates the compliance requirement.

q: A team stores backups in S3 Standard-IA but retrieves 40 percent of the data every week for analytics, and retrieval fees now exceed the storage saving. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Moving the data to Glacier Instant Retrieval will remove retrieval fees
The workload's access pattern is too frequent for Standard-IA; those objects should return to S3 Standard or Intelligent-Tiering, where per-retrieval fees do not erase the storage discount
Standard-IA always costs less than Standard regardless of access frequency
Retrieval fees can be waived by enabling S3 Versioning
explain: Infrequent-access classes trade lower storage price for per-GB retrieval charges, so frequent reads can make them more expensive overall. Frequent-access data belongs in Standard or the frequent tier of Intelligent-Tiering, not in colder classes with their own retrieval pricing.

q: Regulatory archives must be kept for 10 years, are never expected to be read except in a legal emergency where a retrieval time of several hours is acceptable, and cost is the priority. Which S3 storage class fits best?
options: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for millisecond access
EFS Standard for archival file storage
S3 Glacier Deep Archive, the lowest-cost class, with retrieval times measured in hours
S3 Standard with Multi-AZ replication
explain: Deep Archive offers the lowest storage price for decade-long, almost-never-accessed data when hours-long retrieval is acceptable. Instant Retrieval pays a premium for millisecond access the scenario does not need, and Standard or EFS pricing is far higher for cold archives.

q: A media library needs archive storage that still allows occasional immediate previews, so millisecond retrieval from the archive tier is required. Which S3 Glacier class provides that?
options: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with bulk retrieval
S3 One Zone-IA with object lock enabled
S3 Glacier Deep Archive with expedited retrieval
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which offers millisecond retrieval for infrequently accessed data at a lower storage cost than Standard-IA
explain: Glacier Instant Retrieval is the archive-tier class built for millisecond access to rarely read data. Flexible and Deep Archive retrievals take minutes to hours regardless of the retrieval option chosen, so they cannot meet an immediate-preview requirement.

q: An Amazon EBS gp2 volume delivers 400 provisioned IOPS but the application needs 8,000 IOPS at 250 MB/s throughput, and the team wants to avoid paying for io2 volumes. Which migration meets the need most cheaply?
options: Migrate to an io2 Block Express volume sized for 64,000 IOPS
Stay on gp2 and increase the volume size until its size-based IOPS reach the target, regardless of wasted capacity
Migrate to an EBS gp3 volume, which independently provisions IOPS and throughput above its baseline at a lower price than gp2 and well below Provisioned IOPS volumes
Replace the volume with instance store storage
explain: gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from volume size, providing up to high IOPS and throughput at a low per-GB price, which fits an 8,000-IOPS need without io2 pricing. Growing gp2 purely for IOPS wastes capacity spend, and io2 Block Express is priced for far more demanding workloads.

q: A database volume truly requires sustained 40,000 IOPS with sub-millisecond latency and multi-attach resilience, and gp3 cannot meet its performance ceiling. Which EBS choice is justified despite its higher price?
options: An io2 (Provisioned IOPS SSD) volume sized to the required provisioned IOPS
A Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volume
A gp3 volume with its baseline 3,000 IOPS
A Cold HDD (sc1) volume
explain: io2 exists for mission-critical workloads whose provisioned IOPS and latency needs exceed gp3's ceiling, so its premium is justified only there. HDD classes and baseline gp3 cannot deliver 40,000 IOPS at sub-millisecond latency.

q: Amazon EFS file systems hold project data that is hot during a project and then untouched for months. Which EFS feature reduces cost for the cold data without manual migration?
options: Enabling EFS replication to a second Region for all projects
EFS Provisioned Throughput mode set to the maximum rate
Mounting the file system from every Availability Zone simultaneously
EFS Lifecycle Management transitioning files to the Infrequent Access storage class after a set period of inactivity
explain: EFS lifecycle policies automatically move inactive files to EFS Infrequent Access at a lower storage price and back on access. Provisioned Throughput at maximum and multi-Region replication raise cost, and mount topology does not tier cold files.

q: An Amazon DynamoDB table serves a spiky retail workload whose traffic varies 20-to-1 between quiet nights and sale events, and provisioned capacity is mostly idle. Which capacity mode best fits the cost profile?
options: Provisioned capacity sized for the sale-event peak at all times
DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode, which charges per request and removes the need to provision for peaks
Global tables replicated to five Regions on provisioned capacity
Provisioned capacity with a very large minimum and no auto scaling
explain: On-demand mode prices actual requests, suiting unpredictable or spiky traffic where provisioned peak capacity would sit idle most of the time. Provisioning for the peak or replicating globally multiplies the idle-capacity waste.

q: A DynamoDB table has a stable, predictable request rate that the team can forecast accurately for the next year, and it runs continuously. Which capacity strategy is most cost-effective?
options: Provisioned capacity with auto scaling (and Reserved Capacity where the commitment fits), which prices sustained throughput below equivalent on-demand request volume
Global tables with on-demand mode in every Region
Provisioned capacity set to ten times the forecast peak
On-demand capacity at all times regardless of volume
explain: At high, steady throughput, provisioned capacity is cheaper per unit than on-demand per-request pricing, and auto scaling plus reserved commitments trim it further. On-demand wins on spikiness, not on sustained predictable volume.

q: A production Amazon RDS database runs at a constant size 24 hours a day and will do so for at least the next two years. Which purchase option reduces its cost without changing its performance?
options: Aurora Serverless capacity purchased per hour of wall-clock time
On-Demand DB Instances with a larger instance class
Spot Instances for the RDS primary instance
Reserved DB Instances for that engine, instance class, and Region with a one- or three-year term
explain: Reserved DB Instances discount a steady, long-lived RDS footprint in exchange for a term commitment, exactly matching a constant two-year database. RDS has no Spot option, oversizing raises cost, and Aurora Serverless follows a different engine and billing model.

q: A development Amazon Aurora database is used only during weekday business hours and sits idle at night and on weekends. Which Aurora option best aligns cost with that usage?
options: RDS Reserved Instances with a three-year All Upfront payment
Aurora provisioned instances sized for peak load running around the clock
Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 with a minimum capacity that can scale down during idle periods (including toward zero where configured), paying for capacity in proportion to use
Aurora Global Database replicated to three Regions
explain: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity with actual load and can shrink dramatically when the database is idle, suiting intermittent dev usage. Always-on provisioned capacity, global replication, and three-year commitments all pay for time the database is unused.

q: An Amazon Aurora cluster's bill is dominated by per-million I/O charges because the application performs constant small writes, while its storage and instance costs are modest. Which Aurora configuration targets that specific cost?
options: S3 Intelligent-Tiering applied to the Aurora data files
Aurora I/O-Optimized, which includes I/O in a higher instance and storage price instead of charging per I/O, benefiting I/O-intensive workloads
Aurora Standard configuration with a larger writer instance
Aurora Serverless with provisioned concurrency enabled
explain: Aurora I/O-Optimized removes per-I/O billing in favour of higher instance/storage rates, which wins when I/O volume is high and predictable. Enlarging instances on Standard configuration leaves per-I/O charges untouched, and S3 tiering does not apply to Aurora storage.

q: A company commits to steady usage across Amazon RDS, Amazon Aurora, Amazon ElastiCache, and Amazon MemoryDB and wants a single flexible database discount commitment. Which instrument provides that?
options: Database Savings Plans, which commit to an hourly database usage amount and apply across supported database services, families, and Regions
Reserved DB Instances that can be exchanged between engines at will
Spot Instances pooled across the database fleet
Individual EC2 Instance Savings Plans for each database host
explain: Database Savings Plans are the cross-service commitment for the managed database family, trading an hourly commitment for discounts that follow usage across engines and instance families. Reserved DB Instances are narrower per-engine commitments, and database workloads cannot run on Spot.

q: An S3 bucket holds 50 TB of objects averaging 40 KB each, and a lifecycle rule moves them to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, yet the saving is smaller than expected. Which S3 pricing detail explains the shortfall?
options: Standard-IA charges double for objects smaller than 1 MB as a penalty
Standard-IA bills a minimum billable object size (128 KB) and a minimum storage duration, so very small objects and short stays erode the nominal per-GB saving
Lifecycle transitions are billed at Glacier Deep Archive retrieval rates
Small objects are automatically replicated to three Regions at extra cost
explain: Infrequent-access classes impose a 128 KB minimum billable size and minimum duration charges, which materially affect small-object workloads. There is no double-charge penalty or automatic extra replication; the shortfall is the minimum-size and duration mechanics.

q: A backup strategy keeps hourly EBS snapshots for 90 days through manual scripts, and snapshot storage grows without bound because nothing expires old copies. Which service automates retention so backup cost stays bounded?
options: AWS Backup with no vault or plan defined
S3 Lifecycle rules applied to the EBS volumes
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM), which creates snapshots on a schedule and deletes them automatically when the retention count or age is reached
CloudWatch alarms that email the team when snapshot count is high
explain: DLM's lifecycle policies exist precisely to schedule snapshot creation and enforce retention-based deletion, bounding snapshot spend. Alarms only notify, S3 lifecycle does not govern EBS snapshots, and an undefined Backup plan performs no automation.

q: A company must centralise backup for Amazon RDS, Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and DynamoDB with per-workload retention policies and reporting on backup cost. Which service provides that central management?
options: S3 Cross-Region Replication configured per resource
Manual snapshot scripts maintained by each application team
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager alone, for all four services
AWS Backup, which applies backup plans with retention rules across supported services and reports protected resources and jobs centrally
explain: AWS Backup is the cross-service backup service with plans, vaults, retention, and central reporting; DLM covers EBS (and related) lifecycle only. Per-team scripts fragment retention enforcement, and S3 replication is not a backup manager for databases and volumes.

q: Compliance requires database backups to be retained for one year, but the team currently keeps every daily backup in the same high-cost vault storage indefinitely. Which retention redesign preserves compliance at lower cost?
options: Delete backups older than 30 days and rely on a policy document
Set the AWS Backup plan's lifecycle to transition older backups to cold storage where supported and to expire backups after the one-year retention limit
Keep all backups in warm storage forever to simplify audits
Copy every backup to three additional Regions
explain: Backup lifecycle rules — cold-storage transition plus expiry at the compliance horizon — are the cost lever built into AWS Backup plans. Indefinite warm retention overpays, early deletion breaks compliance, and extra Regions multiply the retained footprint.

q: CloudWatch Logs costs climb because verbose debug logs from a production application are retained forever and ingested at full volume year-round. Which combination most reduces log cost while preserving useful observability?
options: Set every log group's retention to never expire
Stream all logs to a second Region for backup by default
Increase the log level to debug on all services for completeness
Filter or sample debug logging at the source, set a finite retention period on the log groups, and export only the data that needs long-term retention to cheaper S3 storage
explain: Log cost is driven by ingestion volume and retained gigabytes over time, so reducing verbosity at the source, expiring on schedule, and archiving selectively to S3 attack both drivers. Indefinite retention and more debug output are the causes, not the cure.

q: A team publishes hundreds of high-resolution custom CloudWatch metrics that are queried only as hourly averages in monthly reports. Which practice lowers metric cost while keeping the reports accurate?
options: Aggregate metrics before publishing (for example with statistic sets or pre-aggregation) and publish at the resolution the reports actually need, instead of paying for high-resolution storage on every raw data point
Keep high-resolution metrics forever in case of an audit
Duplicate the metrics into a second namespace for reporting
Publish each metric once per second to improve report precision
explain: Custom metric pricing scales with the number of metrics and stored resolution; pre-aggregation preserves the averages the reports consume at a fraction of the ingestion and storage cost. Higher frequency, duplication, and indefinite retention all raise the metric bill.

q: An Amazon S3 bucket contains objects that must be kept for a fixed legal hold period, after which they have no value. Storage cost review shows the bucket never uses lifecycle rules. Which minimal configuration solves the cost problem?
options: A bucket policy that denies all delete actions forever
S3 Versioning enabled with no lifecycle rules for old versions
An S3 Lifecycle rule that transitions the objects through cheaper storage classes during the hold where access allows and expires them automatically at the end of the hold period
Object Lock in governance mode with no expiration date
explain: Lifecycle transition plus expiration aligns storage price with the object's useful life and guarantees deletion when the hold ends. Versioning without lifecycle accumulates noncurrent versions, and a permanent delete deny or dateless lock makes the cost problem permanent.

q: A DynamoDB table used for session data sees each item read and written a few times and then never touched again, yet the table stores years of dead sessions. Which feature removes the dead data without ongoing scan-and-delete jobs?
options: Replicate the table globally so old items are archived elsewhere
Enable DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL) on an expiry attribute so items are deleted automatically after their session lifetime at no additional throughput cost
Convert the table to on-demand mode to delete items for free
Run a nightly provisioned scan that deletes expired items item by item
explain: TTL deletes expired items automatically in the background without consuming provisioned throughput, which fits session expiry exactly. Scan-and-delete jobs burn read and delete capacity continuously, and neither global replication nor a capacity-mode change removes expired items.

q: An Amazon RDS instance is oversized for its workload, but the team fears downtime from resizing during business hours. Which additional database cost lever requires no resize at all?
options: Add read replicas in three Regions for reporting
Enable Multi-AZ so the standby shares the primary's cost
Review storage configuration — for example moving from gp2 to gp3 storage or removing over-provisioned IOPS — and purchase Reserved DB Instances for the existing steady footprint
Increase the backup retention period to 35 days
explain: Storage type and commitment discounts change the bill without an instance resize: gp3 storage is cheaper than gp2 at equal performance for most workloads, and Reserved Instances discount unchanged steady usage. Multi-AZ, longer backup retention, and extra replicas all add cost.

q: A workload writes large binary objects to Amazon EBS volumes attached to EC2 instances and keeps them for years, paying block-storage prices for what is effectively object storage. Which migration most reduces storage cost?
options: Move the binaries to Amazon S3 with lifecycle tiering to Glacier classes as they age, reserving EBS for data that truly needs block semantics
Upgrade the volumes from gp3 to io2 for better durability pricing
Snapshot the volumes hourly and retain all snapshots
Enable EBS multi-attach so more instances share each volume
explain: S3 with lifecycle tiering prices long-lived object data far below EBS per-GB rates and adds Glacier tiers as data cools. io2 premiums, multi-attach, and unbounded snapshot retention all increase block-storage spend for data that does not need a block device.

q: An Aurora MySQL cluster is used for a reporting workload that runs two heavy queries each morning and is idle the rest of the day. Which deployment keeps the reporting capability at the lowest database cost?
options: Purchase three-year Reserved Instances for the peak-sized cluster
Replicate the cluster with Aurora Global Database for reporting locality
Provision a dedicated Aurora writer and two readers sized for the morning peak, running continuously
Use Aurora Serverless v2 for the reporting cluster (or a reader that scales with load) so capacity is paid for mainly during the morning query window
explain: Serverless capacity that tracks the two-query daily pattern avoids paying peak provisioned rates for 22 idle hours. Peak-sized always-on clusters and long commitments priced on that peak institutionalise the waste.

q: A team stores database backups as manual RDS snapshots and shares copies to a second account, keeping every snapshot ever taken. Snapshot charges now rival the database's own cost. Which governance change addresses the root cause?
options: Disable automated backups to reduce the snapshot count
Move to automated backups or AWS Backup with a defined retention period so snapshots expire on schedule, and audit shared manual snapshots for expiry as well
Share the snapshots to a third account for safekeeping
Convert manual snapshots to EBS snapshots for cheaper storage
explain: Unbounded manual snapshot retention is the root cause; a managed retention policy with automatic expiry — including an audit of shared copies — bounds it. Sharing to more accounts or converting formats preserves the unbounded growth.

q: An application performs frequent full-table scans on a DynamoDB table for a daily report, consuming large read capacity that dwarfs the application's transactional cost. Which redesign lowers the reporting cost most?
options: Replicate the table to a second Region and scan the replica
Double the table's provisioned read capacity permanently
Export the table data to Amazon S3 (for example with DynamoDB export to S3) and run the daily report with Athena or a similar analytics tool instead of scanning the operational table
Enable DAX so the scans are served from cache
explain: Moving analytical scans off the operational table onto an S3 export queried by Athena prices the report as analytics storage and queries rather than DynamoDB read units. More provisioned capacity, caching scans in DAX, and replica scans all keep paying table throughput for an analytics job.

q: A company's Amazon S3 bill shows a large share of spend on objects in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval that are accessed every few days by a customer-facing feature. Which diagnosis is most likely correct?
options: Retrieval frequency has no effect on Glacier class costs
The fix is to enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
Glacier Flexible Retrieval is the cheapest class for frequently accessed data
The data was tiered too aggressively for its actual access frequency; it belongs in S3 Standard-IA or Glacier Instant Retrieval, where retrieval pricing and latency suit regular access
explain: Flexible Retrieval charges per retrieval and takes minutes to hours, so regular customer-facing access makes it both slow and unexpectedly expensive. Warmer infrequent-access tiers price and perform correctly for data read every few days.

q: An EC2-based file server uses Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) volumes for a latency-sensitive metadata workload, and performance complaints push the team toward the most expensive fix first. Which EBS assessment should come before any purchase?
options: Confirm the workload's actual IOPS, throughput, and latency profile; most general workloads are served cheapest by gp3 with independently tuned IOPS and throughput rather than by Provisioned IOPS volumes
Replace all volumes with sc1 Cold HDD to cut cost first
Purchase io2 Block Express volumes for every file server immediately
Disable CloudWatch metrics so performance data cannot mislead the team
explain: gp3's independently adjustable IOPS and throughput satisfy most workloads at the lowest SSD price, so measuring the real profile prevents an unnecessary jump to io2 pricing. Cold HDD worsens a latency problem, and removing metrics removes the evidence the decision needs.

q: A SaaS product stores per-tenant exports in Amazon S3, and tenants download each export once within a week and never again, while exports must be kept for 90 days. Which storage design fits this access pattern?
options: Store exports in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from creation so the single download is as cheap as possible
Store exports in S3 Standard or Standard-IA for the first download window, then use a lifecycle rule to transition them to a Glacier class until the 90-day expiry deletes them
Keep exports in S3 Standard for a full year in case a tenant returns
Place exports on an EFS file system with Provisioned Throughput
explain: The pattern is one early download then silence: a warm tier serves the download cheaply and quickly, lifecycle tiering cuts the remaining 80-plus days of storage price, and expiry enforces the 90-day limit. Deep Archive from creation would make the expected download slow and retrieval-charged.

q: A team wants to cut observability spend and proposes deleting all application metrics and shortening all log retention to one day across production. Which response best balances cost and operability?
options: Apply cost-effective observability selectively — aggregate low-value metrics, filter noisy logs, and tier retention by value — while keeping the metrics and logs needed for incident response and SLOs intact
Move all logs to Glacier Deep Archive with a one-day retrieval expectation
Keep every metric at one-second resolution to be safe
Approve the proposal because observability data has no operational value
explain: Observability cost optimisation is about matching fidelity and retention to operational value, not eliminating visibility on production systems. Blanket deletion blinds incident response, while maximum resolution everywhere preserves the overspend the review targeted.

q: An Amazon ElastiCache cluster runs a large memory-optimised node 24 hours a day for a cache whose working set fits in a quarter of its memory. Which action most reduces cache cost without changing the application?
options: Add a second cluster in another Region for symmetry
Enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover on every development cache
Right-size the cluster to a smaller node (including a Graviton family where supported) based on measured memory and CPU utilisation
Purchase the largest node as a Reserved Instance for three years
explain: Cache cost follows node size and count; measured headroom of 75 percent means a smaller (and possibly Graviton) node serves the same working set for less. Extra Regions, unnecessary Multi-AZ on dev caches, and committing to the oversized node all preserve or grow the waste.

q: A database team must choose between Aurora I/O-Optimized and Aurora Standard for a new write-heavy cluster, and it has reliable I/O volume forecasts. Which decision rule is correct?
options: Choose based on which configuration has the shorter name in the console
Always choose Standard because its instance price is lower
Always choose I/O-Optimized because it is newer
Estimate the per-I/O charges under Standard configuration from the forecast; if those charges exceed the I/O-Optimized price premium for instances and storage, choose I/O-Optimized
explain: I/O-Optimized trades higher instance and storage rates for zero per-I/O billing, so the breakeven is a calculation from forecast I/O volume — high-I/O workloads win, low-I/O workloads overpay. Recency or headline instance price alone cannot decide it.

q: A growing S3 bucket has no lifecycle rules, and analysis shows 20 percent of its bytes are incomplete multipart uploads and superseded object versions. Which cleanup yields immediate saving with no application change?
options: Add S3 Lifecycle rules to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a few days and expire or tier noncurrent versions on a defined schedule
Enable bucket default encryption with a customer-managed key
Replicate the bucket so the waste exists in two Regions
Turn on S3 access logging for the bucket
explain: Incomplete multipart parts and noncurrent versions are billed storage that lifecycle rules can remove automatically — a pure saving with no application impact. Encryption, logging, and replication do not delete the wasted bytes; logging and replication add more.

q: A company runs Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for a workload whose compute needs swing between near-zero overnight and moderate peaks twice a day, on an engine and architecture that support serverless database options. Which evaluation should the architect lead with?
options: Add two read replicas so the peaks are shared across three instances
Purchase a three-year Reserved DB Instance sized for the twice-daily peak
Evaluate Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 (PostgreSQL-compatible) against the RDS footprint, because its capacity scaling matches a near-zero-to-moderate swing better than a fixed provisioned instance
Move the workload to DynamoDB without reviewing access patterns
explain: A near-zero trough makes fixed provisioned capacity — especially a peak-sized reservation — mostly idle spend, so a serverless database evaluation leads. Replicas multiply idle capacity, and a database-engine migration without access-pattern analysis is not a cost decision.

q: A company with 800 on-premises servers needs a data-driven business case and portfolio assessment before committing to migration waves. Which approach should the solutions architect recommend first?
options: Migrate all servers immediately with Application Migration Service and assess costs after cutover
Purchase Reserved Instances for the estimated fleet before any discovery is performed
Decommission the oldest servers first without dependency mapping to reduce scope
Use AWS Migration Evaluator and application discovery to inventory servers, model costs, and prioritize the portfolio
explain: Migration Evaluator combined with discovery data builds a defensible business case from actual utilization and licensing. Migrating or buying commitments before assessment guesses at sizing, and decommissioning without dependency mapping risks breaking applications.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: During discovery, a team finds a critical application whose server dependencies are unknown, so it cannot be safely grouped into a migration wave. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Move the application alone and discover its dependencies from production errors after cutover
Run agent-based discovery to map inbound and outbound dependencies, then assign the application to a wave based on those dependencies
Place the application in the first wave to surface problems early
Exclude the application permanently from the migration portfolio
explain: Agent-based discovery reveals process and network dependencies so wave planning avoids severing connected components. Moving first and learning from outages is reckless, and exclusion ignores a critical workload.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A migration factory must move 300 VMware virtual machines to EC2 with minimal redesign and continuous replication until cutover. Which service is designed for this rehosting pattern?
options: AWS DataSync
AWS Application Migration Service (MGN)
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS)
AWS Elastic Beanstalk
explain: MGN performs block-level continuous replication for lift-and-shift rehosting of servers to EC2. DMS migrates databases, DataSync moves file/object data, and Beanstalk is an application platform, not a server replication tool.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A firm wants to assess and transform a large VMware estate, including automated discovery and wave planning for modernization, rather than manually scripting each move. Which AWS offering best fits?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
Amazon Route 53 Resolver
AWS Transform for VMware
AWS WAF
explain: AWS Transform for VMware automates assessment, dependency mapping, and migration/modernization planning for VMware workloads. Parameter Store, Route 53 Resolver, and WAF have no migration transformation role.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A legacy Oracle database must move to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. The engines differ, so schema conversion is required. Which combination should be used?
options: AWS DataSync to copy the database files directly into Aurora
AWS DMS alone with a full load and no schema conversion
Application Migration Service to replicate the Oracle host into Aurora
AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to convert the schema, then AWS DMS with change data capture for ongoing replication
explain: SCT converts heterogeneous schemas while DMS with CDC keeps the target in sync for a low-downtime cutover. DMS alone cannot convert incompatible objects, DataSync does not migrate databases transactionally, and MGN replicates servers, not database engines.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company only needs a one-time homogeneous migration from on-premises MySQL to Amazon RDS for MySQL during a weekend window, with no engine change. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A strangler fig refactor of the database into microservices before any data moves
AWS DMS full-load migration, optionally using native MySQL replication or backup/restore because the engines match
AWS Transform for mainframe conversion of the MySQL schema
AWS SCT must rewrite every table because the source and target engines are identical
explain: Homogeneous migrations need no schema conversion because engines match; DMS full load or native tools suffice. SCT conversion, mainframe transformation, and a refactor add unnecessary work.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Petabytes of on-premises NFS file data must move to Amazon EFS and then stay synchronized until the final cutover weekend. Which service best handles the transfer and incremental sync?
options: Amazon Elastic Disaster Recovery
AWS Backup
AWS DataSync
AWS Database Migration Service
explain: DataSync is purpose-built for large-scale file and object data transfer with scheduling, verification, and incremental synchronization. DMS is for databases, Elastic Disaster Recovery replicates servers for DR, and Backup protects AWS resources.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A monolithic .NET application on Windows servers will be replatformed to managed containers with minimal code change, removing the need to patch guest operating systems. Which target is most suitable?
options: Amazon EC2 with self-managed Docker installed manually
AWS Lambda with the entire monolith deployed as a single function zip
On-premises VMware retained with a VPN connection
Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate
explain: ECS on Fargate replatforms containers onto a managed, serverless compute layer without guest OS patching. Self-managed EC2 keeps the patching burden, a monolith rarely fits Lambda constraints, and staying on premises is not a migration.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A team is decomposing a monolith into microservices incrementally, routing new functionality to new services while the legacy system continues running. Which pattern describes this refactor?
options: Strangler fig pattern
Backup and restore pattern
Rehosting pattern
Big-bang cutover pattern
explain: The strangler fig pattern incrementally replaces monolith functionality behind a facade or router until the old system can retire. Rehosting changes no architecture, big-bang replaces all at once, and backup/restore is a DR strategy.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An organization wants to retire an application whose data must be retained for seven years for compliance, but the application itself has no future business use. In migration portfolio terms, what should happen?
options: Repurchase the application as a SaaS product solely to store its old data
Refactor the application into microservices before shutting it down
Retire the application and archive its data to low-cost storage that meets retention requirements
Rehost the application unchanged to EC2 and keep it running indefinitely
explain: Retiring removes the workload while archived data satisfies retention at low cost. Running or refactoring a useless application wastes spend, and buying SaaS just for archival is disproportionate.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Leadership asks why some applications are scheduled in later migration waves even though their servers are simple to move. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Simple servers must always wait because MGN cannot replicate them early
Wave planning groups applications by dependencies, business criticality, and risk, not by server simplicity alone
Later waves are reserved only for the largest servers by disk size
Applications are waved alphabetically by application name
explain: Waves sequence interdependent components together and balance risk and business events. Disk size, alphabet, or a fictitious MGN limitation do not drive sound wave planning.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company plans to replatform a self-managed PostgreSQL database to a managed service to reduce patching, backups, and failover administration without changing its application SQL. Which target best achieves this?
options: Amazon Redshift
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL
Amazon Neptune
Amazon DynamoDB
explain: RDS for PostgreSQL keeps the same engine and SQL while AWS manages patching, backups, and Multi-AZ failover. DynamoDB, Redshift, and Neptune require data-model or query changes.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An enterprise wants to modernize a COBOL mainframe workload by refactoring it to Java running on managed AWS services. Which AWS service is specifically designed for mainframe modernization?
options: AWS Mainframe Modernization
Amazon SageMaker
AWS Migration Hub
AWS Outposts
explain: AWS Mainframe Modernization provides tooling and runtimes to refactor or replatform mainframe workloads, including automated COBOL-to-Java conversion. Migration Hub orchestrates tracking, SageMaker is ML, and Outposts extends AWS on premises.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A database migration must keep source and target synchronized for weeks while application testing runs against the target, then cut over in minutes. Which DMS feature enables this?
options: S3 Cross-Region Replication of the database backup files
Change data capture (CDC) ongoing replication after an initial full load
AWS DataSync scheduled file copies
A one-time full load task run once at the start of testing
explain: CDC continuously applies source changes after the full load, so the target stays current during testing and cutover is brief. A single full load goes stale, and file-copy mechanisms do not apply transactional changes.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A solutions architect must choose between rehosting and refactoring a differentiating customer-facing application that is constrained by its legacy architecture. Which reasoning best supports refactoring?
options: Any application older than five years must be refactored by policy
Refactoring avoids all testing because new code is inherently more reliable
Refactoring is always cheaper than rehosting for every workload
The application provides competitive advantage and its current architecture blocks needed agility and scaling, justifying the higher refactor effort
explain: Refactor effort is justified where business differentiation and architectural constraints demand change. It is neither universally cheaper nor test-free, and age alone is not a decision criterion.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A retailer cannot migrate during its November and December peak freeze. How should this constraint shape the migration plan?
options: Schedule migration waves outside the freeze window and use the freeze period for discovery, testing, and readiness work
Cancel discovery until after the freeze ends
Ignore the freeze because cloud cutovers are risk-free
Plan the largest cutover for the peak weekend when traffic validates performance
explain: Business constraints such as freeze periods drive wave timing; preparation can continue safely during the freeze. Cutting over at peak maximizes risk, and pausing all work wastes the window.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company discovers through portfolio assessment that a commercial off-the-shelf application is available as a SaaS product with equivalent features. Which migration strategy does adopting the SaaS version represent?
options: Retain
Rehost
Replatform
Repurchase (drop and shop)
explain: Repurchasing replaces the application with a SaaS offering. Rehost moves it unchanged, replatform makes limited platform changes, and retain keeps it in place.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An application depends on a licensing model that is not supported in the cloud and has no business owner requesting a move this year. What is the most defensible portfolio decision?
options: Rehost it immediately and resolve licensing after cutover
Retire it without consulting the business owner
Retain the application on premises for now and revisit it in a later planning cycle
Refactor it in the first wave to force a licensing change
explain: Retain is appropriate when technical blockers and lack of business demand make migration premature. Moving first creates compliance risk, and retiring without an owner decision is improper.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A team will replatform a Java application from on-premises Tomcat servers to a managed container service, keeping the code largely intact but changing the deployment unit. Which benefit is the primary driver?
options: Conversion of the application into event-driven functions automatically
Zero operational responsibility for capacity, security, and configuration
Elimination of all application testing because containers never fail
Reduced infrastructure management while preserving application behavior and most code
explain: Replatforming trades self-managed servers for managed container infrastructure with minor changes. It does not eliminate testing, auto-convert code to functions, or remove all operational duties.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: To prepare mainframe batch jobs for modernization, architects need an inventory of programs, dependencies, and complexity before choosing refactor or replatform. Which activity should come first?
options: Rewrite the highest-volume batch job in Java without analyzing its callers
Decommission the mainframe scheduler before mapping job dependencies
Use AWS Mainframe Modernization assessment/discovery tooling to analyze the mainframe codebase and dependencies
Move batch files with DataSync and declare the modernization complete
explain: Mainframe assessment reveals code and dependency complexity that determines the right pattern. Rewriting, decommissioning, or moving files without that analysis risks breaking interdependent jobs.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A migration wave failed its first cutover rehearsal because a downstream reporting system was not migrated or connected. Which planning artifact would most likely have prevented this?
options: A larger instance size for the migrated application servers
An additional backup taken immediately before cutover
A post-cutover survey of business users
A dependency map and wave plan that include downstream consumers in the same wave or provide interim connectivity
explain: Dependency mapping ensures consumers and providers move together or stay connected. Bigger instances, surveys, and backups do not fix a missing dependency plan.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A firm wants to adopt serverless for a new image-processing feature extracted from its monolith, with spiky, unpredictable demand and no servers to manage. Which design best fits?
options: S3 events triggering AWS Lambda functions, with results stored in Amazon S3 or DynamoDB
A fixed fleet of EC2 instances sized for peak load running 24/7
Keeping image processing inside the monolith and adding more on-premises servers
A single large container running continuously on a self-managed host
explain: Event-driven Lambda scales with spiky demand and removes server management. Fixed fleets over-provision, and expanding the monolith contradicts the extraction goal.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Which metric set is most useful when right-sizing EC2 targets during portfolio assessment?
options: Actual CPU, memory, network, and storage utilization collected over a representative period
The number of users in the application's login table only
Peak utilization from a single one-hour snapshot on the busiest day ever recorded
The vendor's original nameplate capacity printed on the hardware
explain: Representative utilization data prevents both over-provisioning and undersizing. Nameplate specs and single snapshots misrepresent real demand, and user counts alone say nothing about resource use.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company uses AWS DMS and discovers that some source tables lack primary keys, causing replication performance and consistency concerns. What is the best remediation?
options: Ignore the issue because CDC works identically without keys
Delete the affected tables from the migration scope permanently
Switch the migration to DataSync so table keys no longer matter
Add primary keys or unique indexes to the source tables (or use supplemental logging/limited LOB handling appropriately) before ongoing replication
explain: DMS CDC relies on keys to apply updates and deletes efficiently and correctly; remediating the source schema is the fix. DataSync does not migrate databases, ignoring the issue risks inconsistency, and dropping tables loses data.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An architect proposes using Application Migration Service to move a database from Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL to save licensing costs. Why is this proposal flawed?
options: MGN replicates the server and its storage as-is, so the workload would still run Oracle on EC2 rather than converting to Aurora
MGN only works for databases smaller than 1 TB
MGN automatically converts Oracle schemas to PostgreSQL during replication
MGN cannot replicate any server that runs a database
explain: MGN is a lift-and-shift server replication tool; it preserves the engine, so licensing and conversion goals require DMS/SCT to Aurora instead. It does replicate database servers, within documented limits unrelated to a 1 TB cutoff.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A migration program needs a central place to track progress across MGN, DMS, and multiple accounts as waves execute. Which service provides that orchestration and tracking view?
options: AWS Migration Hub
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon CloudWatch
Amazon Inspector
explain: Migration Hub tracks migration progress across AWS and partner tools in one console. CloudWatch monitors metrics, CloudTrail audits API calls, and Inspector finds vulnerabilities — none orchestrate migrations.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A workload with steady, predictable file-transfer needs must move continuously changing media files from on-premises storage to S3 over several months. Which DataSync capability is most relevant?
options: DMS CDC applied directly to the media files
One manual copy at project start with no further synchronization
MGN block replication of the file server into S3
Scheduled, incremental DataSync tasks that transfer only changed files with data integrity verification
explain: DataSync schedules incremental transfers and verifies integrity, keeping S3 current over a long migration. A single copy goes stale, and DMS/MGN do not write file data into S3 as a managed transfer.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company wants to modernize a legacy application by first rehosting it, then incrementally optimizing once it is stable in AWS. Why is this sequenced approach often recommended?
options: Modernization must always precede migration to be effective
It reduces initial migration risk and timeline while creating a path to modernize with cloud-native services after the move
Sequencing eliminates the need for testing at cutover
Rehosting permanently prevents any later modernization
explain: Move-then-modernize balances speed and risk: land safely first, optimize second. Rehosting does not block later change, modernization need not come first, and cutover testing remains essential.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A team is replatforming an on-premises Microsoft SQL Server database to Aurora MySQL-compatible to exit commercial licensing, but the application uses T-SQL stored procedures. What is the greatest migration risk to plan for?
options: The color scheme of the management console after migration
The physical size of the data files during transfer
Inability to create any backups on Aurora MySQL
Incompatible stored procedures and SQL dialect differences requiring SCT assessment and code conversion
explain: Heterogeneous moves fail most often on dialect and stored-procedure incompatibility, which SCT assessment surfaces early. File transfer is routine with DMS, and Aurora fully supports backups.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: During a wave rehearsal, application performance on EC2 is poor because the target instance was sized from allocated on-premises capacity rather than actual use. Which assessment practice prevents recurrence?
options: Right-sizing from collected utilization metrics in the discovery and portfolio assessment phase
Adding a second Availability Zone to the same instance
Enabling detailed monitoring after users complain
Always choosing the largest available instance family
explain: Discovery utilization data drives right-sizing; allocated capacity overstates need but mismatched instance choice still harms performance/cost. Largest instances waste money, and monitoring alone does not size targets.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A global firm wants a repeatable migration factory: standardized landing zone, wave runbooks, and automated replication for hundreds of applications. Which element is most critical to factory throughput?
options: Standardized patterns and automation for common migration paths (rehost, replatform) so teams are not designing each move from scratch
Delaying the landing zone until after the first 100 applications move
Manual checklists performed by a single engineer for all waves
A unique, hand-crafted architecture for every application regardless of similarity
explain: A factory depends on repeatable patterns, automation, and a ready landing zone. Bespoke designs, single-person manual work, and a missing landing zone destroy throughput.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An application owner insists on refactoring a low-value internal tool that is used by five people and will be replaced next year. What should the architect recommend instead and why?
options: Retire it today without providing the replacement
Convert it to a multi-Region active-active design
Refactor it first because all internal tools deserve microservices
Rehost or retain the tool, because refactor investment cannot pay back before its planned replacement
explain: Migration strategy must match business value and remaining life; a short-lived low-value tool merits rehost or retain. Refactoring or active-active design grossly over-invests.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company migrating SAP and non-SAP workloads wants to validate that target Aurora and RDS configurations will meet performance before cutover. Which step best de-risks this?
options: Skip testing because managed databases always outperform on-premises systems
Convert all databases in a single weekend without rehearsal
Run proof-of-concept migrations with DMS test tasks and load/performance testing on the target databases
Test only after production cutover when real users generate load
explain: POC migrations with representative load expose target performance and conversion issues before commitment. Managed services are not automatically faster, and production is not a test environment.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Which scenario is the best fit for AWS DataSync rather than AWS Storage Gateway or a manual copy?
options: Block-level replication of a running application server for cutover
Real-time conversion of COBOL programs to Java
Automated, high-speed transfer of millions of files from an on-premises NFS share to Amazon S3 with bandwidth scheduling and verification
Transactional replication of an Oracle database to Aurora
explain: DataSync excels at large-scale, verifiable file/object transfers with scheduling. Databases need DMS, running servers need MGN, and COBOL conversion is a mainframe modernization task.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An organization plans to break a monolith into microservices owned by separate teams, each with its own database. Which principle is central to this refactor?
options: A single shared database that all microservices update directly
Domain-driven decomposition with bounded contexts, so each service owns its data and can deploy independently
Deploying all services together in one release train forever
Keeping all business logic in one shared library that every service must redeploy to change
explain: Bounded contexts and per-service data ownership enable independent deployment and scaling. Shared databases and lockstep releases recreate monolith coupling.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A legacy application cannot be modified, but its file-based integration must move to AWS ahead of the application itself. Data must appear in S3 for new analytics while the legacy app still writes files on premises. Which approach bridges the transition?
options: Copy files manually by email attachment to the analytics team
Block all analytics until the application eventually retires
Use DataSync to replicate the file data to S3 on a schedule while the legacy application remains the writer
Refactor the legacy application despite the constraint that it cannot change
explain: DataSync provides interim data movement without touching the unmodifiable application. Manual copies are unreliable, and waiting stalls the business need.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A migration business case shows high projected savings, but the assessment ignored software licensing costs for commercial databases and OS on EC2. What is the most likely consequence?
options: The savings estimate becomes more accurate by omitting a major cost
Licensing never affects cloud migration economics
The business case overstates savings, and the portfolio decision may change once license-inclusive modeling is applied
AWS automatically waives all third-party license costs on EC2
explain: Licensing is a major migration cost driver; omitting it inflates savings and can flip strategy choices (for example toward Aurora or Linux). AWS does not waive third-party licenses.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A team must migrate a 40 TB Oracle database with only a 4-hour cutover window. Online replication is required. Which design meets the window?
options: Weekly tape backups shipped to AWS and restored at cutover
DataSync copying live database files during the window
DMS full load followed by CDC ongoing replication, with cutover when replication lag approaches zero
A dump-and-restore performed entirely inside the 4-hour window
explain: Pre-syncing with full load + CDC makes the window only about final catch-up and switch. Offline dump/restore of 40 TB cannot fit 4 hours, and copying live database files is not transactionally safe.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An enterprise modernizes its integration layer by replacing a legacy ESB with event-driven services. Which AWS combination best supports this refactor?
options: Amazon EventBridge and Amazon SQS/SNS with Lambda or ECS services consuming events asynchronously
A single EC2-hosted ESB scaled vertically without limit
Direct database links between every pair of applications
Nightly CSV file drops as the only integration mechanism
explain: EventBridge plus queues/topics decouple producers and consumers in an event-driven refactor. A monolithic ESB, point-to-point DB links, and batch files preserve the legacy coupling.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Before migrating, a company wants to know which applications are idle 'zombie' workloads consuming data-center resources. Which discovery output identifies them?
options: A list of applications sorted by contract renewal date
The number of printers on each office floor
Utilization analysis showing servers with consistently near-zero CPU, memory, and network activity over the observation period
The physical rack location of each server
explain: Zombie detection comes from sustained near-zero utilization in discovery data. Contract dates, rack locations, and printers do not indicate workload activity.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A solutions architect is asked to replatform a stateless web tier so it gains managed scaling and deployment with almost no code change, while the team keeps its existing WAR deployment model initially. Which consideration is most accurate about choosing containers over functions here?
options: Lambda can run any unmodified WAR file with no time or packaging limits
Containers on ECS Fargate preserve the existing deployment model and runtime, whereas Lambda would require repackaging the app around function and event constraints
Containers cannot scale automatically under any configuration
ECS requires managing and patching the underlying host operating systems on Fargate
explain: Replatforming favors minimal-change targets; ECS/Fargate keeps the WAR model without host patching. Lambda imposes packaging and execution limits and cannot run an arbitrary WAR unchanged.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A mainframe replatform project wants to keep COBOL code largely as-is but run it on AWS-managed mainframe runtime instead of refactoring to Java. Which AWS Mainframe Modernization option fits?
options: Rehosting the physical mainframe hardware into an AWS data center
Replatforming to the AWS Mainframe Modernization managed runtime (for example, Micro Focus/Bull-based runtime) without a language rewrite
Refactoring with automated COBOL-to-Java conversion tooling
Replacing all batch jobs with Lambda functions in the first phase
explain: Mainframe Modernization supports both refactor (to Java) and replatform (managed runtime preserving COBOL). Physical mainframe hardware cannot be rehosted into AWS, and wholesale Lambda replacement is not the replatform path.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A migration wave includes a database, its application servers, and a batch scheduler that must move together because they exchange files hourly. What is the correct wave-planning decision?
options: Move components in alphabetical order regardless of exchanges
Move the database first and the scheduler three months later with no interim plan
Assume hourly file exchanges will tolerate a multi-week outage
Keep the three components in the same wave (or provide tested interim file connectivity) so the hourly exchange is never severed
explain: Interdependent components that exchange data frequently belong in the same wave or need interim connectivity. Separating them without a bridge breaks the business process.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company wants to use AWS Transform capabilities for a .NET Framework application that must move to .NET on Linux containers to cut Windows licensing. This is best described as which activity?
options: Modernization/transformation of the application codebase and platform, beyond a simple rehost
A backup strategy, because containers store application data
A retire decision, because Linux cannot run .NET workloads
A rehost, because the application code and OS remain identical
explain: Transform tooling assists code and platform modernization such as .NET Framework to modern .NET on Linux. The code/OS change means it is not a rehost, and modern .NET runs well on Linux.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: Which discovery method provides the deepest dependency data for servers that will be migrated with tight cutover windows?
options: Agent-based discovery (Discovery Agent/Application Discovery Service agent) collecting process, performance, and connection data over time
A single interview with the application owner
Reviewing purchase orders for the original hardware
Scanning public DNS records for the company domain
explain: Installed agents observe real connections and performance continuously, giving the deepest dependency evidence. Interviews, purchase records, and DNS provide only partial, static views.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A portfolio contains 200 applications; 60 are candidates for SaaS replacement, 90 for rehost, and 50 need detailed assessment. What does this exercise represent?
options: Rationalization of the portfolio into migration strategies (the 7 Rs) to prioritize effort and waves
A chaos engineering experiment
A backup retention policy decision
A disaster recovery failover test
explain: Assigning 7 R strategies across the portfolio is rationalization, the core of portfolio assessment. It is unrelated to DR testing, chaos experiments, or backup retention.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A DMS replication task shows high latency because a single large table without a primary key is being replicated with row-by-row lookups. Which additional DMS design choice can help large-table throughput?
options: Reduce the target database storage to force smaller transactions
Segment the large table and use parallel load settings (for example, table segmentation by ranges) for the full load phase
Convert the migration to a manual CSV export
Disable all logging so failures are invisible
explain: Table segmentation enables parallel full-load threads for large tables. Disabling logging hides problems, shrinking storage hurts, and manual CSV abandons managed replication.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An architect recommends serverless adoption for an infrequently used internal API with bursty traffic that currently runs on an always-on server. Which outcome is the strongest justification?
options: The API gains a fixed monthly cost identical to the server
Cost and operations shift to pay-per-request with automatic scaling and no idle server to patch or pay for
Serverless removes the need to design authentication for the API
Traffic bursts will be rejected once a concurrency ceiling design is ignored
explain: Bursty, infrequent workloads are ideal for Lambda/API Gateway economics and zero idle cost. Serverless does not remove auth design duties or make capacity planning irrelevant.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A firm migrating to AWS must prove to auditors how each application was assessed and why its strategy was chosen. Which practice best supports this governance need?
options: Delete discovery data after each wave to save storage
Record rationale only verbally in stand-up meetings
Maintain discovery data, assessment outputs, and strategy rationale in the migration portfolio tooling (Migration Hub/Migration Evaluator) as the system of record
Keep decisions in individual engineers' notebooks
explain: Auditable migration governance needs a retained system of record linking evidence to decisions. Notebooks, verbal decisions, and deletion defeat auditability.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A workload consists of Windows file shares used by a design team that must move to AWS with SMB access preserved and minimal application change. Which target and transfer pairing fits best?
options: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server as the target, with DataSync (or Robocopy/DMS-style file migration tooling) transferring the share data
Amazon Neptune as the target with DataSync loading graph data
AWS Lambda as the target file system
Amazon DynamoDB as the target with DMS converting files to items
explain: FSx for Windows preserves SMB/NTFS semantics for Windows shares, and DataSync moves the file data. NoSQL, graph stores, and functions are not SMB file targets.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company plans phased strangler-fig modernization behind Amazon API Gateway. How does API Gateway support the pattern?
options: It converts REST calls into database transactions on the monolith
It automatically rewrites monolith code into microservices
It acts as the facade, routing some paths to the legacy system and others to new microservices so functionality migrates incrementally
It blocks all traffic to the legacy system from day one
explain: Strangler fig needs a routing facade; API Gateway directs each route to old or new implementations during gradual replacement. It does not rewrite code or force an immediate full cutover.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: An organization discovers that 30% of its portfolio is interlinked through a shared authentication service. How should wave planning respond?
options: Migrate the shared authentication service early (or dual-run it) so dependent applications can move in subsequent waves without losing authentication
Ignore the shared service because authentication is not a dependency
Duplicate the authentication database per application without synchronization
Migrate all dependent applications first and authentication last
explain: Shared services are foundational dependencies; landing or dual-running them early unblocks later waves. Moving dependents first or ignoring the dependency guarantees failures.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A team replatforms from self-managed Cassandra to a managed, Cassandra-compatible service mindset but is told to stay with the listed managed targets in the migration plan: RDS, Aurora, ECS, and Lambda. Which statement is most accurate?
options: There is no direct Cassandra-equivalent among RDS/Aurora, so the plan needs either a containerized Cassandra on ECS as an interim replatform or a data-model refactor — it should not claim RDS is a drop-in replacement
RDS for MySQL stores wide-column data identically to Cassandra
Aurora PostgreSQL accepts Cassandra CQL natively with no changes
Lambda can host the Cassandra cluster statefully without storage services
explain: Honest assessment matters: RDS/Aurora do not speak CQL or replicate Cassandra's model, so ECS-hosted Cassandra or a refactor is required. Claiming a drop-in SQL replacement would break the application.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: What is the primary purpose of a migration readiness assessment before large-scale waves begin?
options: Evaluate organizational, operational, security, and platform readiness so gaps are remediated before they stall migration at scale
Replace the need for a landing zone
Guarantee AWS will waive migration service fees
Certify that every application has already been migrated
explain: Readiness assessment finds people/process/platform gaps early. It does not certify completed work, replace the landing zone, or affect fees.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A database team chooses DMS with a minimal-downtime approach for an e-commerce database. Which cutover practice is essential?
options: Delete the source database before validating the target
Change application connection strings randomly over the following week
Cut over while replication lag is at its daily peak to test resilience
Validate data with DMS validation, monitor replication lag to near zero, stop writes briefly, and switch connection strings/DNS in a rehearsed runbook
explain: Safe cutover requires validated data, near-zero lag, and a rehearsed switch. Cutting over at peak lag loses transactions, and deleting the source before validation removes the fallback.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A business requires RTO of 15 minutes and RPO of 1 minute for a critical ordering system, at the lowest cost that meets those targets. Which DR strategy is most appropriate?
options: Warm standby with a scaled-down but functional environment in the DR Region that scales up on failover
Multi-site active-active across four Regions regardless of cost
Pilot light with no data replication configured
Backup and restore to a single Region
explain: Warm standby continuously replicates data and keeps core services running small, meeting tight RTO/RPO without full active-active cost. Backup/restore is too slow, pilot light without replication misses the RPO, and four-Region active-active over-delivers on cost.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A workload can tolerate RTO of 24 hours and RPO of 12 hours, and cost is the dominant concern. Which DR strategy fits best?
options: Multi-site active-active
Backup and restore, with backups copied to the DR Region
Pilot light with continuously running application servers at full size
Warm standby at full production capacity
explain: Loose RTO/RPO makes backup and restore the cheapest valid strategy. The other options keep costly capacity running for requirements that do not demand it.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: What does RPO define, and how does it drive DR design?
options: RPO is the number of backups retained per year
RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, and it determines replication frequency/continuity (for example, continuous replication versus periodic backups)
RPO is the percentage of uptime guaranteed in a contract
RPO is the time allowed to restore service after an outage
explain: RPO bounds acceptable data loss in time, so a small RPO forces continuous or frequent replication. Restoration time is RTO, uptime percentage is availability/SLA, and retention count is a backup policy detail.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A company wants continuous block-level replication of on-premises servers to AWS so it can fail over with an RPO of seconds and RTO of minutes, without maintaining a full second data center. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval restore jobs
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
AWS DataSync nightly tasks
AWS Backup
explain: Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates server storage to a staging area in AWS for low RPO/RTO failover. Backup is periodic, Glacier restores are slow, and nightly DataSync cannot deliver seconds-level RPO.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: After a DRS failover drill, the recovered instances launch with an outdated instance type because the launch template was never updated after a production change. Which practice prevents this drift?
options: Assume replication of data also replicates target launch configuration
Run drills less frequently so drift is noticed less often
Disable launch templates and configure instances manually during a disaster
Regularly review and update the Elastic Disaster Recovery post-launch actions and launch settings, and include template verification in DR drills
explain: DR launch configuration must be maintained and drill-verified as production evolves. Data replication does not carry target launch settings, and manual configuration during a disaster is slow and error-prone.
domain: Domain 4: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

q: A multi-Region application must fail DNS traffic over automatically when the primary Region's health checks fail, with clients seeing minimal stale DNS. Which Route 53 configuration is most appropriate?
options: A single A record with a 24-hour TTL pointing only at the primary Region
